articles.title: Russian Drill Simulates Incursion and ‘Security Zone’ in Tsentr-2026 Games
articles.body:
Russian armed forces practiced transitioning from defensive operations to a counter-offensive and carving out a “security zone” inside the territory of a neighboring state during the large-scale strategic military exercise Tsentr-2026, according to official Kremlin dispatches and Russian defense ministry briefings.
The maneuvers, conducted between Sept. 28 and Oct. 3, were formally designated to practice repelling conventional aggression on the Central Asian strategic vector and ensuring military security across the Caspian Sea basin.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
However, operational details presented to Russian President Vladimir Putin revealed that the drills incorporated cross-border offensive actions.
Reporting to Putin on the progress of the maneuvers, Russian Deputy Defense Minister Yunus-Bek Yevkurov stated that after repelling an adversary’s opening assault, coalition forces launched a large-scale counter-offensive.
Yevkurov detailed that starting Oct. 2, troops rehearsed operations to “liberate seized territory” and establish a “security zone on adjacent territory” belonging to the opposing state.
Putin traveled in person to the Chebarkul military training ground in the Chelyabinsk region on Friday, Oct. 2, to observe the concluding phase of the exercises, stating that Russian formations were directly integrating operational tactics and doctrine developed during the full-scale war in Ukraine.
Russia Plans Record $200B Defense Budget as Healthcare, Education, Face Cuts
Central Asian vector
While Russian defense officials did not formally name the hypothetical neighboring adversary, defense analysts at Ukrainian military portal Militarnyi noted that Kazakhstan most closely matches the operational geography of the scenario.
Kazakhstan shares an extensive land border with Russia’s Chelyabinsk region where the Chebarkul training facility is situated, represents a central political entity in Central Asia, and possesses an extensive coastline along the Caspian Sea.
Analysts emphasized that while the operational design closely mirrors regional geography, the identification of Kazakhstan remains an analytical assessment rather than an officially confirmed element of Moscow’s war games.
The strategic maneuvers involved significant firepower across multiple domains. Four Russian long-range strategic bombers conducted simulated strikes against designated “critical infrastructure” of the adversary, supported by tactical aviation, artillery units, strike drones, mechanized armored columns, and surface combatants of the Caspian Flotilla.
According to Russian defense ministry figures, the Tsentr-2026 exercise mobilized more than 47,000 military personnel, over 2,000 pieces of heavy weaponry and military hardware, 90 combat and transport aircraft, and 77 naval ships and support vessels.
Operations were executed across 11 designated military ranges and the maritime zone of the Caspian Sea. Moscow additionally hosted foreign military contingents from Belarus, China, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, Pakistan, and Tajikistan.
European pre-war legislation
The offensive maneuvers in Central Asia coincide with heightened defense vigilance across NATO’s eastern flank, where frontline European governments are preparing for prospective cross-border escalation.
In Poland, the Ministry of National Defense confirmed on Friday that it is drafting comprehensive legislation to introduce a formal “pre-war” phase of defense readiness, enabling early troop deployments and institutional mobilization before martial law is legally declared.
The draft statute is designed to bridge the regulatory gap between peacetime governance and wartime mobilization, linking national operational plans directly to NATO’s Response System.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has repeatedly warned that Europe has entered a “pre-war era,” cautioning that allied intelligence dispatches indicate Moscow is evaluating hybrid drone and missile strikes against nations supporting Kyiv, which the Kremlin could portray as accidents to test the resolve of NATO’s Article 5 collective defense guarantee.
The legislative drive also follows escalatory rhetoric from senior Russian officials directed at frontline European states. Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev threatened Lithuania in September with destruction if it rescinded restrictions on nuclear weapons, asserting NATO would not risk global war to defend Vilnius.
Days later, Kremlin security aide Nikolai Patrushev threatened that Moscow could deploy its “entire arsenal” against Poland, claiming Warsaw could be destroyed within days following Polish warnings that the alliance would decisively defeat any conventional Russian attack.

articles.title: Ukrainian Mirage 2000 Downs Russian Cruise Missile With Cannon
articles.body:
A Ukrainian Air Force Mirage 2000-5F multi-role fighter jet has intercepted and destroyed a Russian S8000 “Banderol” compact cruise missile using its onboard 30mm automatic cannon, marking the first confirmed gun kill of the munition type by the French-supplied aircraft.
The close-range interception was reported by French Aid to Europe, an open-source research initiative monitoring Western military assistance delivered to Kyiv, with defense portal Militarnyi independently detailing the engagement.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to military monitoring data, the Ukrainian fighter pilot bypassed conventional guided air-to-air missiles, relying instead on one of the aircraft’s two internal 30mm DEFA 554 automatic cannons.
Each cannon carries an onboard ammunition capacity of 125 rounds and can fire at a rate of up to 1,800 rounds per minute, giving the aircraft rapid close-in ballistic engagement capabilities against low-flying targets.
Downing an aerial target with automatic cannon fire demands close visual proximity and aggressive maneuvering compared to engaging targets at standoff ranges with guided missiles.
According to manufacturer specifications, the Russian Banderol maintains an operational cruising speed between 520 and 560 kilometers per hour, with maximum dash speeds reaching 620 to 650 kilometers per hour across an operational flight range of up to 500 kilometers.
Close-range gun engagement
Military analysts noted that neutralizing high-speed targets with gun rounds offers substantial cost efficiency by conserving scarce and expensive air-to-air munitions.
Russian Ballistic Missiles and Drones Hit Kyiv, Killing 1
At the end of September, France delivered a fresh consignment of MICA heat-seeking and radar-guided air-to-air missiles alongside specialized 30mm high-explosive incendiary rounds to maintain operational readiness across Ukraine’s Mirage fleet.
The S8000 Banderol, developed by Russian defense contractor Kronshtadt, is engineered as a low-cost, compact cruise missile tailored for saturation barrages against urban logistics, transportation hubs, and utility facilities.
The weapon is propelled by a Chinese-manufactured Swiwin micro-turbojet engine and carries a high-explosive fragmentation warhead weighing more than 114 kilograms, containing roughly 49.5 kilograms of high-grade explosive filler.
Its small radar cross-section, low-altitude flight profile, and turbine velocity have posed operational hurdles for mobile ground-based gun crews, requiring the Ukrainian Air Force to commit combat aircraft to patrol interception sectors.
Late-night information: the Mirage 2000-5F was the first western fighter aircraft to destroy a Russian S8000 Banderol cruise missile with the cannon. In 2025, France took 4️⃣ Mirage 2000-5F from its Air Force’s stocks and transferred them to Kyiv. pic.twitter.com/rtg8LMeocP
— French Aid to Europe 🇨🇵 🇪🇺 (@aidefranceukr) October 1, 2026
French fighter fleet
France delivered its initial batch of renovated Mirage 2000 fighters to Ukraine in early 2025, fulfilling commitments announced by French President Emmanuel Macron to reinforce Ukrainian airspace defenses following the earlier supply of American-built F-16 fighters.
Independent defense estimates place the Ukrainian Air Force’s operational Mirage fleet between 12 and 15 airframes.
The delta-wing French aircraft have been integrated into Ukraine’s layered territorial air defense network, tasked with intercepting cruise missiles and loitering munitions while retaining strike capacity to deploy Western standoff ordnance such as SCALP-EG cruise missiles.
In March 2025, a Ukrainian Mirage 2000 recorded its first confirmed operational victory by intercepting a Russian Kh-101 strategic cruise missile.
The fleet has sustained operational strains amid continuous air patrols. In July 2025, a Ukrainian pilot safely ejected from a Mirage 2000 after experiencing an in-flight equipment failure during a defensive sortie, resulting in the loss of the airframe without causing casualties on the ground.

articles.title: Ukraine Will Hit Russian Refineries in Response to Moscow's ‘New Doctrine’ of Airstrikes
articles.body:
Ukraine will double down on attacking Russian oil refineries in response to a new policy of airstrikes by Moscow designed to force people to abandon Kyiv and other cities, but will not target civilians, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Ukrainian intelligence has obtained documents showing that Russian leader Vladimir Putin had issued a “new doctrine” of military attacks on a much broader range of civilian targets ahead of winter, Zelensky said.
“We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure ... logistics ... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities,” Zelensky said. “This is the goal of the operation.”
Driving the shift in policy, Zelensky said, was Putin's desire to appear strong at a time when his military was losing ground in a key frontline region and sustaining higher levels of casualties.
The Kremlin was not available to comment on Saturday. But in a statement urging foreign nationals to leave Kyiv, the Russian Foreign Ministry said Moscow would continue to systematically hit targets in what it said were retaliatory strikes for Ukrainian attacks on Russia in recent months.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilians.
Counteroffensive in Donbas
Zelensky said an ongoing Ukrainian counteroffensive, code-named “Vivaldi,” had recaptured around 140 sq km (54 sq miles) of Ukraine's eastern Donbas region, which Russia has said it must control in its entirety as a condition for any peace deal.
In recent weeks, U.S. President Donald Trump's administration has sought to revive talks to end the four-year-old conflict — Europe's bloodiest since World War Two.
The U.S. leader last month urged Ukraine to refrain from hitting Russian oil installations, saying that was sending global diesel prices surging.
But Zelensky, speaking as air raid sirens blared outside the gilded halls of the presidential offices, said he had received no indications from Russia that Putin was interested in peace talks or discussing a ceasefire on energy infrastructure.
Over the past week, the Ukrainian capital has come under persistent attack by Russian drones and missiles targeting energy and telecoms assets, road and rail infrastructure. For the first time, Russia has targeted the bridges across the Dnipro River connecting east and west Kyiv.
Zelensky said Ukraine would respond to the change in tactics by Moscow, but would not respond in kind by targeting civilian infrastructure indiscriminately.
“We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners: what gives money to them for this war,” Zelensky said in English. “But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects.”
Support from Europe
After the Trump administration invited Putin to attend a G20 summit in Miami in December and discussed business deals with Russian envoys, Zelensky urged Washington not to normalise relations with Russia before ensuring a return to peace.
Zelensky said he would be happy to meet Putin for peace talks at the G20, but he warned the U.S. not to believe in “illusions” that Russia would end hostilities if it gained control of Donbas.
“It's not fair just to normalize,” said Zelensky, dressed in his trademark black T-shirt and military-style jacket. Any resumption of economic and diplomatic ties with the West had to be in return for peace, he said: “Because peace is more important than any kind of economy.”
While the U.S. has proposed resuming trilateral talks in the coming weeks in the UAE, Zelensky noted that an exact date and location for the technical-level conversations had not been set.
Ukrainian officials warn that Russia has stockpiled hundreds of ballistic missiles ahead of an expected winter onslaught against electricity and water infrastructure. Last winter, the worst of the war, Russian strikes left swathes of the country without electricity and heating for days at a time.
Since the summer, Moscow has also begun launching dozens of fast and relatively cheap jet-powered Shahed drones a day at Ukraine, whose air defenses have struggled as its previous generation of interceptor drones are too slow to catch them.
Zelensky said Ukraine had been forced to rely heavily on its fighter aircraft — F-16s and MiGs — to down around 60% of the Russian jet-powered drones, but supplies of 20 mm ammunition for the planes were running low.
Kyiv was urgently working on other solutions — including boosting its jamming capabilities, he said. In the second half of October, it should receive its first shipment of small, cheap air defense missiles capable of hitting the new Shaheds.
Last week, Zelensky said Ukraine was developing five models of new interceptor drones capable of downing the jet Shaheds. Fresh from a meeting with his defense chiefs, he said tests on two of those models showed a modest success rate of around 30%.
“We'll have to scale it,” he said. “I hope that with all these things, with all these elements, we'll find a way.”
Ballistic threat
Ukraine announced the first combat use this week of its own domestically made ballistic missile — the FP-7, which has a range of around 250 km (155 miles).
Zelensky said he had called the manufacturer Fire Point to pressure executives to quickly finish a longer-range model, the FP-9, which the company has said could hit Moscow.
“I said to them, ‘Where is my FP-9?’” said Zelensky, with a grin. “We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be (ready) this autumn, I'm sure.”
Zelensky said a recent spate of Russian drone incursions and hybrid attacks in Europe were an effort to intimidate European populations and to divide support for Ukraine.
Some European leaders were starting to understand this, he said, and toughen their position.
Russia says such accusations are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria.
After talks with European officials in Brussels this week, Ukraine found funding to proceed with orders for drones that it needs to keep fighting at the start of 2027, Zelensky said.
Ukrainian officials had worked on a plan with European partners to plug a $27 billion hole in Kyiv's defense budget this year.
The plans involve a combination of the reallocation of Ukraine's own budget resources, bilateral assistance, and using “money credits” from next year's portion of a €90 billion EU loan, Zelensky said.

articles.title: Valtersson exposes NATO military exhaustion, Russian air superiority, US strategic defeat  in Iran
articles.body:
Valtersson exposes NATO military exhaustion, Russian air superiority, US strategic defeat in Iran
TEHRAN — In the latest joint X Space broadcast co-hosted by the Tehran Times and Sputnik, military analyst Mikael Valtersson—a former officer of the Swedish Armed Forces specializing in air defense, former defense politician, and chief of staff with the Sweden Democrats—provided an incisive assessment of shifting global strategic realities.
Valtersson detailed Russia's undeniable air superiority in Ukraine, the severe depletion of European military stockpiles, and the profound economic and strategic defeat suffered by the United States in its military confrontation with Iran. Highlighting the collapse of Western security narratives, Valtersson underscored how Washington's reckless interventions have eroded American soft power, exposed NATO's structural vulnerabilities, and accelerated the long-term contraction of the U.S. military footprint across the Middle East.
Sputnik Question: Following the quiet abandonment of Ukraine's publicized 40-day drone campaign, how have the air war dynamics shifted between Russia and Ukraine—particularly given reports that Russian reconnaissance and jet-powered drones are flying virtually unopposed over Kyiv to film strike impacts in high quality, while sustained strikes target Odesa's port infrastructure?
The Ukrainian 40-day drone campaign was a classic PR stunt designed for Western public consumption. Once it failed to paralyze Russia's economy or force political concessions, Kyiv simply ceased mentioning it altogether. Western media coverage remains egregiously biased, seizing on isolated incidents to accuse Russia of targeting civilians while ignoring major Russian operational successes. In reality, civilian casualty rates in Ukraine remain remarkably low compared to military losses—a standard of restraint that should be commended in modern warfare.
Russian air superiority across the theater is absolute and manifest. Ukraine possesses a critical deficit of high-end air defense assets, such as Patriot missile batteries, which are rationed sparingly to protect select high-value sites in Kyiv. Furthermore, Ukraine lacks the medium-level air defense systems necessary to counter Russia's newer jet-powered drones, leading to at least a tripling of successful drone penetrations. The sight of Russian reconnaissance drones loitering over Kyiv to capture high-resolution strike footage highlights this total air defense breakdown.
Beyond the capital, key maritime hubs like Odesa demonstrate the extent of Ukrainian vulnerability. Russia's daily, sustained strike campaign against Ukrainian shipping and harbor infrastructure in Odesa has proceeded virtually unopposed for three months, devastating Ukraine's grain export capacity and striking a fatal blow to its national economy.
Tehran Times Question: U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly claimed that the war in Iran could be concluded within two weeks. Given Iran's capture of a second U.S. unmanned submarine in the Strait of Hormuz and the heavy expenditure of U.S. air defense interceptors during Iranian strikes on Jordan's Muwaffaq Salti air base, what is the reality of Washington's military posture and strategic standing?
The claim that the war with Iran will end in two weeks is completely detached from military reality. Such a timeframe would require the United States to offer Iran an extraordinarily favorable deal, as Tehran holds the superior strategic position and will not accept a bad peace arrangement.
Trump faces mounting domestic political pressure over soaring fuel prices and impending midterm election losses, leaving Washington with minimal leverage. Trump's bombastic statements—claiming Iran is "totally destroyed" and declaring the "greatest victory in world history"—indicate that he is either becoming demented or simply lying, as his assertions directly contradict operational facts on the ground.
Tactically and technologically, a strategic deadlock has set in that favors Tehran. Iran's capture of a second U.S. unmanned submarine in the Strait of Hormuz represents a major intelligence harvest, providing Iranian engineers direct access to advanced American technology. Operationally, the limits of American air defense were laid bare during the Iranian attack on Jordan's Muwaffaq Salti air base. U.S. forces expended an immense volume of interceptors—firing approximately 70 Patriot missiles and over 12 THAAD interceptors—yet Iranian missiles still penetrated the defense grid, destroying or damaging around 10 aircraft. Washington cannot sustain this rate of interceptor expenditure without compromising its global force posture. Ultimately, this war represents a catastrophic strategic defeat for U.S. influence, missile reserves, and global soft power, while significantly elevating the strategic standing of both Iran and China.
Sputnik Question: What realistic military options remain for European nations seeking to sustain Ukraine, given the severe exhaustion of Western weapon stockpiles, unsustainable Ukrainian casualty figures, a dark winter outlook, and rising political volatility within Europe?
European nations have virtually no viable military options left to alter the war's trajectory. European defense inventories are thoroughly drained, and because the United States must prioritize replenishing its own critically depleted stockpiles, Europe cannot expect American rearmament assistance for years. At best, European aid can temporarily delay a complete Ukrainian military collapse, but it cannot support effective offensive operations.
The human toll on Ukraine is mathematically unsustainable. Citing data acknowledged by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk from Ukrainian military sources, Ukraine is losing roughly 28,000 soldiers per month to deaths and severe injuries—totaling approximately 325,000 casualties per year. In the territory currently controlled by Kyiv, the population is probably below 20 million, with two million men actively dodging military service. Ukraine is exhausting its human reserves far faster than it can draft replacement personnel, pointing toward a dark and difficult winter as Russian forces methodically strike critical logistics and energy infrastructure. While reckless political rhetoric from European elites carries risks of unintended escalation reminiscent of 1914, shifting domestic political dynamics—such as the growth of AfD and BSW in Germany and the National Rally in France—will likely force a significant reduction in European military backing for Kyiv in the years ahead.
Tehran Times Question: How are Washington's claims of maintaining complete control over the Strait of Hormuz received by the European public, and how is energy inflation shaping European attitudes toward U.S. foreign policy?
Mikael Valtersson Answer: Official assertions by the U.S. administration that it controls the Strait of Hormuz and that commercial shipping has returned to normal are treated as a complete joke by the European public. If an election for U.S. president were held in Europe today, Donald Trump would receive perhaps 5 to 10 percent of the vote, reflecting deep public cynicism toward official Washington narratives. Unlike the heavily slanted coverage of Ukraine, European media reporting on the Middle East has been noticeably more neutral, allowing citizens to see through American propaganda.
Furthermore, Western public perception of Iran has shifted noticeably. Prior to the war, European discourse focused almost exclusively on human rights allegations; today, public debate centers on Iranian resilience and the realization that Washington's military aggression was a grave error. The public increasingly views the conflict as a blunder driven not by American or European security interests, but by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's desperate attempt to avoid domestic prosecution and prison. Economically, European citizens are suffering under severe energy inflation. Having cut off cheap Russian energy due to sanctions, Europe exposed itself to global market shocks resulting from Middle Eastern volatility. While European governments temporarily buffered price spikes through domestic tax cuts on fuel, long-term economic damage remains inevitable, fueling public resentment against both Washington and European political elites.
Sputnik Question: How valid are Western accusations regarding Russian hybrid threats, and under international law, what legal rights does Russia possess to target European supply lines directly sustaining Ukraine's war effort?
Accusations regarding hybrid warfare merely highlight Europe's profound internal security vulnerabilities. European governments lack the security infrastructure and manpower needed to guard their vast industrial and economic assets, leaving localized vulnerabilities exposed to disruption.
 
Under established international law, European states have long since crossed the threshold into active co-belligerency. European governments do not merely offer passive sympathy; they provide direct budgetary support, heavy combat systems, operational training, intelligence, and equipment repair services. European direct budget support is the absolute operational backbone of the Ukrainian state; if Western economic budget support were withdrawn, the Ukrainian economy would collapse within three to six months, completely destroying its capability to maintain a defense. Drawing a historical parallel to U.S. material support for the British Empire prior to World War II and Germany's subsequent declaration of war, Russia possesses full legal justification under international law to target European logistical vectors and military infrastructure sustaining the enemy war effort.
Tehran Times Question: What does the permanent withdrawal of U.S. military forces from Iraq signal regarding the durability and strategic utility of American military bases across the Middle East?
The permanent withdrawal of U.S. forces from Iraq signals a structural decline in the American regional presence. Far from acting as strategic assets or instruments of deterrence, U.S. facilities across the Middle East have transformed into acute strategic liabilities and prime targets for regional defense forces.
For regional host nations, housing American facilities has backfired spectacularly. Rather than securing U.S. protection, regional host states have found their local infrastructure exposed to collateral damage and military strikes during broader regional escalations. Crucially, regional leaders feel deep resentment toward Washington's unilateral behavior; Gulf state politicians have openly complained that they were not even consulted or informed prior to U.S. strikes, learning through media reports that American forces had launched attacks from or near their sovereign territory without their knowledge. As regional allies realize that hosting American bases yields zero security benefits while incurring enormous security costs, they will increasingly demand the removal of U.S. troops, permanently diminishing Washington's military footprint in the region.

articles.title: Ukraine fired its first FP-7 ballistic missile in combat. Its maker says next version will do what Ukraine needed since 2022
articles.body:
- Ukrainian forces have fired a Fire Point FP-7 ballistic missile in combat for the first time
- The launch heralds a new phase of the wider war: the ballistic phase
- Soon both Ukraine and Russia will be able to bombard each other with hard-to-intercept missiles
Ukraine has fired its new Fire Point FP-7 ballistic missile in anger for the first time, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Thursday, 1 October.
Kyiv hasn't said what the missile targeted or how much damage it caused. The Wall Street Journal, citing an unnamed source, reported that it struck a target in Russian-occupied Ukraine. Zelensky was ecstatic on social media. "Thank you for the result," the Ukrainian president wrote. "Next up: production. Glory to Ukraine!"
The FP-7 can hit back at Russia, but it can't stop the Iskander ballistic missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities. Its twin is meant to. Fire Point is building an interceptor version, the FP-7.X, as the core of Freyja, its bid for a cheaper alternative to the American Patriot, and the company aims for a first ballistic missile interception by mid-2027.
Kyiv drone- and missile-maker Fire Point, most famous for its FP-1 and FP-2 one-way attack drones and FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, has been hard at work on ballistic missiles for at least a year. Ballistic missiles can cost millions of dollars per round, making them much more expensive than a $50,000 drone or $500,000 cruise missile.
But the extra expense buys a lot more destructive potential. An FP-1 packs a 60-kg warhead; an FP-7's warhead weighs about 200 kg. While an FP-1 might motor as far as 1,000 km, it's slow and fairly easy to shoot down. An FP-7 possesses less range—up to 250 km under the best conditions—but it streaks through the atmosphere at several times the speed of sound, making it extremely difficult to intercept.
The only Russian air defense systems that stand any chance of swatting down an incoming FP-7 are also among the most in-demand in the Russian inventory and thus the most over-stretched: the S-400 surface-to-air missile batteries.
Ukrainians know better than anyone the kind of damage and terror ballistic bombardment can inflict. Since effectively running out of Patriot surface-to-air missiles earlier this year, Ukraine has been unable to defend itself against weekly Russian bombardment that now usually includes several Iskander ballistic missiles.
The Russian bombardment threatens to disrupt commerce, throttle electricity generation, and grind down Ukrainian morale at a critical juncture in Russia's wider war on Ukraine. Ukrainian troops are holding their own along the 1,200-km front line, but behind the front line everyday Ukrainians are suffering under missile and drone impacts.
That suffering will only get worse as winter closes in, temperatures drop, and the Russians resume intensive attacks on the electrical grid, potentially depriving millions of people of household heating. Ukrainian batteries firing FP-7s can't directly prevent Russian attacks. But they can retaliate for the attacks.
Expect the ballistic tit for tat to intensify. It may not be the first Ukrainian ballistic missile fired in anger: in June, Russia said it shot down a Ukrainian ballistic missile over Moscow, and Kyiv never said what it was. But the FP-7 is the first Kyiv has confirmed using in combat, and it has the range and payload to inflict serious damage on targets inside Russia. But an even more powerful Ukrainian missile, the Fire Point FP-9, is coming soon. It reportedly ranges 850 km with an 800-kg warhead.
Trending Now
The ballistic phase
The FP-7 can smash Russian depots, air bases, and factories in oblasts bordering Ukraine. The FP-9 could wreak havoc as far as Moscow. The only major constraint on the Ukrainian bombardment will be Fire Point's production capacity, and Kyiv's ability to finance that production.
The Ukrainians will be incentivized to produce as many FP-7s—and, later, FP-9s—as possible. The same factories that produce surface-to-surface FP-7s will also churn out a surface-to-air variant, the FP-7.X.
That missile, which is overall similar to the standard FP-7 but includes a sophisticated seeker head, is the main munition for Ukraine's new mostly homemade air defense system being developed by Fire Point and various foreign partners under the auspices of the European missile defense program Freyja.
Ukraine has five ways to stop Russia’s Iskanders. Only one arrives before the strikes on the grid begin
If the FP-7.X works as advertised and Fire Point can scale production, it could bolster Ukraine's defenses against Russian ballistic missile strikes while the standard FP-7 and its bigger cousin the FP-9 retaliate for Russian ballistic missile strikes.
A new phase of the wider war is about to begin—the ballistic phase, where both sides can pummel the other with hard-to-intercept missiles.
The side that makes the most and best missiles, for offense and defense, will prevail in the coming ballistic fight.

articles.title: US-led initiative tightens efforts to block weapons from reaching Iran, stop nuclear proliferation
articles.body:
The United States and countries participating in the Proliferation Security Initiative (PSI) pledged on Friday to step up efforts to prevent the transfer of weapons, materials, equipment, and technologies to and from Iran that could support the development of weapons of mass destruction and delivery systems, including unmanned aerial vehicles.
The countries issued a joint statement marking one year since the reinstatement of six UN Security Council resolutions imposing restrictions on Iran under the snapback mechanism.
Among the measures announced were closer intelligence-sharing between participating countries, streamlined procedures for transferring information, and interdiction and prevention measures targeting Iranian proliferation activity.
The statement also expressed support for the US sanctions campaign Operation Economic Outcast and called on all UN member states to implement the reinstated resolutions.
“We call on Iran to return to fulfilling its nonproliferation commitments and to cooperate fully with the International Atomic Energy Agency,” the statement said.
Trump: ‘Very soon, you’re going to see things happening’
The declaration of increased cooperation followed remarks by US President Donald Trump this past week that “things will happen in Iran very soon,” as he said Tehran’s military and economic capabilities had been severely damaged during six months of war.
“Very soon, you’re going to see things happening,” Trump said, later declaring that the United States would “win this war very quickly, one way or another.”
“In Iran, we’ve been there for six months, with 18 dead. By the way, even one is too many, but they lost 4,500,” Trump said. “We lost 18, and very soon you’re going to see things happening, very soon.
Trump claims near-total control of Strait of Hormuz
“But you have a country there that’s been almost completely destroyed. Their economy is in bad shape. They have inflation of more than 300%.”
Trump later addressed developments in the Strait of Hormuz, saying Washington had achieved near-total control of the area.
“Over the last week in the Strait of Hormuz, where we have almost total control, I would say total control, but every once in a while they put a mine there and disrupt things a little,” he said. “But we have, in effect, almost total control of the Strait of Hormuz.”
Trump also said the volume of oil passing through the strait over the previous three days had reached unprecedented levels.
“And in fact, over the last three days, more oil has come out of the Strait of Hormuz than at any other point in history,” he said. “I’m not just talking about the period since the war. I’m saying at any point in history. There was pent-up demand that had accumulated.”
Axios reported that Trump attended a secret meeting on Iran and Yemen chaired by US Vice President JD Vance and attended by top administration national security aides at Camp David on Friday.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, White House envoy Steve Witkoff, CIA director John Ratcliffe, and Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine all attended the meeting, according to the report.
The report cited three US officials, who told Axios that “things were decided, or at least deeply discussed.”
The White House refused to respond to an Axios request for comment.
The high-level, closed-door meeting comes amid reports that both the US military and Saudi Arabia are preparing to step up military activity in the region.
The US military is considering a major expansion of its naval presence in the Middle East in the coming weeks, including the deployment of three aircraft carriers and accompanying warships to provide greater operational flexibility, The Washington Post reported Friday.
The report said the buildup could also include an additional 20,000 troops, on top of the roughly 50,000 already deployed in the region, as well as up to 150 fighter jets and additional destroyers to defend against missile attacks.
Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, is considering a significant military offensive against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen aimed at breaking the group’s hold on key coastal areas and securing Red Sea shipping routes, Reuters reported Friday.
The planned operation is intended to reverse gains made by the Houthis last month, when they advanced along the coast and seized control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, according to people familiar with the plans, including Gulf and Yemeni officials and Western diplomats.
The operation, which could be launched in the coming weeks, would be led on the ground by Yemeni forces overseen by Riyadh and supported by Saudi airstrikes, according to six people familiar with the preparations.
Reuters and Ariella Roitman contributed to this report.

articles.title: Ukraine will hit Russian refineries in response to Moscow’s ‘new doctrine’ of airstrikes
articles.body:
Ukraine will hit Russian refineries in response to Moscow’s ‘new doctrine’ of airstrikes
- Ukraine will intensify attacks on Russian oil refineries in response to Moscow’s new doctrine targeting civilian infrastructure to force evacuations, but will avoid hitting civilian objects.
- Ukrainian forces have recaptured around 140 sq km in Donbas amid ongoing counteroffensive, while facing persistent Russian drone and missile strikes on Kyiv’s energy and infrastructure.
- Ukraine develops new defence systems against Russian drones, announces first use of domestic ballistic missile FP-7, and secures funding with European partners to sustain defence through 2027.
AI generated
KYIV - Ukraine will double down on attacking Russian oil refineries in response to a new policy of airstrikes by Moscow designed to force people to abandon Kyiv and other cities, but will not target civilians, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Ukrainian intelligence has obtained documents showing that Russian leader Vladimir Putin had issued a “new doctrine” of military attacks on a much broader range of civilian targets ahead of this winter, Zelensky said.
“We saw documents and we know that they allow them attack infrastructure... logistics... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities,” Zelensky said. “This is the goal of the operation.”
Driving the shift in policy, Zelensky said, was Putin’s desire to appear strong at a time when his military was losing ground in a key front-line region and sustaining higher levels of casualties.
The Kremlin was not available to comment on Oct 3. But in a statement urging foreign nationals to leave Kyiv, the Russian Foreign Ministry said Moscow would continue to systematically hit targets in what it said were retaliatory strikes for Ukrainian attacks on Russia in recent months.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilians.
Counteroffensive in Donbas
Zelensky said an ongoing Ukrainian counteroffensive, code-named “Vivaldi”, had recaptured around 140 sq km of Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, which Russia has said it must control in its entirety as a condition for any peace deal.
In recent weeks, US President Donald Trump’s administration has sought to revive talks to end the four-year-old conflict – Europe’s bloodiest since World War II.
The US leader in September urged Ukraine to refrain from hitting Russian oil installations, saying that was sending global diesel prices surging.
But Zelensky, speaking as air raid sirens blared outside the gilded halls of the presidential offices, said he had received no indications from Russia that Putin was interested in peace talks, or discussing a ceasefire on energy infrastructure.
Over the past week, the Ukrainian capital has come under persistent attack by Russian drones and missiles targeting energy and telecoms assets, road and rail infrastructure.
For the first time, Russia has targeted the bridges across the Dnipro river connecting east and west Kyiv.
Zelensky said Ukraine would respond to the change in tactics by Moscow, but would not respond in kind by targeting civilian infrastructure indiscriminately.
“We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners: what gives money to them for this war,” Zelensky said in English. “But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects.”
Support from Europe
After the Trump administration invited Putin to attend a Group of 20 summit in Miami in December and discussed business deals with Russian envoys, Zelensky urged Washington not to normalise relations with Russia before ensuring a return to peace.
Zelensky said he would be happy to meet Putin for peace talks at the G-20, but he warned the US not to believe in “illusions” that Russia would end hostilities if it gained control of Donbas.
“It’s not fair just to normalise,” said Zelensky, dressed in his trademark black T-shirt and military-style jacket. Any resumption of economic and diplomatic ties with the West had to be in return for peace, he said: “Because peace is more important than any kind of economy.”
While the US has proposed a resumption of trilateral talks in the coming weeks in the UAE, Zelensky noted that an exact date and location for the technical-level conversations had not been set.
Ukrainian officials warn that Russia has stockpiled hundreds of ballistic missiles ahead of an expected winter onslaught against electricity and water infrastructure.
Last winter, the worst of the war, Russian strikes left swathes of the country without electricity and heating for days at a time.
Since the summer, Moscow has also begun launching dozens of fast and relatively cheap jet-powered Shahed drones a day at Ukraine, whose air defences have struggled as its previous generation of interceptor drones were too slow to catch them.
Zelensky said Ukraine had been forced to rely heavily on its fighter aircraft – F-16s and MiGs – to down around 60% of the Russian jet-powered drones, but supplies of 20mm ammunition for the planes were running low.
Kyiv was urgently working on other solutions – including boosting its jamming capabilities, he said. In the second half of October, it would receive the first shipment of small, cheap air defence missiles capable of hitting the new Shaheds.
Last week, Zelensky said Ukraine was developing five models of new interceptor drones capable of downing the jet Shaheds. Fresh from a meeting with his defence chiefs, he said tests on two of those models showed a modest success rate of around 30%.
“We’ll have to scale it,” he said. “I hope that with all these things, with all these elements, we’ll find a way.”
Ballistic threat
Ukraine announced the first combat use this week of its own domestically made ballistic missile – the FP-7, which has a range of around 250km.
Zelensky said he had called the manufacturer Fire Point to pressure executives to finish quickly a longer-range model, the FP-9, which the company has said could hit Moscow.
“I said to them, where is my FP-9?” said Zelensky, with a grin. “We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be (ready) this autumn, I’m sure.”
Zelensky said a recent spate of Russian drone incursions and hybrid attacks in Europe were an effort to intimidate European populations and to divide support for Ukraine.
Some European leaders were starting to understand this, he said, and toughen their position.
Russia says such accusations are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria.
After talks with European officials in Brussels this week, Ukraine had found funding to proceed with orders for drones that it needs to keep fighting at the start of 2027, Zelensky said.
Ukrainian officials had worked on a plan with European partners to plug a US$27 billion (S$34 billion) hole in Kyiv’s defence budget this year.
The plans involve a combination of the reallocation of Ukraine’s own budget resources, bilateral assistance and using “money credits” from 2027’s portion of a €90 billion (S$130 billion) EU loan, Zelensky said. REUTERS

articles.title: Russia Threatens to Strike Defense Plants in NATO Countries
articles.body:
What is fundamentally new about Zakharova’s statement?
Previously, similar statements from Russia mostly concerned targets inside Ukraine or transport convoys within Ukraine. Now, for the first time, Russia is officially and directly threatening defense plants on the territory of NATO and EU countries, which represents a step toward further escalation.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
At the official diplomatic level of the Foreign Ministry, the Kremlin is effectively legitimizing potential Russian strikes against targets in sovereign NATO nations.
In response, EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius stated that if Russia strikes factories on European territory, it would fall under NATO’s Article 5 on collective defense and trigger a military response.
An aide to Kubilius clarified that this refers specifically to a direct Russian strike, rather than the acts of sabotage that have recently increased at EU arms plants.
At present, NATO does not have a clear position on the conditions for invoking Article 5, which undoubtedly encourages Russia to continue escalating and testing the limits.
The implications
It seems that after Zakharova’s statement that European factories producing weapons for Ukraine are potential military targets for Russia, the question of such a strike should no longer be “will it happen?” but rather “when will it happen?”
The trigger for this statement was Poland’s readiness to locate production of Patriot interceptor missiles for Ukraine. Moscow has thus already publicly formulated the argument it could use to justify such a strike.
Switzerland Allocates $162M for 8 Ukraine Recovery Projects
Before Feb. 24, 2022, many analysts were wrong because they tried to determine whether Putin had already made a final decision to go to war. It was more reliable to look at other things: whether the Kremlin had the capabilities, preparations, political justification, and willingness to take risks. The same logic should be applied now.
Russia already has significant strike-drone capabilities, is expanding sabotage operations and drone activity in Europe, is testing NATO’s response, and is now openly identifying European arms factories as potential targets. The threshold for a strike may therefore be lower than it appears.
A particularly important signal would be a shift in Kremlin rhetoric from “we have the right to strike” to “we warned you”: statements that specific countries or factories “will bear responsibility for the consequences” would indicate further preparation for action.
Russia would most likely launch such a strike if it became convinced that NATO’s response would be limited to sanctions, stronger air defenses, additional military assistance to Ukraine, diplomatic measures, or other steps that stopped short of a direct strike on Russian territory.
The risk would increase if Moscow concluded that previous acts of sabotage, cyberattacks, drone incidents, and other operations in Europe had not produced unacceptable consequences for Russia.
For the Kremlin, such episodes have not only operational but also intelligence value: they reveal the speed of the allies’ response, the level of unity, and the practical limits of that response. If the Russian leadership sees that even after Russia’s involvement has been confirmed, the response remains limited, this could reduce the perceived risk of taking the next step.
Such a decision would become more likely if the Kremlin could carry out an attack in a way that made rapid and unequivocal attribution difficult. For Moscow, a scenario in which responsibility could be denied or remain subject to political debate – at least in the initial stage – would be significantly safer.
The first step, therefore, might not be a demonstrative launch of Geran drones from Russian territory but the use of other types of UAVs, sabotage groups, maritime platforms, intermediaries, or other tools that leave room for uncertainty.
Another condition would be political fragmentation within NATO. The Kremlin would likely count on disputes over whether a particular incident constituted an armed attack, whether Article 4 or Article 5 should be invoked, what the response should look like, and whether it is worth risking a broader conflict over a single damaged facility. If Moscow expected a slow or ambiguous decision-making process, this could create a window of opportunity for a limited attack.
Another key factor would be its assessment of the US position. For the Kremlin, what matters is not only America’s formal commitment to NATO but also Washington’s willingness to support a rapid and forceful response to a single limited strike.
Any signs that the US is politically focused on other issues, that Washington and its European allies disagree, or that it is reluctant to broaden the conflict could be perceived by Moscow as favorable conditions for testing the limits of what it can get away with.
As with the war against Ukraine, we are unlikely to see a specific order to launch such a strike. That is why indirect indicators, including rhetoric used to justify it, should be taken seriously. Zakharova’s statement means that a public justification for a possible strike on military-industrial facilities outside Ukraine has likely already been formulated.

articles.title: Russia shows Pantsir air defense on Belarus-built chassis
articles.body:
- Russia showed a Pantsir-S1M air defense system on a Belarusian MZKT-7930-312 chassis during its Tsentr-2026 exercise.
- Belarus reportedly received a 2024 order for 18 such chassis, and Ukraine destroyed one MZKT-based Pantsir near Mariupol in February.
Russia has shown an upgraded Pantsir-S1M air defense system mounted on a Belarus-built MZKT-7930-312 chassis during its Tsentr-2026 strategic exercise, the first official confirmation that the gun-and-missile system now rides on the heavy Minsk-built chassis.
Until now, the configuration was known only from a leaked supply contract and from a single vehicle that Ukrainian drone operators destroyed near Mariupol in February. Russian officials did not say how many Pantsirs have been built on the new chassis, which units operate them, or whether the switch will extend across the fleet.
Tsentr-2026 ran from Sept. 28 to Oct. 3, with its main stage held on Oct. 2 at the Chebarkul training range in Russia’s Chelyabinsk region. President Vladimir Putin watched part of the drills on Oct. 1. Russia’s Defense Ministry said more than 47,000 troops and over 2,000 pieces of equipment took part. Rostec’s “Russian Weapons” project told Rossiyskaya Gazeta that Pantsir systems were demonstrated during the exercise.
The Pantsir combines short-range surface-to-air missiles with twin 30 mm cannons and its own radar. Russia uses it as the inner layer of its air defense, protecting long-range S-300 and S-400 batteries, airfields and other key sites from aircraft, cruise missiles and drones. The standard version sits on an 8×8 KamAZ-6560 truck, with export versions on the German MAN SX45 and some units on Russia’s BAZ-6309.
The MZKT-7930 is a heavy 8×8 military platform built by the Minsk Wheeled Tractor Plant in Belarus. Russia already uses it for some of its most important systems, including the Iskander ballistic missile launcher, the Bastion coastal defense system and elements of the S-400. A Pantsir on the MZKT-7930 first appeared only as a display mock-up at the MAKS air show near Moscow in 2009.
In early 2024, the Belarusian plant received an order from Russia for 18 MZKT-7930-312 chassis to carry Pantsir systems, according to an investigation reported in April by Ukrainian outlet Obozrevatel. That summer, Pantsir maker KBP, based in Tula, reported successful tests of the chassis. The documents showed the trucks would carry the 72V6 combat module used by Russia’s own armed forces, and the investigation said some vehicles may have been finished as an MZKT-7930-415 version with an armored cab and a different windshield layout.
The first visual evidence of the pairing came from the battlefield. In late February, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces struck a Pantsir-S1 mounted on an MZKT-7930 near the former Azovstal steel plant in Mariupol, The Defence Blog reported. The vehicle carried add-on screens meant to protect it from drone strikes.
Ukraine has made Pantsirs a priority target. Open-source tracking group Oryx had recorded at least 52 Russian Pantsir systems destroyed or damaged, and Ukrainian officials have claimed that about half of Russia’s deployed Pantsirs have been knocked out, a figure that has not been independently verified.

articles.title: SOS - Ukraine’s Looming Dark Winter Demands Decisive Action
articles.body:
Russia’s winter playbook is running again, and its logic is evident. Missile and drone attacks have spread from regional power centers to the core of Kyiv’s infrastructure – high-voltage substations and main bridges over the Dnipro River.
Moscow is not trying to hide what it’s doing. The aim is to paralyze the capital, make life there impossible, and choke the supply lines for troops and equipment to the east.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Western sympathy won’t intercept the missiles over the Dnipro, and it certainly won’t turn on heat in a hospital when the power goes out. If Ukraine’s partners really want to help the country survive this winter, then they need to stop offering sympathy and concern and start changing policy.
That starts in Washington. For months, the US administration has operated in a strange operational double standard: Ukraine will defend itself against incoming missiles, but it shouldn’t attack the airfields and bases inside Russia from where those attacks are being launched, nor the energy-generating sites that sustain the Kremlim’s war effort.
For air defense crews to hunt cruise missiles seconds before they collide – rather than blowing up bombers on the tarmac or storming missile depots in Kursk and Belgorod – is a losing strategy. The US must drop all target restrictions on ATACMS soon.
At the same time, Washington should stop tying military aid to slow domestic procurement schedules and instead fund Ukrainian defense factories directly. Kyiv is developing long-range drone missiles and tactical ballistic systems that are cheaper, faster to deploy, and free from foreign political restrictions. Europe, meanwhile, must take greater responsibility for security in its own neighborhood rather than waiting to see what the US Congress does next.
Ukraine Strikes Russian Drone Site, Crossing, Belgorod Hubs
The first fix is air defense. Firing two-million-dollar interceptors at fifty-thousand-dollar Shahed drones is a quick way to run out of ammunition. European partners that own Patriot, NASAMS, and IRIS-T systems need to hand batteries over directly to help cover cities and transit points like the bridges of Kyiv.
To counter daily drone swarms, European funding should go toward building Ukraine’s mobile fire teams. That’s the only way to clear the lower skies without burning through high-end missile stocks amid ballistic threats. Small teams with thermal scopes, pickup trucks, searchlights, and jammers are the only way to get out of there.
The second solution is the grid. Trying to fix up massive, centralized power plants when bombs are still falling is a waste of time and money. European aid needs to stop making those long-term post-attack repairs and focus on physical armor and decentralization.
Electrical transformers, the hardest components to replace, should be housed in reinforced concrete shelters that can take direct shrapnel hits. Aid should target mobile gas turbines, industrial generators, and battery storage units in the cities on the generation side. If a city can run its water pumps and district heating on local micro-grids and the main power plant is destroyed, it loses most of the terror value.
Europe must stop holding back money. Around $200 billion in frozen Russian central bank assets is in European accounts, most of it at Euroclear in Belgium. For years, lawyers have been debating whether to touch this money while Ukrainian cities get flattened. European leaders need to take these assets and not just skim the annual interest but use them directly for Ukrainian weapons buying and grid repairs.
Making the aggressor pay for the damage isn’t just a nice idea; it’s basic common sense. None of these choices require complex diplomacy or grand ideological speeches. They are practical decisions: let Ukrainians hit back at the sites bombing them, give them the hardware they need to keep the power on, and use Russian money to pay for it.
And finally, President Trump should not be allowed to evade implementing the important sanctions law targeting Russia and its partners that Congress finally passed recently, and he signed. Ignoring it is an insult to US democracy and an unfriendly act against Ukraine at a critical moment.
Ukraine has proven for four and a half years that it can hold the line. It is long past time for its partners, even though they have already given critical but inconsistent support, to show the same backbone.

Russia struck a key bridge in Kyiv connecting the left and right bank of the Dnipro river overnight Saturday, as Moscow steps up its aerial campaign against Ukraine.
Traffic was suspended on the capital’s Northern Bridge and emergency services were deployed to the scene amid damage to the road and trolleybus cables on the crossing, Kyiv major Vitaly Klitschko said on Saturday. Around 500,000 people commute from the Dnipro’s left bank to the river’s right bank daily, with eight bridges connecting the two sides in total.
That follows several similar attacks by drones on the Southern Bridge in Kyiv in recent days, forcing the temporary suspension of vehicle movement and huge traffic jams.

Separately, the UN-linked International Atomic Energy Agency said four strikes in recent days had threatened safety and security” at the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, including reportedly disabling an off-site radiation monitoring station.
Moscow has stepped up its bombing campaign in recent weeks against Ukraine’s civil and critical infrastructure, targeting residential areas, energy facilities, sea terminals and data centers, setting the stage for a dire winter for Kyiv. In the past week alone, Russia has launched more than 190 missiles and drones, mostly targeting energy infrastructure.
The Russian foreign affairs ministry issued a statement on Saturday warning “foreign nationals and diplomatic personnel against remaining in” Kyiv.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has ordered his troops to abandon the rules of war, Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the FT this week.

articles.title: The winter war: Ukraine is prepping for another season of Russian attacks before the cold sets in
articles.body:
On Sept. 23, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov once again voiced Moscow’s rejection of a Ukrainian proposal to halt fighting along the current front line. Now Kyiv is preparing for another series of strikes on its critical infrastructure that appear intended to freeze the country during the upcoming winter and result in a humanitarian disaster. Ukraine’s military and civilian institutions have already begun preparing for what they expect to be an especially difficult Russian campaign, with energy companies inspecting equipment and stockpiling fuel while apartment associations buy up generators.
In September, air raid alerts have sounded in Kyiv every day — and almost continuously. Jet-powered Shahed drones circle over the city, disrupting the work of municipal services, shops, businesses, and public institutions. A new operating protocol took effect on Sept. 10, introducing a “yellow” alert level for Shaheds and a “red” level for missiles. Under a yellow alert, most businesses and institutions now remain open.
The changes do not apply to schools, which are still required to suspend classes during air raid alerts. Schools without underground classrooms have moved children to online learning. Across Ukraine more broadly, local authorities have been given discretion over how to respond to alerts.
In August and September, central government officials held a series of meetings with businesses. Entrepreneurs were advised to consider setting up air defenses on their own, to cooperate with existing volunteer territorial defense formations (known by the Ukrainian acronym DFTG), and to move warehouses underground.
Russian forces have been striking warehouses belonging to home improvement retailer Epicentr and delivery company Nova Poshta for years, but the logistical networks of supermarket chains recently started coming under systematic attacks for the first time. Strikes on warehouses reduced the range of goods available in stores in August, though the situation had largely stabilized by mid-September.
As fall begins, everyone in Ukraine seems to be asking the same question: how can the country make it through a winter of relentless strikes? It is already clear that the infrastructure responsible for heating and other fundamental civilian services will be among Russia’s targets.
The military shield and the front line
Ukraine needs interceptors to defend against ballistic and cruise missiles. But increasingly frequent attacks by jet-powered drones have created another challenge.
A volunteer (call sign Max) with a Kyiv Region DFTG told The Insider that his unit formed teams of interceptor-drone pilots in preparation for the winter campaign, alongside its regular gun and mobile fire teams. Training began in mid-spring, and by the end of summer, most volunteers had passed examinations and received certificates — along with combat interceptor drones.
But a problem emerged: older interceptor drones work well against conventional Shaheds traveling at speeds of up to 250 kilometers per hour, but new interceptors designed to take out jet-powered Shaheds have only recently completed testing. Russia is expected to use both conventional and jet-powered Shaheds during the fall and winter, meaning crews are expected to use different interceptors depending on the target.
Volunteer formations are part of Ukraine’s Territorial Defense Forces (TDF) and their supply system tends to lag somewhat behind those of the Unmanned Systems Forces, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), and the National Guard. Newer technologies only reach the TDF and volunteer groups after they have been tested by regular units.
By Sept. 20, videos had emerged showing jet-powered Shaheds being intercepted by high-speed fixed-wing interceptor drones and Sting S quadcopters.
“We have to remember that there is no such thing as 100% effective air defense. Some missiles and Shaheds will get through any defenses. That is why residents should always follow the recommendations of Ukraine’s Defense Forces. New Ukrainian interceptor drones are more maneuverable and can engage targets at greater distances and altitudes than the usual weapons used by ground-based fire teams. But they cannot offer a complete guarantee either. The same applies to Russia, where they are also technologically behind. So if power stations, thermal power plants, and combined heat-and-power plants burn here this winter, there is an even greater likelihood that they will burn in Russia as well,” Max said.
Ukraine’s new interceptor drones are more maneuverable and can hit targets at greater ranges and altitudes, but they cannot provide a complete guarantee against Moscow’s aerial attacks
A Kyiv volunteer territorial defense formation commander called Asgard said his unit has gun teams equipped with a wide range of weapons “from 5.45 mm up to 23 mm,” along with interceptor-drone crews. “The biggest target was probably a cruise missile we shot down in 2024. Believe it or not, we brought it down with a 7.62 mm Maxim machine gun manufactured in 1942.” Unsurprisingly, Asgard’s unit also engages jet-powered Shaheds.
There has been no particular need for “retraining” this year, the Kyiv DFTG commander said. “Every day we face new challenges and learn. Before, they were ordinary Shaheds. Those are very easy targets for us now. We still have work to do with the jet-powered ones.”
Ukraine’s small mobile air defense units shoot down conventional Shaheds in 95% to 99% of cases, but their success rate against jet-powered versions is no more than 40% to 60%. Volunteer formations hope that rate will increase soon as interceptor-drone teams receive more high-speed drones of their own.
At the front itself, winter could provide Ukraine with some advantages, according to Silver, an FPV drone pilot who flies fiber-optic-controlled drones.
“There will be more work in winter. First, the leaves will fall, which will make things easier. Even now we manage to fly fiber-optic drones through forests, but without the ‘greenery’ [the military term for dense seasonal foliage] we will create far more problems for the Russians. Second, we will rely on skill, quality, and careful planning rather than quantity. We are changing our approach, adapting technically and improving our skills. Everyone is talking about AI-equipped drones now, but artificial intelligence will not replace the person who still decides which target to send it toward. I’ve worked with AI-assisted terminal guidance, and it works!”
Even if Russia carries out another mobilization, conditions will become harder for Russian soldiers in winter, according to a Nemesis bomber-drone pilot who has flown 1,000 combat missions over a year and a half.
“The Russian military is adapting too, changing tactics and infiltrating our lines. Maybe they have something new prepared for us. But overall, we’re ready. We’ll see how their mobilization goes and how many more targets we have along the line of contact,” the pilot said.
Front-line cities
About 127,500 people live in the Ukrainian-controlled portion of the Kherson Region — about a quarter of the prewar population. In the city of Kherson itself, 63,000 out of the prewar population of 283,000 remain — roughly 22%.
The situation there is difficult. Russian forces deliberately target energy and heat-generating facilities in an effort to deprive residents of basic services. Strikes take place around the clock, with explosions heard roughly every two minutes. Since the area was liberated in November of 2022, the regional administration has recorded 400,000 Russian attacks involving more than 900,000 munitions.
Elvina Osmanova, head of the Kherson regional administration’s domestic and information policy department, told The Insider that between three and 10 guided aerial bombs (known by the Russian and Ukrainian abbreviation KAB) are dropped on Kherson each day. “They hit infrastructure sites one after another, including the combined heat-and-power plant, and essentially everything responsible for electricity, heating, gas, and water supplies.”
Alongside guided bombs, Russian forces make extensive use of conventional drones, a particular problem for Kherson, Nikopol, and other cities within a 20-kilometer range of the front line. Osmanova lists off the drone types that most frequently attack the city: “FPV drones, Mavics, cheap Molniya kamikaze drones, and other systems. Most of them use fiber-optic control, which makes them difficult to stop. As many as 5,000 drones can be launched at Kherson in a week.”
Still, food deliveries still make it to central Kherson, Osmanova said:
“The city has a sufficient supply of food. But the Russians deliberately destroy trucks and kill drivers transporting bread and other foodstuffs, so issues with deliveries cannot be ruled out. Due to constant shelling, some parts of Kherson are already effectively dead — riverside areas such as Antonivka, Voyenne, Korabel, and several others near the Dnipro. They haven't had normal municipal services for a long time.
Last winter, there were times when people went 10 days without electricity or water. Right now, one district of the city has been without power for 14 days. In other areas, electricity has been restored through the heroic efforts of utility workers. Many have unfortunately been wounded or killed. Drones deliberately target workers while they repair infrastructure.
We understand that the Russians will only increase their attacks in the fall and winter. The number and severity of enemy attacks are increasing every day. Kherson may end up without electricity and heating not just for hours or days but for prolonged periods, and we're preparing for that. We're adapting our anti-drone system — detection systems, electronic warfare, and mobile fire teams — and increasing physical protection for important facilities.”
Shelters are another major focus. Osmanova said 307 protective structures have been repaired and 439 mobile shelters installed in crowded public areas. Protection for critical infrastructure is also being strengthened through backup power, additional physical defenses, and alternative systems intended to allow facilities to continue operating after Russian attacks.
“The Russians attack any kind of transportation with drones: mopeds, passenger cars, trucks, ambulances, municipal vehicles, and public transit,” Osmanova said. “Last week alone, about 40 vehicles were damaged or destroyed. We are doing everything possible to protect the city’s supply routes, including covering roads and streets with anti-drone nets. About 270 kilometers of roads have already been protected that way.”
Zarina Zabrisky, an American journalist with Byline Times who lives in Kherson, told The Insider that residents are preparing for winter however they can. Residents with standalone, private houses were able to heat their homes with firewood in previous winters and are preparing to do so again — and many of them have generators. Zabrisky’s apartment has access to a supply of natural gas, which she used to heat her home last winter.
At the same time, the local administration is advising residents — particularly older people, those with limited mobility, and families with children — to seriously consider temporarily relocating to safer parts of Ukraine. The authorities say they are prepared to assist at every stage, including organizing evacuation, finding housing, providing humanitarian aid, and offering psychological and legal assistance.
Kyiv
Locals in Kyiv are not counting on an energy ceasefire. Instead, they are preparing for something resembling a repeat of last year. The main difference is that the upcoming winter is expected to be milder, with frequent thaws.
Vyacheslav Hryb, who heads three condominium associations in Kyiv, told The Insider how preparations are going:
“We’re buying additional inverters, checking the generators, and connecting elevators to them. If the power goes out, our calculations show the elevators can operate for five to six hours. Heating should also be fine. We have a large building and a 110-kilowatt generator that powers the cold-water supply, hot-water supply, and heating.
Last year, the unprecedented cold made everything harder, and after the strikes, many buildings had to drain water from their heating pipes. Restarting the heating at minus 22 Celsius [about negative 8 degrees Fahrenheit] was what you might call an advanced-level challenge. The instructions say it’s impossible, but we pulled together and managed to get it running.”
Kyiv’s energy situation is among the most difficult among Ukrainian cities not located near the front. Last winter, residents of several buildings on the eastern bank of the Dnipro went without centralized heating for around a month after heating pipes burst. Electricity schedules were largely maintained, with power generally available for four hours followed by four hours without it.
Kyiv’s energy situation is among the most difficult of Ukraine’s non-frontline cities
Residents are now buying batteries and inverters in order to be more self-sufficient. Buildings with condominium associations are generally better prepared, often with generators or high-capacity battery and inverter systems that can keep heat, water and elevators running during outages. But only about 2,000 of Kyiv’s more than 10,000 residential buildings have these associations.
Other buildings are serviced by municipal housing offices, commonly known by the Soviet-era abbreviation ZhEK. Their residents therefore often have to go to special “Points of Invincibility” set up by city authorities and Ukraine’s State Emergency Service to warm up and charge their devices.
The Zhytomyr phenomenon
The city of Zhytomyr is located less than 100 miles from Kyiv, but last winter it did not even suffer widespread short-term power cuts. Vitaliy, a Zhytomyr resident, told The Insider that while Kyiv spent days at a time without electricity, Zhytomyr experienced only a handful of outages, none lasting more than an hour:
“Specialists had told me before that Zhytomyr had inherited many military factories from the Soviet era. It was also an early adopter of power systems designed for wartime conditions. The city developed a distributed energy system, which is why, despite repeated attacks, we did not face major disruptions or prolonged power outages last winter or the winter before.”
In Ukrainian cities where power distribution has been managed effectively, utility services remain close to prewar levels. Residents of Kyiv — and perhaps soon Moscow and St. Petersburg — can only look with envy at Zhytomyr.
The overall state of Ukraine’s energy system
The risk of new large-scale attacks remains one of the most serious and unpredictable factors facing Ukraine this winter. DTEK, the country’s largest private energy company, is preparing for a range of possible scenarios.
“First and foremost, we are repairing and restoring thermal power plants around the clock after attacks,” the company told The Insider. “There is not a single DTEK generating unit that has not been damaged or destroyed during the years of the full-scale war, and some units have had to be rebuilt several times.”
At the same time, the company is carrying out scheduled equipment repairs in order to improve reliability during the winter. It is also stockpiling fuel and supporting the operation of mines, machine-building facilities, and repair businesses. DTEK spent more than 7.6 billion hryvnias ($170 million) on those efforts in the first half of 2026 alone. Since the start of the full-scale invasion, it has spent more than 51 billion hryvnias ($1.2 billion) restoring thermal generation, supporting its businesses, and preparing for wartime winters.
In the first half of 2026, DTEK invested 3.3 billion hryvnias ($74 million) in repairing and modernizing power grids. Since the start of the full-scale invasion, investment in that area has exceeded 15 billion hryvnias ($335 million). The company says its central goals are to restore as much available capacity as possible, maintain sufficient supplies for emergency repairs, and be prepared to respond as quickly as possible to new attacks.
DTEK is advising Ukrainians to use electricity carefully, particularly during periods of peak demand, and says it will do everything possible to minimize the effects of attacks. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, meanwhile, said the government would prepare the country’s air defense network for the winter.
“This is extremely difficult, but it has to be expanded. Absolutely everyone is working on it: the Defense Ministry, the Foreign Ministry, and the Foreign Intelligence Service. The obvious challenge, as you know, is missiles for the Patriot system. But we are working on that as well,” Zelensky told reporters Sept. 25. “Separately, we are working on our own anti-ballistic air defense system. That is the FREYJA system. We will work on all of this so there is no collapse.”
Zelensky also said Ukraine would retaliate for attacks on its energy system by striking not only Russian oil refineries — but its energy facilities as well.

articles.title: As Russia expands attacks on Kyiv, Ukraine prepares to hit Moscow’s oil industry harder in response
articles.body:
Ukraine will intensify strikes on Russian oil refineries in response to Moscow’s expanded campaign against Ukrainian infrastructure, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an interview with Reuters on 3 October.
Russia has increased attacks on Kyiv in recent weeks, hitting energy and telecommunications infrastructure, roads, railways, and bridges across the Dnipro. Zelenskyy said Ukraine would respond by targeting the Russian energy infrastructure that helps finance the war.
Russia expands attacks on Kyiv
Russian forces have broadened their strikes on infrastructure in and around Kyiv in recent weeks, with attacks increasingly affecting systems that support civilian life.
Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence obtained documents indicating that Russian authorities had approved a broader policy for targeting infrastructure, including logistics, roads, schools, and hospitals. He said the goal is to put pressure on residents to leave Kyiv and other major cities.
Russia has also begun targeting bridges across the Dnipro, which connect the eastern and western parts of the capital.
Ukraine targets Russia’s war economy
Ukraine plans to keep striking Russian oil refineries because they generate revenue that supports Moscow’s war effort, Zelenskyy said.
The policy puts Kyiv at odds with US President Donald Trump, who has urged Ukraine not to attack Russian oil facilities, arguing that such strikes contribute to higher global diesel prices.
Zelenskyy said he sees no indication that Moscow is prepared for either peace talks or an agreement to halt attacks on energy infrastructure.
Ukraine prepares for a new wave of air attacks
Ukraine is also preparing for intensified Russian attacks on its energy system over the winter. Ukrainian officials say Russia has stockpiled hundreds of ballistic missiles for a new campaign against electricity and other critical infrastructure.
Russia has also expanded its use of fast jet-powered Geran drones, launching dozens each day since the summer.
Ukrainian F-16s and MiG aircraft are intercepting around 60% of these drones, according to Zelenskyy, but ammunition for their 20 mm cannons is running low. Ukraine is increasing the use of electronic warfare and expects a first shipment of small, inexpensive air defense missiles designed to counter the jet-powered drones later in October.
Ukraine is developing five interceptor drone models to counter Russian Shaheds. Two have already undergone testing, with Zelenskyy putting their current interception rate at around 30%.
Ukraine expands its strike capabilities
Ukraine is also expanding its long-range strike capabilities. It has used its domestically produced FP-7 ballistic missile in combat for the first time, with a range of about 250 kilometers, while work continues on the longer-range FP-9.
At the same time, Kyiv is working with European partners to secure additional funding for its defense needs. Ukraine has found financing to order drones for early 2027 and is working to close a $27 billion gap in this year’s defense budget through its own resources, bilateral assistance, and financing linked to the EU’s €90 billion loan package.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s ability to sustain its defense and expand its strike capabilities will remain central as Russia prepares for another winter campaign.
