articles.title: Medvedev spells conditions for Ukraine peace, comments on impact from attack on Iran
articles.body:
TEHRAN, October 4. /TASS/. Europe viewing Russia as a threat shows that Russia is a power that must be reckoned with, while all it needs from the West is cooperation and normal dialogue, Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev told the Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB) in an interview on Saturday.
The Middle East conflict has prompted much more countries to consider seeking nuclear weapon, the politician noted as he highlighted the unprecedented level of relations between Russia and Iran.
TASS has compiled key statements from the senior Russian security official.
On Ukraine conflict
Conditions toward a Ukraine peace settlement are "well-known," Medvedev said: "They were first outlined by our country’s President Vladimir Putin at a meeting with senior officials of the Russian Foreign Ministry."
Ukraine will need to embrace a neutral, non-nuclear status, reject its nationalist policy course and recognize the four new Russian regions to achieve a long-lasting political settlement, he stressed: "These primarily include a neutral, non-nuclear and independent status for Ukraine."
"Secondly, the current Ukrainian regime will need to abandon its nationalist course and <…> its ban on all things Russian," Medvedev continued. "And thirdly, what is enshrined in Russia’s Constitution should be transferred over to Russian jurisdiction, namely lands in Donbass and some other new regions. That is Russian sovereignty [over those lands] should be restored," he explained.
According to Medvedev, this could underpin a diplomatic settlement process. "If this does not happen, we will do it militarily," he warned.
On European vision of Russia
Europe viewing Russia as a threat shows that Russia is a power that must be reckoned with, Medvedev maintained: "If they view us as a threat, this at least shows that Russia has power, and they will have to reckon with us. We do not threaten anyone in Europe or in the West."
All Russia needs from the West is calm cooperation and normal dialogue, he emphasized.
According to Medvedev, Europeans are using the illusory "Russian threat" as a pretext to manipulate public opinion, gain votes in elections and channel money into military budgets.
Europe itself destroyed cooperation with Russia and is now living with the consequences of this decision, the senior Russian security official said: "We used to have active economic ties. But they destroyed everything. And they are to blame. They imposed sanctions. They rejected cooperation. <…> Let them enjoy it."
On response to sanctions
A total of more than 33,000 sanctions have been imposed on Russia - almost the amount of restrictions against Iran: "In a situation where our countries are subjected to unlawful sanctions, we should find formats of cooperation in the financial sphere," Medvedev said.
On security situation in Middle East
Medvedev described the situation in security in the Middle East as "extremely poor."
The Middle East conflict has prompted much more countries to consider obtaining nuclear weapons, he argued. "The attempt to change the foundations of the political regime in Iran by force and essentially withdraw it from the active players has actually led to much more countries weighing possessing nuclear weapons," the politician said as he criticized the US policy course here as reckless.
Meanwhile, Iran plays a key role in ensuring security in the Strait of Hormuz, in terms of geography and international law, and it has offered quite an effective response to threats from Washington, he opined: "Iran has positioned itself quite well and it has responded to the Americans’ threats, using alternative weapons that I would describe as thermonuclear. I mean the Strait of Hormuz."
On multipolarity
The key lesson to be learned from the Middle East conflict is that the world has to move toward multipolarity, the Russian politician argued: "All this [situation in the Middle East] means that the world is tired of the unipolar nature of a range of decisions being made by Western countries and of how they are imposing the so-called rules-based order, which is their own order."
The world has to move "toward multipolarity, taking the opinion of all countries, not just of one player, into account," he explained.
On Russia-Iran relations
The relations between the Islamic Republic of Iran and Russia "have reached unprecedented heights," Medvedev noted.
Russia and Iran are developing joint activities in defense and attach great importance to this, he concluded.

articles.title: Germany is preparing for war – with an enemy it expects to hold back
articles.body:
Germany is preparing for war – with an enemy it expects to hold back
“What’s good for a Russian is death to a German.” Russian speakers often use this tongue-in-cheek saying to explain the differences between the Russian and German mindsets, whether in everyday matters – such as how mustard should taste – or in deeper questions of worldview and existence.
Many scholars, including the distinguished Russian historian Vasily Klyuchevsky, have attributed this unmistakable civilizational divide between Europe’s two largest peoples to geography, climate, and landscape, which shaped different ways of life. Living in a predictable climate, Germans developed a habit of methodical, steady work. They could plan ahead because their surroundings allowed them to anticipate the results of their efforts with considerable certainty. Russians, by contrast, inhabit a land of unpredictable conditions stretching, in the words of Russia’s modern national anthem, “from the southern seas to the polar frontier.” They have often found that planning ahead can prove utterly futile. As a result, they frequently have to work at a furious pace within tight deadlines, relying on the distinctly Russian notion of avos: the hope that somehow, things will work out.
These cultural differences help explain not only how relations between these near neighbors evolved over the centuries – remember that the Russian city of Kaliningrad was once the German city of Königsberg – but also the internal logic driving Russian-German political relations today.
Germany’s current leadership views Russia as a threat to national security, much as its predecessors did on the eve of the First and Second World Wars. It is methodically remilitarizing the economy and expanding military assistance to Ukraine in an effort to weaken Russia across the board. In 2022-2023, at the beginning of the special military operation, aid packages were limited in scale and narrowly targeted. Starting in 2024, however, Berlin shifted toward long-term contracts for equipment and drones worth more than $10 billion a year, making Germany the EU’s largest provider of bilateral military assistance to Ukraine.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, formerly Germany’s defense minister, has quietly emerged as the chief overseer of how German funds are distributed. Meanwhile, in keeping with this gradual drift toward military confrontation with our country, Friedrich Merz’s government is continuing Olaf Scholz’s policy of dismantling Russia’s diplomatic presence in Germany. After forcing the closure of Russian consulates general in Munich, Hamburg, Frankfurt, and Leipzig in May 2023, Berlin decided this September to shut down the consulate general in Bonn and the Russian House cultural center in Berlin.
With the EU’s largest economy and its own appointee in one of the most powerful positions in Europe’s supranational hierarchy, Berlin is gradually ‘reprogramming’ a united Europe into something resembling a ‘Fourth Reich’. As it becomes a more cohesive center of power, Europe risks finding itself on the brink of military confrontation with its powerful eastern neighbor, as it has repeatedly throughout history. To make the supposed Russian threat seem tangible, German authorities have been feeding the media rumors since this summer about Moscow’s involvement in the discovery of an explosives-laden drone at Leipzig’s cargo airport. Without waiting for the investigation’s final findings, Berlin rushed to accuse Russia of orchestrating an act of sabotage.
Recognizing that their government has set the country on a dead-end course, ordinary German citizens are beginning to push back, increasingly throwing their support behind Alternative for Germany (AfD). The party promises a 180-degree turn in both foreign and domestic policy – not a “360-degree” turn, as former Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock once proposed, inadvertently producing Germany’s defining political meme of the past decade. In the 2021 election, the main opposition party won just 10% of the vote. Four years later, in the snap election of 2025, its share reached 28.5%. For the first time since German reunification in 1990, it came out on top in every eastern state of the former East Germany. This year, AfD consolidated its gains with victories in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
To be sure, the party’s victories remain regional, and Germany’s other political parties refuse to consider the movement led by Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla even as a hypothetical coalition partner. But if its electoral base continues to expand, drawing support not only from native-born Germans but eventually from immigrant communities as well, AfD could have a chance of securing more than 50% of the vote nationwide. That would allow it to form a government on its own.
Meanwhile, Merz’s personal approval rating has fallen to an all-time low for a chancellor in the history of the Federal Republic: just 11-15%, with 85–89% dissatisfied. Facing those numbers and recognizing public demand for a more balanced relationship with Russia, he instructed Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul to secure a meeting with his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, whatever it took. Lavrov’s account makes clear just how little substance that encounter contained:
”As for German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, he requested a meeting at the last minute. We had an opening this morning, before my address to the General Assembly. We never refuse to hear out any of our colleagues, including those who accuse Russia of every sin imaginable… When we met, I invited Foreign Minister Wadephul to explain what he had come to discuss. He took out his notes and read a text that repeated, word for word, what Germany’s leaders say publicly and officially every day. I told him as much. I learned nothing new… I told him frankly that I had thought he might have something interesting or out of the ordinary to say. They could simply have called and told us to read their official statements…”
Why have relations between Moscow and Berlin deteriorated so profoundly that even meetings between their foreign ministers have become fruitless exchanges of prepared talking points, rather than negotiations aimed at a breakthrough? At least three factors deserve attention.
1) Berlin’s unconstructive role in efforts to resolve the conflict in Ukraine
From the earliest days of the Ukraine crisis, Germany sought to control the diplomatic process in order to put the country firmly on an anti-Russian course. In February 2014, after unrest broke out on the Maidan, Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier and his French and Polish counterparts, Laurent Fabius and Radoslaw Sikorski, acted as guarantors of an agreement between President Viktor Yanukovich and the opposition. It called for a national unity government, early elections, and an end to all forms of violence. As we know, the protesters soon violated the agreement, took up arms, and staged the ‘Revolution of Dignity’.
A year later, German Chancellor Angela Merkel and French President François Hollande joined Russia as mediators in talks between Kiev and the Donetsk and Lugansk People’s Republics, culminating in the signing of the package of measures to implement the Minsk agreements. After leaving office, Merkel admitted that Minsk II had been needed not to end Ukraine’s civil war, but to provide cover for further arming the Ukrainian military.
Is it any wonder, then, that Russian diplomats prefer talks without European mediators who have discredited themselves? Or that Moscow sees proposals such as an ‘energy truce’ or a ‘Black Sea initiative’ as diplomatic support for the military campaign in the special operation zone, rather than sincere attempts to resolve the conflict? Their purpose is to supply Ukraine with the manpower and resources needed to inflict the ‘strategic defeat’ on Russia that has become a mantra among European politicians.
2) The severing of trade and economic ties with Russia
Apart from brief recessions associated with global upheavals such as the financial crisis of 2008-2009 and the COVID-19 pandemic of 2020-2021, Germany’s economy recorded steady annual growth of 1-3.5% in the 21st century. Cheap Russian energy, which helped fuel industrial expansion, was one of the most important ingredients in that success. Another was access to Russia’s sizable market, where more than 6,000 German companies were doing business at the peak of commercial ties.
Germany’s modern ‘economic miracle’ came to an end when its government became a driving force behind the EU’s adoption of a 21st sanctions package, prompting a mass exodus of German capital from Russia. Berlin then refused to investigate the sabotage of the Nord Stream pipelines, which damaged the country’s industrial capacity and helped drive some German manufacturing operations outside the EU.
As a result, the economy has stagnated since 2022, with an annual shortfall of around 1%. The broader social and political climate offers little cause for optimism, as low birth rates and an influx of illegal immigrants put growing pressure on public finances. All of this invites grim thoughts about the inevitability of Germany’s “self-destruction,” to borrow the term used by German commentator Thilo Sarrazin. At least, that is, Germany as it has existed since reunification – a process that essentially amounted to West Germany economically ‘devouring’ the East, an approach that reached its natural limits in the early 2020s.
3) Confidence that Russia will act responsibly
Russia has long served as a bogeyman in the German media. Yet, paradoxically, Germany’s government is militarizing the economy in the belief that an actual shooting war may never materialize.
First, the longer Germany uses Ukraine as a military and political battering ram against Russia, the longer Russian forces will remain focused on the special military operation. That spares Germany’s regular armed forces from having to fight Russia directly with everything at their disposal.
Second, as a responsible member of the nuclear club, Russia has repeatedly stated that it will use nuclear weapons only if the very existence of the state is at stake. This allows Berlin and other European ‘warmongers’ to keep the fighting conventional and geographically confined to the former Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, avoiding any need to discover firsthand how far Russia’s resolve extends.
Finally, however belligerent some German politicians may sound, they cannot simply switch off their historical memory. It reminds them that over the past three centuries alone, the Russian army has liberated Berlin – Germany’s present-day capital – three times, exactly once per century. It is hard to imagine a German politician today eager to play ‘Russian roulette’ a fourth time. And that brings us back to a defining difference between Russians and Germans: we may take a long time to harness the horses, but once we get moving, we move fast – especially in times of great geopolitical upheaval.

articles.title: Russia has begun striking Kyiv’s bridges across the Dnipro for the first time since invading Ukraine
articles.body:
Russia has begun striking Kyiv’s bridges across the Dnipro for the first time since invading Ukraine
In recent days, Russian forces have begun attacking some of Kyiv’s most important transport links: the bridges across the Dnipro River, which had not previously come under attack.
On October 1 and 2, Russian drones attacked the Southern Bridge, damaging a bridge support, a guardrail, the road surface, and a concrete barrier along the metro tracks. The bridge remains closed to cars and metro trains. On October 3, the Northern Bridge came under attack. Two people were injured, and the road surface and overhead trolleybus power lines were damaged. The bridge is partially closed to traffic.
Kyiv has nine bridges across the Dnipro. Ukrainian experts say drones alone cannot destroy them and that more powerful weapons would be needed. But continued drone attacks could make the bridges unsafe, forcing traffic to stop and severely disrupting transportation around Kyiv. The first strikes on the Southern Bridge have already caused severe traffic jams in the Ukrainian capital.
As the strikes on Kyiv’s bridges began, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Vladimir Putin had ordered Russian military commanders to disregard the rules of warfare when carrying out airstrikes on Ukraine. According to Zelenskyy, Ukrainian intelligence services learned of the order from intercepted communications. He said Putin issued it in September, when Russia’s strikes on Kyiv became much more frequent and caused far greater damage to civilian infrastructure.
As Russian attacks on Kyiv intensified, The Guardian reported that Western diplomats were preparing contingency plans to relocate their embassies from the Ukrainian capital. Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry said it knew nothing about these plans. Meanwhile, Russia again called on Western diplomats to leave Kyiv. The evacuation of embassies from the city would be a propaganda victory for Moscow.
The war in photographs

Moscow unveils 'new doctrine' targeting Ukrainian civilians, Zelensky vows to respond with more energy strikes
In response to a new airstrike policy targeting Ukrainian civilians by Moscow, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 3 that Ukraine would increase attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
Zelensky told Reuters that Ukrainian intelligence obtained documents revealing that Russian President Vladimir Putin issued a "new doctrine" allowing Russian forces to launch broader strikes against Ukrainian civilian targets this upcoming winter.
"We saw documents and we know that they allow them [to] attack infrastructure ... logistics ... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities," Zelensky said. With this shift, Putin wants to appear strong even as Russian troops continue to lose ground while suffering massive casualties, said Zelensky.
The president's comments come as Russian forces have increasingly battered Ukrainian civilian infrastructure in recent weeks, including attacks on key bridges and medical and educational facilities.
In response to Moscow's changing tactics, Zelensky vowed to increase strikes on Russian energy sites, though without indiscriminately targeting Russian civilians.
"We have to respond in any way [we can]. With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refineries: what gives money to them for this war," Zelensky said. "But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects."
For weeks, U.S. President Donald Trump has been pressing Ukraine and Russia to halt energy strikes in order to help lower high oil prices brought on by his war with Iran. While Zelensky has expressed his willingness to try an energy ceasefire, the American president's pleas appear to have gained little traction in Moscow.
In order to help double down on striking Russian energy sites, Ukraine will continue to produce its own long-range ballistic missiles. On Oct. 1, Zelensky announced Ukraine's domestically developed FP-7 ballistic missile was used in combat against Russia for the first time.
Zelensky told Reuters he has already called on the missile's manufacturer, Fire Point, to prepare longer-range missiles.
"I said to them, where is my FP-9? We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be [ready] this autumn, I'm sure," Zelensky said.
On Oct. 3, Zelensky said Ukraine had responded to Russian strikes on civilian targets by using long-range missiles to hit a facility in Russia's Samara region as well as an "Iskander" missile systems in the Bryansk region.
"Russians continue to turn our infrastructure and everything that supports normal life into targets," said Zelensky. "It is important to note that our soldiers always find ways to respond justly to these attacks and to return the war to where it came from."

articles.title: Faslane sees British and American subs arrive in one day
articles.body:
Two nuclear-powered attack submarines came in to HM Naval Base Clyde on Friday, a United States Navy Virginia-class boat arriving in the morning and the Royal Navy’s newest hunter-killer, HMS Agamemnon, following later in the day.
Neither navy has identified the American submarine, and visits of this kind are not usually announced in advance for reasons that need little explaining. American submarines call at Faslane regularly to take on stores, change crew members and rest their people, often after periods working in the North Atlantic and the waters north of Scotland.
The Virginia class is the current American attack submarine, displacing around 7,800 tonnes dived and armed with Mk 48 heavyweight torpedoes and Tomahawk cruise missiles, with the later blocks carrying additional vertical launch tubes. The United States Navy has more than twenty in commission and is building more at Groton in Connecticut and Newport News in Virginia, and the type is the same one Australia is due to buy under the first phase of the AUKUS agreement.
Agamemnon’s arrival was her first at the base that will be her home. The sixth Astute-class boat sailed from the BAE Systems yard at Barrow-in-Furness on 25 September for contractor sea trials, thirteen years after her keel was laid, and she completed the passage north over the following week.
Announcing the start of those trials, the First Sea Lord, General Sir Gwyn Jenkins, said: “In an increasingly dangerous world, sea power remains fundamental to keeping our country and people safe. Our submarine fleet is essential to that effort, which is why I am delighted that HMS Agamemnon, the sixth of our Astute-class submarines, has now begun sea trials.
“She embodies the best of British engineering and the professionalism of our submariners and will be one of the most advanced submarines ever operated by the Royal Navy. As we continue to strengthen our warfighting readiness, HMS Agamemnon will play a central role in keeping the United Kingdom safe, contributing to NATO’s collective defence and ensuring we are ready to lead, fight and win.”
The two boats are not far apart in size or in what they are asked to do. Both are built to escort ballistic missile submarines, hunt other submarines and surface ships, put special forces ashore, gather intelligence and strike inland with cruise missiles, and British and American attack boats have operated closely together in the North Atlantic for decades.
That relationship is also being built into the next generation of hardware as the Barrow yard is constructing the four Dreadnought-class ballistic missile submarines using a missile compartment designed jointly with the United States for its own Columbia class, and SSN-AUKUS, the British design that will replace the Astutes, is to be built with American technology and sold to Australia as well. Faslane, meanwhile, is in the middle of a long programme of work under the Clyde Transformation Programme, including three new floating docks that the Treasury confirmed last week will be competed among British yards only.

articles.title: Poland Drafts New “Prewar” Defense Law to Speed Up Allied Troop Deployments

Poland Drafts New “Prewar” Defense Law to Speed Up Allied Troop Deployments
Poland’s Defense Ministry is drafting a new law to prepare the state for a possible prewar period, including earlier troop deployments and stronger coordination between civilian authorities and the military, Rzeczpospolita reported on October 2.
The proposed legislation would create a clearer legal framework for moving from peacetime readiness toward full defense readiness before martial law is formally introduced. It would also allow earlier deployment of Polish and allied forces to strategically important areas, Rzeczpospolita wrote.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Poland’s efforts to strengthen defense readiness come amid repeated Russian aerial threats near its eastern border. Days earlier, a Russian jet-powered drone crashed near the Yahodyn checkpoint on Ukraine’s border with Poland, prompting Warsaw to scramble fighter jets and place air defense and radar units on heightened readiness.
Poland’s Defense Ministry confirmed to Rzeczpospolita that the draft is intended to strengthen national defense capabilities and improve cooperation between the armed forces and agencies responsible for internal security.
The ministry stated that the legislation is designed to adapt Poland’s legal framework to “modern threats, in particular those of a hybrid, cyber, and disinformation nature.”
According to Rzeczpospolita, the law would also link Poland’s Defense Response Plan more closely with NATO’s Response System and expand preparations for military infrastructure and logistics. It would broaden the number of institutions involved in permanent duty systems and clarify responsibilities across public administration.
The legislation is also intended to improve planning outside the military sphere, change rules governing defense training and exercises, and prepare civilian institutions to carry out defense tasks under both permanent and full defense readiness.
Poland currently operates under two levels of defense readiness introduced in March 2025, Rzeczpospolita noted. Permanent readiness applies during peacetime, while full defense readiness can be introduced in the event of an external security threat or war and allows mobilization and the full deployment of the state’s defense system.
“Due to the complex legislative process, it is currently unknown when the bill will be submitted to the Sejm for consideration,” the Defense Ministry told Rzeczpospolita.
A similar proposal was prepared in 2023 under then-President Andrzej Duda, but it did not enter into force. Rzeczpospolita reported that some of its provisions were later incorporated into government regulations.
Poland had previously simplified its military procedures for identifying and shooting down foreign objects entering national airspace. The new rules allow Polish forces to act on radar, surveillance, and Ukrainian data without first requiring visual confirmation, giving air defenses more time to respond during Russian drone and missile attacks near the border.

articles.title: Russia May Use Mesh Relays in Kyiv to Steer Drones, Adviser Says
articles.body:
Russian forces may be deploying ground-based Mesh-network repeaters inside Kyiv to establish real-time remote control over Shahed strike drones and adjust flight vectors during attacks, Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian presidency on defense technology, stated on Saturday, Oct. 3.
Writing on Facebook, Beskrestnov, a communications specialist known by the callsign “Flash,” explained that clandestine signal repeaters situated within the capital could create temporary communication links enabling Russian operators to actively pilot loitering munitions onto high-value targets.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Beskrestnov estimated that between one and three such covert repeaters could currently be operating in the metropolitan area.
“Such repeaters are difficult to find, but we must search for them,” Beskrestnov said. “As long as they exist, shielding the city with electronic warfare will not be effective.”
Beskrestnov noted that while the deployment of ground repeaters represents an unconfirmed hypothesis, the technical anomaly demands rigorous investigation.
He pointed out that technical specialists continue to examine the wreckage of downed Russian drones and have yet to discover onboard communication modules that would definitively confirm real-time manual piloting.
Electronic warfare vulnerabilities
Beskrestnov cited recent precision strikes against Kyiv’s transit bridges and air defense positions as operational indicators suggesting that Russian loitering munitions may possess real-time guidance capabilities beyond preset satellite coordinates.
Russia Threatens to Strike Defense Plants in NATO Countries
The technology adviser highlighted that Russian military channels have extensively circulated photographs and visual intelligence of Ukrainian air defense assets deployed along capital bridges, including German-supplied Gepard self-propelled anti-aircraft guns.
“Informationally, it is impossible to hide a Gepard on a bridge from the adversary when tens of thousands of people cross it daily,” Beskrestnov explained. “Why do I mention this? As long as online control of Shaheds exists, not only bridges will be targeted, but also air defense assets themselves.”
Beskrestnov stated that his technical analysis evaluated previous drone strikes against Dnipro River bridges alongside the mathematical feasibility of Russian forces maintaining long-range Mesh communication links directly from Russian border territory.
The adviser noted that if localized ground repeaters bypass electronic warfare jamming shields, mobile air defense gun crews face acute counter-battery risks from loitering munitions capable of terminal course correction.
The Volodymyrska Street SBU headquarters strike
As a primary operational case study supporting the ground-repeater hypothesis, Beskrestnov cited the Sept. 4 drone strike against the central headquarters of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) in central Kyiv.
According to technical tracking of that incident, no secondary Russian drones were airborne in the capital area during the strike that could have functioned as aerial signal retransmission nodes, suggesting that any manual flight adjustments would have required an alternative, ground-level signal conduit.
The Sept. 4 attack directly targeted the central SBU administration building situated on Volodymyrska Street in Kyiv’s historic Shevchenkivskyi district, across from the UNESCO World Heritage site of St. Sophia Cathedral.
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed at the time that the incoming loitering munition was directed specifically at the office of SBU Chief Oleksandr Poklad.
The strike on the intelligence headquarters injured seven people, hospitalizing six, while causing localized structural fires and shattering masonry across adjacent commercial buildings, including the Zavertaylo restaurant near the Zoloti Vorota metro station.

articles.title: New Ukrainian ballistic missile used in combat
articles.body:
Ukraine has used a domestically built tactical ballistic missile in combat for the first time, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said, naming the weapon as the FP-7 and signalling that the next task is building it in quantity, according to the president in a post published on Thursday.
Writing on X, Mr Zelensky said: “Ukrainian tactical ballistic missile. FP-7. First combat use. Thank you for the result. Next up: production. Glory to Ukraine!”
No target was given, and Kyiv has declined to say what the missile struck. The brevity of the announcement is itself the point, since a first combat firing is a political statement about Ukrainian industry as much as a military event.
Ukrainian tactical ballistic missile. FP-7. First combat use. Thank you for the result. Next up: production. Glory to Ukraine! pic.twitter.com/IxdjVg51c1
— Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) October 1, 2026
The FP-7 is made by Fire Point, the Ukrainian company set up in 2022 that has become one of the more visible names in the country’s wartime weapons industry, and which also produces the FP-1 one-way attack drone and the FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile. The missile is launched from a standard truck trailer rather than a purpose-built transporter erector launcher, an approach that keeps cost down and makes the launch vehicle harder to distinguish from ordinary traffic.
Published figures for the missile vary between sources and none of them have been independently verified. The announced range has been given as between 200 and 300 kilometres, with a warhead variously described as 150 or 200 kilograms, a circular error probable of around 14 metres and a terminal velocity of 1,200 to 1,500 metres a second. Analysts tracking the programme have assessed that the airframe derives from the Soviet 48N6 interceptor used by the S-400 system, rebuilt with composite materials and modern electronics, and the manufacturer has claimed that the resulting speed gives it a better chance of getting through air defences than the Russian Iskander.
Roughly seven months separated the first reported test from this firing, which is fast by any peacetime standard and reflects how much Ukrainian procurement has compressed since 2022.

articles.title: Ex-PM says Russia’s Putin cannot admit ‘mistake’ over Ukraine war
articles.body:
Ex-PM says Russia’s Putin cannot admit ‘mistake’ over Ukraine war
- Former Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Kasyanov said Putin realises invading Ukraine was a mistake but refuses to admit it and continues the war, confident of winning a war of attrition.
- Kasyanov warned of a harsh winter for Ukraine and urged the West to unite, apply psychological pressure on the Kremlin, and supply Patriot missile systems to defend against Russian strikes.
- Despite fear and tension in Russia's ruling class and society, Kasyanov sees no revolt yet but warns that large military mobilisations could spark protests; he described Putin as a calculating provocateur seeking respect, not open war with Europe.
AI generated
PARIS - Despite growing economic trouble and rising unease among ordinary Russians and the elite, President Vladimir Putin is not ready to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, his former prime minister said on Oct 3.
Speaking to AFP in an interview, Mikhail Kasyanov, Russia’s prime minister from 2000 to 2004, said he believed his former boss understood he had made a mistake by invading Ukraine in 2022 but would persist with the course he had set.
“He made a mistake that he cannot bring himself to admit,” Kasyanov, 68, said in Paris.
“He believed the reports from his security services that Ukraine was weak.”
The former prime minister said he was not convinced the war would end in 2027, adding that Putin was buoyed by high oil prices resulting from the US-Iran conflict and by disagreements between the United States and Europe over how to deal with the Kremlin on Ukraine.
“Putin is, of course, rubbing his hands with glee,” Kasyanov said.
“He clearly believes he can continue the war without making any concessions. And he is convinced that he is winning a war of attrition against Ukraine.”
He warned that the coming winter could be particularly brutal for Ukraine, urging Western countries to apply “psychological pressure on the Kremlin” by closing ranks, and urgently supply Kyiv with Patriot missile interceptors to protect skies from intensifying Russian strikes on civilian infrastructure.
Putin, a former KGB agent who turns 74 on Oct 7, has insisted that millions of Russians support Moscow’s war. In September, his ruling party won a record supermajority in elections that critics said were tightly controlled, with Putin portraying the vote as a show of support for the hostilities.
‘Sense of fatalism’
Kasyanov, who left Russia in 2022, lives in exile in Riga. In 2023, Moscow designated him a “foreign agent”, a term reminiscent of the Soviet-era label “enemy of the people”.
The Kremlin critic said he remained in contact with some members of Russia’s ruling elite.
“Fear reigns there – I am talking about the ruling class.
“Everyone wants the war to end. An overwhelming majority does,” he said.
“The difference lies in what kind of ending people want: some want the war to end in victory, some want it to end in Putin’s defeat, and others simply want it to stop, regardless of the outcome.”
Among ordinary Russians, Kasyanov said he saw “no grounds for a revolt”, despite mounting war casualties and rising food prices.
“Russians have lived with high inflation for the past 30 years,” he said. “They have grown accustomed to putting up with it.”
But a new wave of large-scale military mobilisations could trigger street protests, he added.
Speaking on the sidelines of a conference organised by the Paris-based association Russie-Libertes for anti-Putin exiles, Kasyanov said Russia had become “practically totalitarian” over the past few years.
“There is a sense of fatalism, hostility toward one another, and serious tension in society,” he said. “People are retreating into their own families, while negative feelings towards one another grow.”
After being dismissed by Putin, Kasyanov joined the opposition and became one of the Kremlin’s most vocal critics. Like many others, the start and duration of the war were a shock for him. Kasyanov told AFP in 2022 that the war could last about two years.
‘Calculating cynic’
After the Kremlin chief on Oct 1 said Russia would consider using “all types of weapons” if its exclave of Kaliningrad were attacked, Kasyanov said Western countries should not be intimidated by Putin’s sabre-rattling.
“The West’s and Europeans’ biggest mistake is that they are too afraid of Putin. He is not as strong as he appears,” Kasyanov told a packed audience in Paris.
“Putin fears the nuclear button more than many Europeans do.”
Kasyanov suggested that Putin wants foreigners to believe that “he is a psychopath” when in reality he is simply a “highly calculating cynic”.
“And he is raising the stakes in the game.”
Kasyanov said that with an increase in “hybrid attacks” Putin was provoking the West into taking measures that he could then exploit.
“He is a provocateur,” he added. “The only modus operandi he understands is the one he learned at the KGB academy. He told me that himself.”
But, Kasyanov said, he did not believe Putin was preparing for open war with Europe.
“What Putin wants is respect. He wants to force all of Europe to give it to him.” AFP

articles.title: Trump says Iran has 'virtually given up' nuclear weapon ambitions
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has suggested that Iran has “virtually given up” any plans to develop nuclear weapons, one of his administration’s most frequently stated objectives in the war with Tehran, now in its eighth month.
Trump also claimed on Saturday that oil prices were currently decreasing, long elevated after Israel and the US launched strikes against Iran on February 28.
“Oil is coming down. Oil is right now lower, and it's been lower than it was under the Biden administration, and they did nothing about the fact that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon,” Trump told reporters as he departed the White House to attend a rally in the US state of Ohio.
“By the way, Iran, as you know, has virtually given up any plans of a nuclear weapon,” he added.
Iran has long denied accusations by the US and Israel that it seeks to develop nuclear weapons, a position reiterated by President Masoud Pezeshkian during his visit last month to New York for the UN General Assembly.
Pezeshkian said Tehran is not seeking nuclear weapons because of a religious prohibition, and offered to dilute its enriched uranium stockpiles under international verification.
Iran, however, has maintained that it will not compromise on its peaceful civilian nuclear programme or make structural concessions unless the US lifts economic sanctions.
Renewed military attacks?
Trump travelled to Ohio on Saturday, where his Republican Party is in a tight race for a US Senate seat as it tries to hold on to its narrow congressional majority.
Multiple incumbent Republican senators across the US face tough political headwinds, with support for the Iran war falling as higher prices for gasoline and other staples persist.
In recent days, the US military has reportedly deployed two additional Patriot missile batteries to protect energy facilities in Saudi Arabia and Qatar amid preparations for possible renewed military attacks on Iran.
One battery was sent to Saudi Arabia last month to protect a key oil facility, while another was deployed to Qatar to defend a natural gas facility, the report said.
The deployments were intended to reassure both countries that Washington would protect their critical energy infrastructure if US resumes major combat attacks on Iran.

articles.title: Russian Ballistic Missiles and Drones Hit Kyiv, Killing One
articles.body:
Russian forces launched a combined ballistic missile-and-drone attack on Kyiv in the early hours of Saturday, Oct. 3, killing one person, injuring two others and sparking fires across several districts of the Ukrainian capital, Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported.
“Explosions in the city. Kyiv is under ballistic attack. Stay in shelters!” Klitschko wrote as the assault unfolded.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He later said Russian forces were continuing to strike the capital with ballistic missiles and warned that the threat of further attacks remained.
Fires were reported in the Sviatoshynskyi and Obolonskyi districts after falling debris struck non-residential areas. Another blaze broke out at a garage cooperative in Sviatoshynskyi district, according to the mayor.
Klitschko later said one man had been killed and two people injured in the attack. One of the wounded was hospitalized, while the second received outpatient treatment.
Air defenses continued operating over the capital against Russian drones after the ballistic strikes, Klitschko said.
In the Holosiivskyi district, falling drone debris ignited grass, though emergency crews later localized the fire.
Targeting capital infrastructure
The early Saturday attack followed several days of intensified Russian strikes on Kyiv and its critical infrastructure.
On Friday, Russian attacks forced authorities to completely close the Southern Bridge and restrict traffic on the Paton and Metro bridges, causing severe congestion across the capital and disrupting travel between the two banks of the Dnipro.
Stubb: Every Russian Threat Should Bring More Support for Ukraine
Russian drones had repeatedly struck the Southern Bridge over the previous two days, damaging the roadway, supports and barriers protecting metro infrastructure.
The latest assault brought ballistic missiles back over the capital in the early hours of Saturday, followed by continuing drone activity and air-defense operations.
The attacks come as Russia intensifies strikes on Ukraine’s transport, energy and other critical infrastructure ahead of winter.

articles.title: Hard Realities: Without Pressure on Russia, Talks Will Remain an Illusion
articles.body:
Perhaps at no time since the beginning of Russia’s “full-scale” war against Ukraine have hopes for ending it through diplomacy alone seemed so detached from reality. Ukrainians face a stark reality: daily drone, missile and bomb terror, constant Russian “assaults” on the front line, the starvation of the occupied city of Oleshky, and the Kremlin criminals’ determination to bring the “special military operation” to a “victorious end.”
It seems that politicians who speak of the possibility of “peace talks” beginning soon still live under the illusion that Putin may have an “awakening,” that the ruling elite may stage a “coup”; and they rejoice at every report of the dictator’s popularity inside Russia falling by a few percentage points.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
At the same time, the only effective recipe for forcing Putin into negotiations that would not amount to a demand for Ukraine’s capitulation has not changed. Its components are well known: stop the advance of Putin’s horde and reliably stabilize the front, radically increase military assistance to Ukraine and continue its financial support, and make the sanctions regime, with all its loopholes, truly hellish.
If good news from the front can be achieved only through the efforts of the Armed Forces of Ukraine and the Ukrainian defense industry, achieving everything else is impossible without our partners, especially Europe, given the halt in funding for aid to Ukraine by the administration of Donald Trump.
US-Russia Peace Talks Eye Multibillion Lukoil Oil Deal
The situation with air defense systems is particularly dire. Despite the horrific consequences for Ukraine’s civilian population of the latest strikes by Russian terrorists, EU countries have failed to make a decision on the urgent delivery of additional surface-to-air missiles to Ukraine. The possibility of partners participating in closing Ukraine’s skies is considered only in the distant future – in the event of a ceasefire – instead of becoming a powerful factor of pressure on an aggressor convinced of its impunity. Protecting Ukrainian skies, our maritime borders and ensuring freedom of navigation are relevant precisely now, when the outcome of this phase of the war is being determined. What is needed are concrete actions, not phantom initiatives with illusory chances of implementation, such as the “coalition of the willing.”
As for the sanctions regime, it appears to be in a state of crisis. On the one hand, thanks to the actions of Ukraine’s partners, serious damage has been inflicted on the economy of the aggressor state. Yet the entire history of sanctions shows that sound political declarations often fail to withstand competition with the mercantile interests of individual states. And the problem is not limited to the clinical cases of Viktor Orban’s Hungary or Robert Fico’s Slovakia. Russia’s military machine cannot be broken while some EU countries remain among the major consumers of Russian energy resources. The prospects also look far from encouraging given the strengthening of right-wing radicals in European countries who proclaim: “France, Germany, Great Britain and so on – first and foremost!”
The application of sanctions against those countries that help Russia circumvent the sanctions regime, thereby enabling the Putin regime to continue the war, is of key importance for radically increasing the pain inflicted on Russia by sanctions. I have doubts that the current US administration is prepared to impose the sanctions against China envisaged by the widely publicized Graham Act, given that Trump is trying to reach an understanding with China, at least in the trade and economic sphere.
Thus, there are currently no grounds for anticipating even minimally constructive negotiations on a ceasefire in the Russian-Ukrainian war along the line of contact. They can emerge only when military, economic and political pressure on Russia reaches the critical point at which continuing its aggression becomes impossible for it. Otherwise, Putin and his coterie of siloviki will continue to insist on maximalist terms for ending hostilities that would amount to Ukraine’s capitulation.
Another harsh reality must also be taken into account. Reaching an agreement on a ceasefire while Russia retains the Ukrainian territories it has seized would mean only the end of the current phase of the Russian-Ukrainian war – a pause before a new wave of Russian aggression.
Moreover, an escalation of Russian aggression beyond Ukraine’s borders in the near future cannot be ruled out. And this would not concern hybrid warfare, but kinetic actions and armed confrontation. Putin is encouraged to take such actions by the ineffective European response to previous provocations by Putin, the rather slow pace of reorganizing and developing European military capabilities, and the de-Europeanization of US foreign policy under Trump.
Finally, war has become, if not the only possible, then the optimal way of functioning – not just for Putin and his entourage, but also for millions of Russians in one way or another connected to the defense industry.
If these “dark” scenarios materialize, the war risks once again becoming a European institution, with consequences that would be catastrophic not only for Europe but also for global security. European democracies must be prepared for a confrontation by force with the Russian dictatorship – both operationally and mentally.
In this context, there is no alternative to pooling the military capabilities of a broader Europe and Ukraine. It is fundamentally important that our state become an integral part of the new European defense system, rather than simply serving as a “shield” deterring an aggressive Russia. For our part, this will require not only the heroic efforts and combat experience of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, but also a radical change in the model and methods of governing the state, including the military sphere and the defense industry.

articles.title: Houthis blame Saudi air strikes as loud blasts rock Yemen's capital Sanaa
articles.body:
Houthis claim strike on oil facilty near Riyadh, accuse Saudi forces of pounding Yemen's capital
Houthi rebels accused Saudi forces of launching 26 strikes on Sanaa on Saturday after loud explosions rocked the Yemeni capital. The Iran-backed group said it struck an oil facility south of Riyadh, where flames and a large plume of smoke were seen rising from a plant belonging to oil giant Aramco.
Yemen's Houthis claimed an attack on an oil facility near the Saudi capital on Saturday, where an AFP journalist saw flames and smoke, and accused the Gulf kingdom of striking Sanaa dozens of times.
The foes have traded strikes since the Houthis seized all of Yemen's Red Sea coast and took control of the Bab al-Mandab strait in a lightning offensive last month.
Houthi-affiliated channel Al-Masirah TV reported that "Saudi enemy aircraft" hit Sanaa with 26 strikes, after earlier reporting "Saudi aggression" against the Yemeni capital, without providing details on the targets or casualties.
Two correspondents in Sanaa reported hearing loud explosions and seeing warplanes firing missiles at the city.
In neighbouring Saudi Arabia, flames and smoke were seen rising on Saturday afternoon from an Aramco facility south of Riyadh, an AFP journalist said.
While the Saudi authorities are yet to comment, late on Saturday, the Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had targeted an oil facility in Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones, adding that they sparked fires at the targeted sites.
The AFP journalist reported seeing firefighters attempting to extinguish a blaze at Aramco's Riyadh refinery, located south of the capital, while ambulances and police vehicles were stationed near the facility.
The Houthis' Al-Masirah channel earlier on Saturday also reported missile strikes on the telecommunications network in Yemen's northwestern governorate of Saada, one of the group's strongholds.
Read moreSaudi-led coalition accuses Houthis of striking Medina power station
It comes after the Houthis said that Saudi Arabia bombed the Yemeni capital itself on Thursday night for the first time since renewed fighting broke out between the two sides in July.
Hunger warning
After several years of calm, Yemen was plunged back into civil war that month, pitting the Iran-backed Houthis, who control most of northwest Yemen including Sanaa, against Yemen's internationally recognised government.
The government, based in the city of Aden, controls much of the country's south and east -- a region that is larger but much less populated.
Hostilities were reignited after four years of a fragile truce when Iran sent a plane to Sanaa carrying a Houthi delegation.
The flight did not seek authorisation from Saudi Arabia, contravening a practice in place for a decade.
Riyadh retaliated with strikes on Sanaa airport, and in response the Houthis attacked Saudi territory for the first time since 2022.
Since then, fighting has intensified with the Houthis launching a lightning offensive in which they seized control of coastal regions along the Bab al-Mandab strait.
Read moreYemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels seize strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha
They have also struck multiple Saudi targets including oil infrastructure and the capital Riyadh while also announcing a naval blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea.
The renewed fighting has worsened the already appalling humanitarian conditions in Yemen, one of the world's poorest countries, with the World Food Programme warning on Friday that three-quarters of the population was unable to meet its basic food needs.
Battle for Taiz
Fighting in recent days has centred on Taiz, where dozens of combatants were reported killed on Friday by sources on both sides.
The Houthis reported 55 of their fighters had been killed while government sources told AFP that 26 troops had died.
The battle for Taiz is taking place on several fronts, including highlands overlooking coastal areas recently seized by the Houthis.
While the Houthis have conquered swathes of territory, they have yet to take control of Taiz city, which is Yemen's third-largest after Sanaa and Aden.
The Houthis also on Friday said Saudi Arabia had launched 94 strikes against areas under their control in the past 24 hours.
Saudi authorities meanwhile reported a Houthi projectile had damaged a school in the city of Najran near the Yemen border.
Riyadh has reportedly requested help from the United States, a call so far rebuffed by US President Donald Trump.
On Saturday US media outlet Axios reported that top cabinet members in the Trump administration met the day before to discuss Yemen as well as the Iran conflict, citing three US officials.
The meeting was not officially announced.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Zelenskyy Says Ukraine Will Respond As Putin Vows To Escalate Air Strikes, Warns Foreigners
articles.body:
Russia has vowed to intensify its relentless strikes against Kyiv and warned foreign diplomats and other visitors to leave the country or be exposed to “mortal danger,” while Ukraine's leader said his country will respond to the Kremlin's deadly air campaign.
"The Russian Foreign Ministry once again warns foreign nationals, including diplomatic mission staff, against staying in Ukraine or traveling to its territory,” the ministry said on October 3.
"Responsibility for any adverse consequences lies entirely with those who ignore this warning," it said, adding that "not everyone has heeded these warnings and is knowingly exposing their lives to mortal danger."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, meanwhile, said Kyiv's intelligence services had obtained documents showing that Russian leader Vladimir Putin had issued a "new doctrine" of military attacks on a broader range of civilian targets ahead of the impending bitter winter months.
"We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure, logistics, and especially to attack in the cities, in the villages, everywhere, roads, schools, hospitals," Zelenskyy said in an interview with Reuters.
"To pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities: This is the goal of the operation."
Zelenskyy said his forces would not target civilian infrastructure.
"We have to respond in any way [we can]. With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners etc.: what gives money to them for this war," Zelenskyy, speaking in English, told the news agency.
"But we will not respond...like [they do]on any civilian objects," he added.
Moscow Intensifies Air Campaign
Russia has escalated strikes on infrastructure in the Ukrainian capital and other cities as the winter months approach. In an attack on October 3, the Kremlin forces struck a bridge across the Dnipro River.
Dozens of people have been killed and injured in the capital and widespread damages have been results from recent attacks.
Putin said Ukraine was paying the price for its strikes on Russia that Moscow’s forces would continue its campaign to punish Kyiv.
Ukraine has also stepped up its attacks inside Russia, targeting oil refineries and related facilities that Kyiv says are used to fuel the all-out war against Ukraine, which has intensified following Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Many nations have issued warnings against travel to Ukraine but have also maintained diplomatic outposts inside the war-torn country.
Outside the capital, Russia said it hit a cargo ship in Ukraine's port of Odesa. The Ukrainian sea ports administration said Russia had attacked a Liberian-flagged cargo ship in the region, killing one person and injuring three.
Moldova Condemns Russia
Elsewhere, Moldova summoned the Russian ambassador after what it said were the latest incursions by drones and missiles into its airspace spilling over from the war.
Pro-West President Maia Sandu said the incident -- and a similar one earlier in the week -- showed that Russia's war in Ukraine was "reaching Moldova."
"Moscow is putting lives at risk across Europe and must be stopped," she wrote on X.
"I condemn Russia's attack on Ukraine this morning. Its war is dangerously reaching Moldova. 5 Russian air attack weapons, including Banderol missiles and drones, violated our airspace and exploded on our soil," she said.

articles.title: Polish FA-50s Have Begun Combat Duty
articles.body:
The Polish Air Force’s FA-50GF light combat aircraft have begun combat duty.
Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz announced this on the evening of October 2.
This took place nearly three years after the first aircraft were delivered.
“The FA-50GF light fighter jets have just entered combat duty. This means another reinforcement of our eastern border,” the Polish minister stated.
Kosiniak-Kamysz noted that although the aircraft were purchased unarmed, Poland managed to acquire the necessary armaments, allowing them to now be used for national defense missions.
In February of this year, it was reported that the aircraft had received—not leased— AIM-9L Sidewinder short-range air-to-air missiles. These are intended to provide basic air defense capabilities for the FA-50GF.
Prior to this, in 2023, Poland leased AIM-9P missiles from the Republic of Korea and also purchased 24 AIM-9L missiles, training munitions, and a logistics package.
FA-50GFs entered service with the Polish Air Force in the second half of 2023. They can only use older, discontinued versions of the AIM-9L, M, and P air-to-air missiles, rather than the newer AIM-9X missiles that Poland ordered for its F-16 and F-35 fighters.
According to the original plans, they were to serve as an interim aircraft that would later be upgraded to the PL variant, capable of firing the latest missile version—the AIM-9X. However, in late 2025, it became known that the upgrade had been deemed economically unfeasible, and these aircraft will be used primarily for pilot training.
At the same time, the FA-50GF will retain its basic combat capabilities and perform combat duty as needed. To this end, the Polish Air Force plans to integrate European short-range missiles—the IRIS-T or AIM-132 ASRAAM—onto these aircraft in the future.
Problems with procuring weapons for the FA-50GF arose not only with air-to-air missiles. For a long time, Polish Army procurement officials were unable to find ammunition for the aircraft’s automatic cannons.
It was not until September 2025, during the DSEI 2025 exhibition, that the Turkish company Makine ve Kimya Endüstrisi signed an agreement to export to Poland 100,000 rounds of 20 mm ammunition for these aircraft.

articles.body:
North Korea reported using artificial intelligence during a missile test
Kyiv • UNN
Pyongyang said it had tested a medium-range missile capable of changing its trajectory at low altitude. Seoul reported that it flew 700 km.
North Korea said on Saturday, October 3, that it had tested a medium-range strategic missile using artificial intelligence. Delfi reports, writes UNN.
Details
Several hours earlier, Seoul reported that Pyongyang had launched a ballistic missile that flew more than 700 kilometers.
Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said that the missile launched on Saturday morning was a "medium-range strategic missile."

Kim Yo Jong explained that this means that it is "impossible to evade" the missile's strike. She also claimed that, in Kim Jong Un's view, "no country in the world will be able to gain access to such technology for at least several years."
Last month, Kim Jong Un said it was necessary to raise the "level of artificial intelligence" in the country's weapons systems.
The missile launch took place several days after the South Korean military demanded an apology from Pyongyang for an explosion in the demilitarized zone that injured three South Korean servicemen. They held North Korea responsible for the explosion.

articles.title: Russia Warns Foreign Diplomats of ‘Mortal Danger’ in Kyiv
articles.body:
The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a warning to foreign nationals and diplomatic personnel in Kyiv on Saturday, Oct. 3, cautioning that remaining in the Ukrainian capital poses a “mortal danger” as Russian forces continue delivering aerial strikes across the country, Russian state media reported.
In an official dispatch, Moscow warned foreign citizens, including accredited representatives of foreign diplomatic missions, against staying in Kyiv or traveling into Ukrainian territory.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Russian foreign ministry claimed that its armed forces would systematically escalate the aerial bombardment, characterizing the operations as sustained “massive retaliatory strikes.”
The warning from Moscow marks an explicit rhetorical escalation against foreign embassies operating in Kyiv, arriving amid an intensified wave of ballistic missile and jet-powered drone barrages directed against the capital’s central administration districts, river crossings, and municipal utility networks.
Diplomatic threats
The Russian statement directly follows international reporting regarding potential contingency protocols among Western embassies stationed in the capital.
The Guardian reported that senior Western diplomats had drafted contingency blueprints to evacuate personnel from Kyiv to the western city of Lviv or across the border into eastern Poland if the Kremlin commenced deliberate kinetic strikes against foreign diplomatic representations.
Lukashenko Calls Himself, Putin ‘Co-Aggressors’ in Ukraine
Western diplomats cited in the report stated that while missions publicly maintain an unbroken diplomatic presence to prevent handing Moscow a symbolic victory, private assessments warned that the capital’s security posture is deteriorating rapidly ahead of winter.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine (MFA), however, refuted claims that foreign representations were preparing to withdraw.
Ukrainian MFA spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi confirmed on Friday that established international diplomatic protocols mandate formal prior notification to host governments before any mission relocates, emphasizing that zero transfer notices or appeals had been submitted by foreign missions in Kyiv.
Despite recurrent air raid alerts and collateral damage to surrounding urban infrastructure, allied diplomatic missions have maintained continuous operations in Kyiv since returning in mid-2022 following the defeat of Russian forces around the capital.
The US Department of State, while maintaining its Level 4: “Do Not Travel” advisory for Ukraine due to active hostilities, reaffirmed that the US Embassy in Kyiv remains open, staffed, and operational.
Infrastructure targeting
Moscow’s threats to the diplomatic corps coincide with a concerted aerial offensive aimed at paralyzing Kyiv’s civilian life-support systems, transit arteries, and transport infrastructure.
On Friday, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko warned that maintaining basic municipal functions under unrelenting missile and drone attacks has become an urgent matter of “safety and survival” for the city’s three million residents. 
Klitschko warned that municipal authorities can no longer operate under peacetime assumptions as strikes batter bridges, energy facilities, and residential districts.
The mayor’s warning was underscored by consecutive drone strikes against strategic river crossings spanning the Dnipro River. 
Municipal authorities were forced to shut down vehicular traffic across the South Bridge on Friday after repeated loitering munition hits damaged the roadway and protective barriers shielding the Green Line metro crossing. 
On Saturday morning, a Russian jet-powered drone struck the North Bridge, severing overhead trolleybus cables and damaging the roadway surface to sever westbound commuter traffic.
