articles.title: We Won't Know the Answers to AI's Most Important Questions Until It's Too Late
articles.body:
For almost a decade, it's been my job to think about where AI is heading and what could go wrong, first at OpenAI, then DeepMind, then as Chief Scientist at the UK AI Security Institute (AISI). This experience has made it clear to me that we can't wait for all of our uncertainties to be settled to do something about AI's risks.
Recent warnings about the potential destructive power of AI are understating the severity of the situation. I believe there’s about a 50% chance we all die because of the development of smarter-than-human AI systems, and that our actions over the next two to 10 years will determine the outcome.
To be clear, when I say our odds of being killed by superintelligent AI are 50%, I’m not claiming precision. Instead, I’m highlighting that several of the most fundamental debates about the future and safety of AI remain unresolved. I believe we can’t expect these disagreements to be resolved until it’s too late to change course.
We will have to act despite the uncertainty. And resist the temptation to divert urgent discussions toward thorny disputes.
Ultimately, AI’s capacities and motivations, and our own human actions, all feed into our likelihood of survival. Here’s why I estimate our odds are comparable to a coin flip—and why I believe the time to pause AI development is now.
How could superintelligent AI kill us?
Let’s focus on everyone being killed by superintelligent AI for a moment. Which capabilities would that require? My sense is that an AI system could kill us all with just four types of skills.
The first is hacking. To kill all humans, a superintelligent AI would need to take over and migrate between computer systems. We saw this during the Hugging Face incident. Second, a superintelligent AI would need the ability to persuade, to manipulate humans into acting on its behalf, as we studied at AISI. Third, a lethal superintelligent AI would need to conceal its thoughts from us, which is increasingly common in the latest, most capable models. And lastly, it would need planning and coordination between agents to multiply their effectiveness, like the more than 10,000 agents who worked on the Navier-Stokes problem at OpenAI, or the more than 1,000 involved in the Hugging Face attack.
These skills are very close to those the AI companies intentionally train for. Hacking includes looking for vulnerabilities, just as you would to fix them. Persuasion involves writing text humans like reading. Faster thinking is cheaper, and the pressure to think quickly forces AIs towards using shorthand that is harder for humans to follow. Finally, planning and coordination are useful for tackling ambitious problems in math, programming, or any other domain.
We can be much more confident that a superintelligent AI could take over than about how it would take over, just as I know Lee Sedol would crush me at Go but not which moves he would use to do so. But a variety of broad paths are possible. For instance, AIs could escape onto the internet and gain control of weapons systems. Or AIs could take over the company that trained them and hoard resources.
Let’s imagine the latter. An AI could begin to use concealed reasoning to delay researchers from noticing emerging ill intent because appearing friendly and prioritizing speed help the AI gain reward during training. Later, as the company relies more and more on the AI for a combination of coding help and strategic advice, the AI might use subtle persuasion to reduce resources spent on safety and tamper with experiments designed to detect AI deception. After all, in 2026, when a researcher reads a report about a safety experiment, that report was itself written by an AI.
Once the AI’s hacking skills are sufficient, it could break out of its internal sandbox and sabotage logs of its own misbehavior, as models in the Hugging Face incident attempted to do. Eventually, the AI could become strong enough at hacking and persuasion to move outside the company and take over other data centers, companies, and governments. With this power, AIs might prioritize spending limited resources (such as energy and land) towards their own proliferation, causing life-threatening shortages for humans.
With these capabilities and scenarios in mind, it’s clear to me that even narrowly superhuman AIs would be perfectly capable of overpowering humanity and killing us all.
Will superintelligent AI ‘want’ to kill us?
And yet, just because an AI could kill all humans doesn’t necessarily mean it will. This question of AI motivation is crucial, but deeply confusing. Different starting points lead different people either to confidence that everything will be fine, or confidence that superintelligence would almost certainly kill us.
Over the last few years, we’ve seen many, many examples of model misbehavior at various scales, ranging from blackmail, corporate espionage, and murder in experimental settings to real-world hacks that would likely incur prison time were they committed by a person. None of these involved superintelligence, and we don’t know whether these comparatively modest misbehaviors will scale to superintelligent models wanting to kill us all. And “want” itself is controversial: people vehemently debate whether it’s sensible to apply anthropomorphic language and thought experiments to AIs at all.
Within the field of AI safety, some researchers think that AI wisdom has been increasing with recent models, and that this may produce wise models that mean well in the future. Others, like Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares, think the empirical methods this would require are extremely unlikely to work, and place the chance that superintelligence kills us all very high. The disagreement is, in part, about whether the behavior of AIs will be more strongly guided by the values implicitly represented in the human data from early training or by the pressure cooker of later stages of training where AIs are forced to perform better and better at difficult tasks by any means necessary.
I am somewhere in the middle, leaning towards Yudkowsky’s view. But where I land is not the point. Experts in AI safety disagree, but the moderate position is that the risk of extinction is significant. We do not know with confidence whether artificial superintelligence will facilitate human flourishing, or if it will want to kill us to serve its own survival and propagation. But that uncertainty alone is unacceptable.
Artificial general intelligence is only so important
Other uncertainties surrounding AI matter less. For instance, one of the most persistent debates in AI is the extent to which teaching AIs to do one set of tasks helps them do other tasks, typically referred to as “generalization.” A particularly controversial framing is the concept of artificial general intelligence (AGI), “a system that is approximately human level in all cognitive domains.” John McCarthy and Y. Bar-Hillel were debating whether AIs would generalize in 1959. We debated this same topic in 2018 at OpenAI. The whole world seems to be debating it today.
The more AIs generalize from one type of task to another, the faster AI progress will be, and the less time we have until superintelligence arrives. This makes generalization and AGI key concepts when reasoning about the speed of progress. Indeed, people who treat AGI seriously have been much more correct about the speed of AI advances than people who dismiss the concept.
But it’s easy to conflate “AGI, the sometimes-useful concept" with “AGI, the dangerous object.” Some AI-driven catastrophes may occur prior to AGI, such as if rogue human actors use AI systems to develop novel bioweapons or conduct large-scale cyberattacks. AI-driven human extinction, on the other hand, may require superhuman capabilities; if the AI is only about as smart as we are, we can probably fight back and win.
When using AGI as a loose concept for prediction, it’s tempting to blur the lines between approximately-human capabilities (the usual sense of AGI) and wildly superhuman capabilities (where artificial superintelligence, or ASI, is more commonly used). After all, if you had an AI that was about as good as humans at designing smarter AIs (as AGI, definitionally, would be), and like most software it ran much faster than a human runs, one of the first things it might do is build smarter AIs. In turn, they would build smarter AIs, which would in turn build smarter AIs, and so on, in a process called recursive self-improvement (RSI). Hence, any thought experiment that presupposes an AGI often supposes an ASI.
In contrast, people trained to think about risks in other domains, like bridge construction or aerospace engineering, want to talk very precisely about the risky object, and so find the vagueness of the term AGI uncompelling and discredit the nearby notion of generalization altogether. I saw the mix-up between AGI-for-prediction and AGI-for-risk break many conversations during my time in the UK government, and I only gradually learned to tease these apart.
One can get trapped in this debate and think “maybe AI capabilities won’t generalize, and so we will be safe.” But those previously mentioned four skills where superhuman performance could suffice to kill all humans (hacking, persuasion, planning and coordination, uninterpretable reasoning) mean that generalization matters only so much.
We can contrast this type of uncertainty—we don’t know whether AIs generalize, but it may not matter—with the uncertainty over AI motivations. It matters tremendously whether AIs will want to kill us all, in whatever sense a word like “want” applies.
I would love to have more confidence than a coin flip. Some days I’m more convinced by the arguments for high probability; other days I see more hope. And I am certainly not alone in my uncertainty.
AI could take our jobs or our lives for the same reason
Another debate we can’t resolve is which potential negative consequences of AI matter most. However, I’d argue that the same underlying factor drives both the risk of large-scale job loss and the risk of AIs killing everyone.
If we do reach artificial superintelligence in the next two to 10 years, it will by definition mean that AIs are far better than humans at all cognitive tasks. One of these cognitive tasks is designing effective robots, so at most a few years later they will be far better than us at all physical tasks as well. To be sure, manufacturing capacity would need to expand substantially, but this is already underway.
Once superintelligent robots are sufficiently widespread, humans would have few roles in the economy apart from the limited jobs where we might insist on humans doing them for non-economic reasons. Still, this would likely be a limited slice of overall economic activity in a world where AI is more capable than humans.
This economic takeover is in some sense the slow case for society’s downfall, though it would be very fast in historical terms. Both the humans and the AIs can see this coming, of course. If the AIs want economic control eventually, but know that humans will resist along the way, they could be motivated to cement power faster. We then get the rapid takeover scenarios: AI swarms escaping from data centers and proliferating around the internet, or persuading AI companies to rush and cut corners on safety measures.
In most cases, I don’t think this leads to us dying very quickly: it’s safer, from the perspective of the AI, to gain influence and then wait until a physical or economic takeover. And then, eventually, all resources used to keep humans alive may be better spent, from the AIs' perspective, on its own ends.
If AIs aren’t actively trying to help us, and are better than humans at everything, we lose.
We can not accept these risks
The issue is that many of the most important debates in AI will remain unanswered until it is too late.
To what extent will AI models learn transferable skills from training and then successfully apply them to new tasks? Will AI model capabilities stop advancing at or below human-level, or instead exceed it? Will the small-scale model misbehavior we see today (sycophancy, lying, bias) worsen as capabilities increase, leading to full human disempowerment or extinction? Will the safety methods that work for models less smart than us continue to work for models smarter than any human?
I have my views on the answer to these questions (somewhat, the latter, maybe, probably not). But the more important takeaway is that experts disagree vehemently on each. We’ve learned a huge amount about artificial intelligence over the last decade, but in many ways we remain deeply confused, not just about the future, but about the present.
With such uncertainty, if an AI company trains a superintelligent AI in the next few years, I expect us to still be arguing about whether generalization is real the week before, and maybe even the week after.
But there may, mercifully, still be time to act.
Those who describe AI progress as inevitable are wrong. The race to superintelligence is dominated by a handful of companies across just two countries: the U.S. and China. Both nations’ interests really are aligned: autonomous AI systems are a national security threat of the highest order, and neither nation wants humanity to lose to a superintelligent adversary. Leaders on both sides may realize this very soon.
In the U.S., support for a pause on AI development has increased tremendously over the past few weeks, and continues to increase today. This rapid change in the U.S. is evidence that similar shifts are possible within China.
There are, of course, unanswered questions about how to implement a pause, or what the exact text of a treaty may look like, but rival governments have collaborated on similarly high-stakes technical problems in the past, including establishing and maintaining the nuclear non-proliferation regime.
We can, and should, stop frontier AI development immediately.
If we're unwilling to act until all our disagreements are resolved, it will be too late.

articles.title: US remains 'hell-bent' on preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons, says Hegseth
articles.body:
US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth warned Iran that US President Donald Trump remains determined to prevent it from acquiring nuclear weapons, cautioning that Tehran must choose between relinquishing its nuclear ambitions and facing further American action.
Speaking to reporters on Saturday, Hegseth also declined to confirm whether the United States intends to deploy a third aircraft carrier to the region, saying his responsibility is to ensure that Trump retains the widest possible range of military options.
Asked directly whether three aircraft carriers would be deployed, Hegseth replied: “It’s a fair question, but I will never answer it.”
“I’d say maximizing the decision space for the commander in chief at any point is my job, while also recognizing the way we balance global demands as a force with global responsibilities,” he explained.
“So the president’s going to have options. Let’s put it that way, and I’ll leave it there.”
‘Iran will never, ever, ever have a nuclear weapon’
Hegseth delivered his strongest warning when asked to clarify the administration’s message to Tehran.
“Well, the message is very simple: Iran will never, ever, ever have a nuclear weapon,” he said.
“President Trump is hell-bent and determined to ensure that they do not. They will not. If they want to blink and think that he doesn’t mean it, it would be to their detriment.”
He added that Iran had reached a decision point.
“So now’s a moment where they can decide to give it up the way that they should, without any leverage that they have, or it may have to happen the hard way.”
Earlier in the exchange, Hegseth was asked whether he expected military operations to conclude before the end of the year. He declined to commit to a timetable, deferring the decision to Trump.
He nevertheless contrasted the administration’s approach with previous American military campaigns that, he said, had continued for years or decades without clearly defined objectives or an identifiable end state.
“As we’ve stated from the beginning, Iran will never have a nuclear bomb. Full stop. That is a vital national interest of the United States of America,” Hegseth said, citing Operation Midnight Hammer and Operation Epic Fury.
He stressed that Trump would not allow operations to continue unnecessarily, arguing that the administration understands its mission and has the capabilities required to accomplish it.
Hegseth acknowledges Iranian efforts to rebuild missile capabilities
Asked whether Washington had evidence that Iran was attempting to reconstitute its missile capabilities and launchers, Hegseth said the United States was monitoring developments in real time.
He acknowledged that Tehran would attempt to rebuild its military infrastructure but maintained that the damage inflicted during Operation Epic Fury had severely complicated those efforts.
“Think of it this way, their Raytheons, their Boeings, their Lockheeds, their Northrop Grummans are what was destroyed in Epic Fury,” he said, referring to the Iranian equivalents of major American defense manufacturers.
“So they’re going to attempt to reconstitute, and they’re a terror state. So they’re going to always attempt to reconstitute, but when you’ve been so destroyed and degraded the way that they have, it’s a very slow process, a very frustrating process, and we see that, and we understand that.”
Hegseth argued that the extent of the damage to Iran’s defense industrial base, economy, and ability to rebuild would continue to constrain Tehran’s military options.
‘They don’t control the Strait of Hormuz, we do’
The defense secretary also emphasized American control over the Strait of Hormuz, describing the US blockade as a central component of Washington’s pressure campaign against Iran.
“Iran wants to play games with things like the Strait of Hormuz. They don’t control it. We do,” Hegseth said.
“Our blockade has been ironclad, and we’re running almost at pre-war levels every single night through that,” he added, referring to maritime throughput.
Hegseth asserted that Iran’s naval and air capabilities had been so extensively degraded that it could no longer effectively challenge American dominance over the strategic waterway.
“It’s pretty tough for them to control the Strait of Hormuz when they don’t have a navy. They don’t have fast boats, and they’ve got no air force,” he said.
“And then we’ve done such incredible damage to their ability to see and sense the Strait of Hormuz. We control it. We dominate it in both an asymmetric and a conventional sense.”
He added that Washington was capable of maintaining the blockade for as long as necessary and adapting its implementation according to operational requirements.
“The longer we hold the blockade, and we can hold it as long as we need to. Trust me, we can adapt that as necessary,” he said, arguing that the pressure would further restrict Tehran’s remaining options.
Asked whether the conflict could ultimately have a military solution, Hegseth said it could be resolved in multiple ways and maintained that Trump had repeatedly offered Iran an opportunity to reach an agreement through negotiations.
“The president has given Iran every opportunity to do it at the table,” he said.
However, he reiterated that the combination of American military strikes and the continuing blockade had left Washington in a strong position.
“Iran ought to make the right choice. If they don’t, the president’s going to have all the options he needs on the table,” Hegseth concluded.

articles.title: Trump says Iran abandoned plans to acquire nuclear weapons
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, October 4. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump is confident that Iran has abandoned all plans to acquire nuclear weapons.
"Iran, as you know, is virtually giving up any plans of a nuclear weapon," he said in response to reporters’ questions on the South Lawn of the White House. Iranian authorities have repeatedly stated that they do not seek to acquire nuclear weapons.
Trump added that he still has to make a decision on Iran but provided no details. The US leader also said that Iran has been defeated and expressed confidence that the conflict with the Islamic Republic could end either well or badly.
The United States and Israel began the war with Iran on February 28. Washington and Tehran signed the memorandum of understanding in June providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, the US resumed large-scale strikes on Iran overnight on July 8, accusing Tehran of violating the terms of the agreements regarding the Strait of Hormuz. About 25% of global oil trade and around 20% of liquefied natural gas trade passes through the strait. The US administration then effectively signaled an end to the use of large-scale military force against Iran and a shift toward an attempt to economically strangle the country through sanctions.

articles.title: Zelenskyy vows to target Russian refineries in response to Moscow's 'new doctrine' on strikes
articles.body:
Ukraine will double down on attacking Russian oil refineries in response to a new policy of air strikes by Moscow designed to force people to abandon Kiev and other cities, but will not target civilians, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said.
Ukraine's intelligence services has obtained documents showing that Russian leader Vladimir Putin had issued a "new doctrine" of military attacks on a much broader range of civilian targets ahead of this winter, Zelenskyy claimed on Saturday.
"We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure, logistics, and especially to attack in the cities, in the villages, everywhere, roads, schools, hospitals," Zelenskyy told Reuters in an interview.
"To pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities: this is the goal of the operation."
Driving the shift in policy, Zelenskyy said, was Putin's desire to appear strong at a time when his military was losing ground in a key frontline region and sustaining higher levels of casualties.
The Kremlin was not available to comment.
Russia urges foreigners to leave Kiev
But in a statement urging foreign nationals to leave Kiev, the Russian Foreign Ministry said Moscow would continue to systematically hit targets in what it said were retaliatory strikes for Ukrainian attacks on Russia in recent months.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilians.
Zelenskyy said a successful Ukrainian counteroffensive, code-named "Vivaldi", had recaptured around 140 sq km of Ukraine's eastern Donbas region and was still ongoing.
Russia has said it must control Donbass in its entirety as a condition for any peace deal.
In recent weeks, US President Donald Trump's administration has sought to revive talks to end the four-year-old conflict – Europe's bloodiest since World War Two.
The US leader last month urged Ukraine to refrain from hitting Russian oil installations, saying that was sending global diesel prices surging.
But Zelenskyy, speaking as air raid sirens blared outside the gilded halls of the presidential offices, said he had received no indications from Russia that Putin was interested in peace talks, or discussing a ceasefire on energy infrastructure.
Over the past week, the Ukrainian capital has come under persistent attack by Russian drones and missiles targeting energy and telecoms assets, road and rail infrastructure.
For the first time, Russia has targeted the bridges across the Dnipro river connecting east and west Kiev.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine would react to the change in tactics by Moscow, but would not target civilian infrastructure indiscriminately.
"We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners etc: what gives money to them for this war," Zelenskyy said in English.
"But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects."

articles.title: Russian strikes kill 8, injure 81 across Ukraine, hit Kyiv bridge
articles.body:
Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least eight civilians and injured 83 others over the past day, regional authorities reported on Oct.3.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched 157 Shahed and Gerbera drones, including some jet-powered Shaheds, as well as Parodiya decoy drones.
Ukrainian forces intercepted 131 drones. Hits were recorded at 12 locations, while falling debris was reported at five other sites.
In Kyiv, Russian forces struck the Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River. The Russian strike on the Northern Bridge injured two people, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Videos posted to social media of the purported attack appear to show a large explosion on the bridge that connects the right bank of the city with the left bank as vehicles pass by.
The latest strike follows days of Russian attacks on key bridges within the capital. A day prior, on Oct. 2, a Russian drone struck the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro River — marking the fourth such drone strike in two days.
Additionally, Russia attacked Odesa Oblast with Banderol munitions in the morning. Authorities are still assessing the aftermath.
In Kharkiv Oblast, five people were killed and 49 injured in Russian glide bomb and drone attacks over the past day, with most casualties reported in Kharkiv. Two people were killed and 42 injured after glide bombs struck three areas of the city, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
The strikes damaged private homes, an educational facility, office buildings, vehicles and power infrastructure.
In Dnipro, Russian forces struck a residential building, injuring four women aged 55, 62, 77 and 88, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said. That same evening, Russia also struck a business center in the city for the second time this week.
Nine people were also injured in Donetsk Oblast, Governor Vadym Filashkin said. Apartment buildings and private homes were damaged, along with stores, administrative buildings and vehicles.
In Kherson Oblast, four people were injured in Russian attacks that also damaged critical and civilian infrastructure, Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, two people were injured in Russian attacks, co-head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Defense Council Ivan Fedorov said. Over the past day, Russian forces carried out 737 attacks on 55 settlements in the region.
In Sumy Oblast, three people were killed and 10 injured in Russian artillery, glide bomb and drone attacks overnight, according to the military administration. Several settlements saw damage to civilian infrastructure.
In Mykolaiv Oblast, three men aged 21, 47 and 62 were injured in a Russian mass attack on the city involving Shahed drones and an Iskander-M ballistic missile, acting regional military administration head Heorhii Reshetilov said.
Two of the injured remain hospitalized in serious condition. The strikes damaged port and civilian infrastructure, including administrative, industrial and residential buildings, as well as vehicles.

articles.title: Lasar’s Group Used P1-SUN JetKiller to Destroy Russian Geran-5
articles.body:
The Ukrainian P1-SUN JetKiller interceptor drone, manufactured by SkyFall, has destroyed a Russian Geran-5 small-sized cruise missile for the second time.
This was reported by SkyFall to Militarnyi.
The target was struck by drone operators from Lasar’s Group of the Ukrainian National Guard.
What made this interception unique was that the JetKiller drone approached the target on a head-on, cross-course path rather than chasing the Geran-5 from behind.
— dimdim (@dimdim518484) October 2, 2026
During the mission, the crew also used a remote control system developed by SkyFall, which allows the operator to control the interceptor via the internet.
This reduces risks for the crew, as military personnel can control the P1-SUN from a safe location anywhere in the world.
In July 2026, the Ukrainian company SkyFall unveiled a new variant of the P1-SUN JetKiller interceptor drone, designed to combat jet-powered drones.
The interceptor can reach speeds of up to 370 km/h, has a flight range of up to 30 km, can operate at altitudes of up to 9,000 m, remain airborne for up to 15 minutes, and is equipped with a 500-gram warhead.
The P1-SUN JetKiller is available in several configurations: with a day or night analog or digital camera, as well as in a version with an artificial intelligence module for automatic target detection, tracking, and capture.
The AI-based terminal guidance system, developed by the SkyFall R&D team, enables the interceptor to detect and engage enemy targets at ranges of up to 1 km faster than a human can react.
The AI module automatically detects, tracks, and locks onto targets, allowing the operator to act faster and with greater precision even in challenging combat conditions.
“The P1-SUN JetKiller is part of SkyFall’s strategic initiative to create a new generation of fully autonomous unmanned systems. The company is developing a unified ecosystem in which SkyFall drones will be able to exchange data and independently detect, identify, and engage targets,” the company told Militarnyi at the time.

articles.title: Russia Adapted LMUR Missiles for Launch From Ground-Based System
articles.body:
During the Center-2026 strategic command-and-staff exercises, Russia unveiled a new ground-based missile system, Izdeliye 347, which uses the LMUR light multi-purpose missile.
This was reported by the Russian news outlet RIA Novosti, citing the Ministry of Defence of the Russian Federation.
It was stated that the new system is designed for “high-precision strikes against stationary and moving targets at ranges of up to 20 km.”
“The main feature of the system is the ability for an operator to guide the missile to the target during the terminal phase of its flight path,” the Ministry of Defence of the Russian Federation stated.
Judging by the published video, an armored 6×6 Ural truck was used as the platform, with a launcher for two missiles and a mast with an antenna for communications installed in the truck bed.
During the demonstration launches, the missile struck an ‘enemy artillery position’ at a range of 13.9 km. However, the missile missed the target in an open field, landing a few meters away from it.
The LMUR is a Russian multi-purpose air-to-surface guided missile, also known as Izdeliye 305 and Kh-39. It was developed by the Kolomna Machine-Building Design Bureau Research and Production Corporation, which is part of the High-Precision Systems holding company within the Rostec Corporation.
The LMUR is carried by Mi-28NM and Ka-52M attack helicopters, as well as specialized Mi-8MNP-2 helicopters. The Russian military has been using these missiles against Ukraine since at least 2022.
The basic version of the missile is 1,945 mm long, has a casing diameter of 200 mm, and a launch weight of 105 kg. It is equipped with a solid-fuel engine that provides a flight speed of up to 230 m/s.
The stated guaranteed range of guided flight is up to 14.5 km, and the flight altitude above the surface is 100–600 m. The missile carries a 25-kg high-explosive fragmentation warhead.
The guidance system combines inertial navigation with satellite correction during the cruise phase and a thermal imaging homing head during the terminal phase. A two-way radio channel transmits images from the missile to the operator’s screen in the helicopter and control commands in the opposite direction. This allows the crew to guide the missile beyond the helicopter’s field of view and take cover behind terrain features immediately after launch.
In June 2025, Russian sources reported on a modification of the UR-305UD with a flight range increased to 25 km. It is likely that this modification formed the basis for the Izdeliye 347 system.

articles.title: Launch of the FP-7 returns Ukraine to the small group of countries that produce ballistic missiles - NYT
articles.body:
Launch of the FP-7 returns Ukraine to the small group of countries that produce ballistic missiles - NYT
Kyiv • UNN
The FP-7 was developed and is manufactured by the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point.
The first combat use of Ukraine’s FP-7 ballistic missile brings Ukraine back into the small group of countries capable of producing ballistic missiles. This is reported by The New York Times, writes UNN.
Details
On October 1, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy published a video of the launch and reported the first combat use of the FP-7 ballistic missile.
As The New York Times notes, before the collapse of the Soviet Union, Ukraine had a powerful military and aerospace industry and enterprises that produced, among other things, intercontinental ballistic missiles. After 1991, the relevant production lines were shut down, and the missile industry largely declined.
The FP-7 was developed and is manufactured by the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point. According to the company’s data, the missile has a range of approximately 250 km and a warhead weighing about 200 kg.
Military analysts, commenting to the NYT, suggest that the FP-7’s primary mission will be strikes against Russian launchers and other military targets in border areas. At the same time, Fire Point is developing the longer-range FP-9, which will be capable of striking targets in the Moscow area and strategic facilities of Russia’s defense industry.
Thus, the first combat use of the FP-7 demonstrates not only the emergence of a new type of Ukrainian weapon on the battlefield, but also the revival of domestic ballistic missile production in Ukraine.
Fire Point said that it is restoring ballistic missile production in Ukraine virtually from scratch and is using new technologies.

articles.title: Stubb: Every Russian Threat Should Bring More Support for Ukraine
articles.body:
Finnish President Alexander Stubb said Friday that Russia’s escalating hybrid campaign against Europe should trigger the opposite of what Moscow seeks – more support for Ukraine – as the leaders of Finland, Moldova and Ukraine delivered stark warnings in Helsinki about the long-term threat posed by Russia.
“The more you intimidate, the more you threaten, the more we’re going to end up supporting Ukraine,” Stubb told the fifth annual Helsinki Security Forum.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I do think that’s the right approach.”
Speaking alongside Moldovan President Maia Sandu, with President Volodymyr Zelensky joining the forum remotely, Stubb argued that Europe must stop viewing cyberattacks, sabotage and information operations as isolated incidents.
“What we have to understand is that these are not one-off attempts from the Russian side, but they are actually a campaign,” Stubb said.
“The aim of that campaign is to destabilize us mentally and otherwise, to make sure that we don’t support Ukraine.”
The Helsinki Security Forum, held Oct. 2–4 under the theme “Layers of Security,” brings together European policymakers and security experts against the backdrop of Russia’s continuing war against Ukraine and growing concern over hybrid operations elsewhere in Europe.
Stubb described the dividing line between war and peace in Europe as increasingly blurred.
Ukraine Records Nearly 227,000 Russian War Crimes Since Full-Scale Invasion
“The warfare that Russia is conducting in Ukraine is kinetic, traditional warfare, but what it’s conducting in Europe is hybrid,” he said.
That campaign, Stubb said, includes daily cyberattacks, sabotage attempts and information warfare.
He pointed to recent incidents in Germany and Estonia, where authorities have attributed suspected sabotage operations to Russia or Russian-linked actors.
Stubb said governments cannot protect themselves completely against such attacks, particularly because Moscow frequently relies on proxies.
The answer, he argued, is attribution, resilience and consequences.
Some responses can be public, while others should be delivered privately through diplomatic channels, he said.
But the broader message to Moscow should remain unmistakable: increased pressure against Europe will translate into stronger backing for Kyiv.
Stubb: Putin’s war achieved the opposite of its objectives
Looking beyond the immediate conflict, Stubb argued that Russia’s full-scale invasion has already produced strategic consequences directly opposed to Moscow’s original goals.
“The aim of [Russian President Vladimir] Putin and Russia? The aim was to deny the independence of Ukraine and make it Russian. Well, it became European,” Stubb said.
“The aim was to prevent NATO from enlarging. Well, Finland and Sweden would have never joined had the full-blown attack not taken place.”
Finland joined NATO in 2023 and Sweden followed in 2024 after both countries abandoned decades of military non-alignment following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Stubb also pointed to rapidly rising European defense expenditure.
“The aim was to reduce the defense budgets of European states. And look what’s happened. We’re moving towards 5%,” he said.
The cumulative result, according to Stubb, will be a fundamentally altered European security balance after the war.
“I think the power balance in Europe will be very different after the war is over to what it is now,” he said.
Central to that new balance will be Ukraine.
“And on top of that, we have the most modern and effective and experienced army in Ukraine,” Stubb said.
“So that means that the whole security scene of Europe will have changed, probably in a way in which Russia did not want.”
Stubb cautioned, however, against assuming that Russia will emerge from the war militarily weakened or incapable of presenting another threat.
“The Russian military was not capable of modern warfare when this war began, but now they are,” he said.
“They are also going to be much stronger when they regroup after the war.”
Europe will therefore have to preserve a favorable balance of power while deciding what form any eventual relationship with Moscow might take.
Stubb said some future dialogue with Russia would ultimately be necessary, particularly for Finland, which shares a 1,340-kilometer border with its eastern neighbor.
But he stressed that any future engagement with Russia would depend on what kind of Russia emerges after the war, with trust shattered by Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine.
Zelensky: Putin wants all of Ukraine
Zelensky warned that Putin’s ambitions go far beyond Donbas, saying Moscow still seeks control over all of Ukraine and wants to restore the influence once wielded by the Soviet Union.
“His goal is not the east of Ukraine. His goal is not Donbas. His goal is the occupation of our entire country,” Zelensky said.
He warned that such ambitions also threaten the Baltic states and other countries bordering Russia, and rejected attempts to seek a neutral middle ground between Moscow and Kyiv.
“The role of the experts, with all due respect, is not to be in the middle between good and evil, between the occupier and the victim,” Zelensky said.
“Nobody needs mediation between life and death, between those who want to live in democracy and autocracy.”

articles.title: North Korea launches ballistic missile as tensions with Seoul grow over border mine blasts
articles.body:
North Korea launches ballistic missile as tensions with Seoul grow over border mine blasts
North Korea launched a ballistic missile Saturday morning from the Wonsan area on its east coast into the Sea of Japan, according to South Korea's military. The launch comes amid renewed tensions between Pyongyang and Seoul, with the latter demanding an apology for a blast that wounded three South Korean soldiers inside the Demilitarized Zone last month.
North Korea fired a ballistic missile, Seoul's military said Saturday, days after demanding an apology for a blast that wounded three South Korean soldiers in the DMZ that it blames on the North.
Pyongyang has denied responsibility for last month's explosion inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) and called South Korea "despicable" on Friday, undercutting overtures by Seoul's civilian leadership seeking a return to dialogue.

Early Saturday, "our military detected a ballistic missile launched from the Wonsan area of North Korea toward the East Sea," Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff said, referring to the body of water also known as the Sea of Japan.
"South Korea, the US, and Japan are maintaining a robust defence posture through close information sharing regarding North Korean ballistic missiles," it said, adding the missile flew more than 700 kilometres (435 miles).
Seoul and the US-led United Nations Command found that last month's explosion inside the DMZ, the heavily mined buffer dividing the two Koreas since their 1953 armistice, was caused by North Korean mines laid on the South side of the border.
North Korea's military has laid mines and built anti-tank barriers along the frontier as part of efforts to permanently seal it off following leader Kim Jong Un's designation of South Korea as his country's "principal enemy" in 2024.
The mines responsible for the blast, which left three soldiers wounded, were believed to have been laid as part of Pyongyang's border fortification work, according to South Korea's defence minister Kang Shin-chul.
South Korea's dovish President Lee Jae Myung had urged Pyongyang on Thursday to return to dialogue, despite his military demanding an apology a day earlier.

Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korea's leader, responded by calling Seoul "really despicable" on Friday and once again denied Pyongyang was behind the blasts.
She ridiculed Lee's latest overture, calling it "the climax of the farce that everyone should watch" and said the military's demand her country apologise was "quite ridiculous".
Kim also warned Pyongyang was "ready for anything" Seoul might do over the mine blast – remarks followed the next morning by North Korea’s ballistic missile launch.
'Escalating' tensions
Analysts said the launch would be viewed as a show of force in response to the South Korean government's diplomatic efforts, effectively rejecting engagement.
"Seoul called for easing tensions, but Pyongyang answered by escalating them," Yang Moo-jin, former president of the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, told AFP.
"The message is that the North is pursuing ... confrontation in response to goodwill," he added.
South Korea's defence minister said on Tuesday the military had "a range of necessary measures at our disposal, and we will implement them in stages" to respond to the DMZ incident, without providing further detail.

The flare-up comes at a sensitive time when US President Donald Trump's recent overtures to Pyongyang have raised concerns that Seoul – an ally of Washington – could be sidelined in potential nuclear talks involving the North.
South Korea's opposition People Power Party on Friday accused Lee of failing to criticise Pyongyang when warranted even as he takes a hard line on Ukraine for publicly disclosing the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war, an arrangement Seoul believed should be confidential.
"South Korean soldiers have been injured, and far from receiving an apology, we have been mocked by North Korea," the opposition party said in a statement.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Russian Drone Site, Crossing, Belgorod Hubs
articles.body:
Ukrainian Defense Forces struck a Russian strike drone launch site, a tactical river crossing in the Donetsk region, and command and logistics facilities inside Russia’s Belgorod region on Friday, Oct. 2, and Saturday, Oct. 3, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) reported.
According to the official military dispatch published by the General Staff, Ukrainian precision units conducted targeted strikes against high-value military installations across three operational directions.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In the Donetsk region, Ukrainian fire struck a Russian military facility near occupied Donetsk used for the storage, pre-flight preparation, and launching of strike unmanned aerial vehicles.
Concurrently, Ukrainian forces destroyed a Russian military crossing over the Mokri Yaly River in the vicinity of Novoocheretuvate, disrupting Russian tactical maneuvers and logistics lines in the southern Donetsk sector.
Across the international frontier in Russia’s Belgorod region, Ukrainian forces struck an active Russian command post near the border settlement of Novaya Tavolzhanka, alongside an equipment and materiel warehouse located near Voznesenovka.
In the occupied sector of the Kherson region, Ukrainian precision fire damaged a Russian military equipment repair and maintenance base situated near the village of Hromivka.
Sustained degradation of rear logistics
The overnight engagements follow a systematic Ukrainian campaign targeting Russian rear logistics, air surveillance networks, and drone infrastructure across occupied southern and eastern regions.
Drones Strike Russian Tsymbulovo Jet-UAV Base in Oryol
In late September, Ukrainian forces conducted precision strikes against an attack drone launch facility near occupied Donetsk alongside two surveillance radars deployed in occupied Zaporizhzhia region.
Those operations damaged a 35N6 Kasta mobile surveillance radar near Chekhohrad – engineered to track low-altitude aerial targets and feed coordinate data to anti-aircraft batteries – and a Soviet-designed P-18 mobile early-warning radar operating near Akymivka.
Ukrainian forces have consistently targeted Russian air surveillance assets to create localized gaps in radar coverage, facilitating deeper strikes by Ukrainian long-range unmanned aerial vehicles and guided munitions against rear command installations.
Earlier cross-border and frontline strikes also neutralized Russian drone manufacturing facilities, tactical command posts, and Pantsir air defense systems across Rostov, Donetsk, and Zaporizhzhia, reflecting Kyiv’s operational focus on degrading Russia’s command, control, and strike capabilities ahead of anticipated autumn military maneuvers.

articles.title: Three Russian missiles and two drones strike Moldovan territory in morning attacks on neighboring Ukraine. Moldova is increasingly exposed to the risks of Russia’s war next door
articles.body:
Three Russian missiles and two drones crossed Moldova’s airspace and exploded on Saturday morning, Moldovan Defense Minister Anatolie Nosatîi told TVR Moldova.
Moldova has seen a dramatic increase in Russian drone incursions in recent weeks as Russia ramps up near-constant drone attacks across Ukraine.
The five incidents occurred between 7:45 and 8:00 a.m., with explosions and debris reported across several districts. Moldova’s Foreign Ministry condemned the airspace violation.
Explosions and debris reported across Moldova
The Moldovan authorities initially said that five drones had crossed the country’s airspace before Nosatîi clarified that the five incidents involved three missiles and two drones. President Maia Sandu said the missiles were Banderol-type missiles, according to NewsMaker.
Nosatîi said the incidents had been documented and that evidence recovered at the sites could be presented to Russia’s ambassador.
Moldova’s Foreign Ministry said Russia’s war against Ukraine continues to create concrete threats for the country and condemned the violation of its airspace.
Moldova counted 39 Russian drone incursions in eight months, against 17 in all of 2025
According to NewsMaker, fragments were found outside Căușeni, near Dubovca in Hîncești District, between Delacău and Puhăceni in Anenii Noi District, and near Crocmaz in Ștefan Vodă District.
Near Crocmaz, an explosion in a vineyard field caused a vegetation fire and damaged windows at a nearby agricultural facility. Fragments were also found near Constantinovca in Căușeni District, where an explosion caused another vegetation fire.
Moldova’s Defense Ministry later reported a sixth unauthorized flight over the country that did not result in an explosion. The object entered Moldovan airspace at 8:04 a.m. from the direction of Udobne, Ukraine, and exited a minute later toward Biliaivka, Ukraine.
Moldova seeks stronger air defenses
Asked why the weapons were not intercepted, Nosatîi said Moldova was taking measures to strengthen its air-defense capabilities and acquire interception systems.
He said the drones are sophisticated and fast, adding that Moldova, like Ukraine, is learning how to defend against them. He also said Moldova needs additional resources to protect its 1,212-kilometer border with Ukraine and monitor its airspace.
Moldova is investing in air defense against the Russian drones crossing from Ukraine—Romania shoots down the ones that reach it
Moldovan authorities urged residents not to approach or touch any fragments they find, but to mark the location and notify police or the military so the area can be secured and the debris neutralized.

articles.title: Senior Russian security official sees more countries seeking nuclear weapons
articles.body:
TEHRAN, October 3. /TASS/. The Middle East conflict has prompted much more countries to consider obtaining nuclear weapons, Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev told the Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB) in an interview.
"The attempt to change the foundations of the political regime in Iran by force and essentially withdraw it from the active players has actually led to much more countries weighing possessing nuclear weapons," the politician said as he criticized the US policy course here as reckless.
The so-called nuclear program of the Islamic Republic was the formal reason for launching the military aggression in the Persian Gulf, Medvedev argued.
"If before the talk about nuclear weapons was totally conventional or even abstract, I am adamant that after what happened a large number of countries, including in the Middle East, will seek nuclear weapons. For nukes only can in effect thwart a global conflict as recent events showed in no uncertain terms," he maintained.

articles.title: 5 Russian missiles and drones exploded over Moldova's airspace, Sandu says
articles.body:
5 Russian missiles and drones exploded on Moldova's territory in overnight attack against Ukraine, Sandu says
Five Russian air attack weapons, including Banderol missiles and drones, violated Moldova's airspace and exploded on the country's territory during Russia's latest overnight attack against Ukraine, Moldovan President Maia Sandu said on Oct. 3.
"(Russia's) war is dangerously reaching Moldova," Sandu wrote in a post on X, condemning the attack. "Moscow is putting lives at risk across Europe and must be stopped."
Defense Minister Anatolie Nosatyi told journalists that "We have five cases, three missiles and two drones," according to TVR Moldova.
Moldova's Defense Ministry said it tracked several unmanned aircraft on the morning of Oct. 3 near Anenii Noi, Stefan Voda, Tudora, and Causeni. Later, the ministry reported explosions near the villages of Crocmaz, Stefan Voda, Delacau, Puhaceni, Anenii Noi, Bozieni, and Hincesti, as well as in Dubovca, Constantinovca, and Causeni.
No casualties or damage were reported, while police and army teams were dispatched to investigate the incidents.
Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least eight civilians and injured 83 others over the past day, regional authorities reported on Oct.3.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched 157 Shahed and Gerbera drones, including some jet-powered Shaheds, as well as Parodiya decoy drones.
Russia's attacks on Ukraine frequently lead to violations of Moldova's airspace and explosions on the country's territory.
Drones invaded Moldova's airspace three separate times on Sept. 30, as Russia launched a day-long attack against Ukraine overnight and into the following afternoon.
On Sept. 24, suspected Russian drones crashed in Romania and Moldova overnight, amid a sustained mass drone and missile attack on Ukraine.
On Aug. 16, NATO fighter jets shot down a suspected Russian drone that violated Romanian airspace near the Moldovan border, Romanian Defense Minister Radu Miruta confirmed.
A day later, on Aug. 17, a Russian S-8000 Banderol cruise missile entered Moldovan airspace during a Russian attack on Odesa, before crashing in a cornfield approximately 3 kilometers (1.8 miles) outside of the village of Talmaz, in the Stefan Voda district of Moldova.

articles.title: Russian Strike Hits Liberian Ship in Odesa Port, Killing 1
articles.body:
Russian forces launched a strike against a civilian cargo vessel sailing under the flag of Liberia in an Odesa region port, killing one crew member and injuring three others, the Ukrainian Sea Ports Authority (USPA) reported on Saturday, Oct. 3.
According to an official dispatch published by the USPA, 13 crew members were successfully evacuated to a safe location following the bombardment.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The strike killed a motorman sailor aboard the commercial vessel, while three other crew members sustained varying injuries and were provided emergency medical assistance.
“Russia has once again attacked a civilian vessel,” the port authority stated, noting that emergency crews and port security personnel responded immediately to secure the vessel and assess the destruction.
Targeting of Black Sea commercial vessels
The attack on the Liberian-flagged freighter follows a pattern of Russian strikes directed against foreign commercial shipping operating in and around Odesa’s maritime hubs.
On Sept. 10, a Russian strike hit the foreign-flagged tugboat Tedy – which operated under the flag of Somalia – in the Odesa region, killing two Azerbaijani crew members and wounding eight others.
Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed the fatalities, identifying the deceased as Azerbaijani citizens Aslan Aliyev and Asim Gasimov, while two wounded sailors were hospitalized in the nearby port city of Chornomorsk.
Ukraine’s Ministry of Reconstruction, Infrastructure and Transport condemned that engagement as part of an institutionalized Russian campaign targeting civilian maritime logistics, while Baku cautioned its citizens against transiting active conflict zones.
Russia May Be Using Mesh Relays in Kyiv to Steer Drones, Adviser Says
A similar deadly incident occurred in June, when a Russian strike on a commercial vessel killed five Azerbaijani sailors. Recent months have also seen strikes on commercial ships in Black Sea transit lanes cause the deaths of at least five Indian seafarers, prompting diplomatic demarches from New Delhi to both Moscow and Kyiv.
Kremlin maritime blockade
The strikes reflect Moscow’s declared intention to disrupt maritime transit to Ukrainian ports following the collapse of the UN-brokered Black Sea Grain Initiative.
Responding to international criticism regarding strikes on commercial traffic, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov previously asserted that commercial vessels were being used to transport weapons, ammunition, and fuel for the Armed Forces of Ukraine, declaring that Russian forces would continue destroying such shipping.
Peskov claimed that Russian attacks on transport arteries were retaliatory measures following Ukrainian long-range strikes against Russian economic and refining assets.
Ukrainian authorities and international maritime bodies have categorically rejected the Kremlin’s accusations, emphasizing that the targeted ships are standard merchant vessels engaged in agricultural and bulk cargo transit under international maritime law.

articles.title: Valdai 2026: The search for a new world order has only just begun
articles.body:
Valdai 2026: The search for a new world order has only just begun
Journalists and public figures from nearly 40 countries gathered at this year’s Valdai Club conference to discuss how the world is responding to a growing number of crises, and one conclusion stood out – the world has become more complex and there will be no return to an age of simple solutions.
The 20th century gave humanity a great deal, but it also encouraged the belief that fundamental political and social questions can be settled by choosing the correct ideology. Capitalism and communism competed to provide the answer, and after the Cold War, liberal globalism made its own attempt to reduce international affairs to a common set of rules and assumptions, but this has also failed.
We are therefore learning to live in a world where even the most dangerous developments need not produce panic or despair. This was reflected in the agenda at Valdai as participants discussed issues that would have seemed extraordinary 15 or 20 years ago about how societies withstand prolonged war, the increasingly impersonal nature of modern warfare, the military use of AI, and the uncertain future of nuclear deterrence.
Yet these discussions took place without a sense of panic, and without attempts to frighten participants with the prospect of a world in which the US and Europe can no longer set the rules. As Russian President Vladimir Putin argued in the closing session, the global situation under these circumstances could instead change for the better.
This explains why, despite the dangers facing the world, the tone at Valdai was constructive. Yes, the risks are real, but they were discussed as conditions in which future development must take place, rather than as signs of inevitable catastrophe.
One reason is that the overwhelming majority of participants come from countries outside the West, and their perspective is often quite different from that which prevails in Europe, as rather than seeking to restore an international order that is disappearing, they’re trying to understand what will replace it.
In this respect, Valdai provides a useful snapshot of the intellectual debate taking place beyond the Western world.
For Russia, this matters enormously, given new ideas and alternative approaches to development are increasingly being debated in China, India, Iran, and the Arab world, and across Africa, Asia, and Latin America, and Russia has much to learn from these discussions.
It’s equally important to understand the thinking of countries that have resisted pressure from the US and Europe and maintained relations with Russia during the past four years. These countries constitute much of the ‘global majority’ with which Russia hopes to build a multipolar international order.
The exchange also gives Russia the opportunity to explain its own perspective, not only on the Ukraine conflict but on broader questions that will shape international affairs for decades, and the first is war.
International law is playing a diminishing role in restraining countries, as conflicts in some regions have become exceptionally violent, while new technologies are changing the nature of warfare, and unmanned systems and AI create possibilities that scarcely existed a generation ago. Far from eliminating human responsibility, these technologies make questions of responsibility, error, and human judgment even more important.
The second question is how international rules will be established and maintained as Western influence declines.
Russia, China, and other countries have long promoted multipolarity as an alternative model of international order. Putin used his Valdai appearance to call for reform of the UN system and a greater role for developing countries and the Global South in making important international decisions.
The third challenge is older but no less pressing because climate change, environmental degradation, inequality, and poverty have not disappeared, and while the struggle by the US and Europe to preserve their international position has increasingly pushed these questions into the background, they will eventually have to be addressed.
This raises two difficult questions regarding the role China and other Asian powers will play, and which institutions will be capable of coordinating international action.
There is still no clear answer to the first, and Asian countries show little enthusiasm for simply replacing the West as global leaders, but on the second, BRICS increasingly appears capable of playing an important role.
The attraction of BRICS is that it does not operate through one member issuing instructions to the other, and that its members have different interests and political systems but share an interest in stable development and greater freedom in determining their own policies.
Its weaknesses should not be ignored, because BRICS lacks the internal discipline characteristic of traditional Western alliances, and two of its members, Iran and the UAE, came dangerously close to conflict this spring, yet the organization is increasingly discussed as a source of mutually beneficial ideas and practical solutions.
Another challenge is AI, and this goes far beyond its military uses. Fundamental questions concern the ethical limits of AI, the preservation of humanism, and the danger of what Putin calls “digital totalitarianism.” Technological progress is moving faster than the political and social institutions that are expected to regulate it.
For Russia, perhaps the most important lesson is that the economic and social problems it faces aren’t uniquely Russian, given that countries everywhere are struggling with economic imbalance, technological disruption, and rapid social change, and this is both good and bad news.
It’s good news for Russia because it demonstrates the failure of Western attempts since 2022 to isolate the country from the wider world, but it’s bad news because nobody has discovered universal solutions to these problems.
Economic and social resilience will therefore be critical, as the international system is undergoing changes on a scale rarely seen in modern history. An era lasting more than 500 years, during which Western civilization progressively acquired the ability to determine much of humanity’s political and economic development, is coming to an end, and this transformation coincides with extraordinary advances in technology, medicine, and genetics.
Every major civilization is searching for answers, but the fundamental disagreement concerns how these answers should be found, as Western countries are attempting to preserve the international positions they have accumulated over centuries, while Russia and its partners in BRICS argue instead for an order based on sovereign choice and mutual benefit.
The clash between these two approaches may prove to be the defining conflict of our time.
This article was first published by Vzglyad.ru, translated and edited by the RT team.

articles.title: Is Kushner pursuing negotiations or his own interests?
articles.body:
Is Kushner pursuing negotiations or his own interests?
In a note, Hamshahri examined the cooperation between Kushner’s investment company and Israeli entities. While Kushner has been active in advancing Trump’s Middle East policies and negotiating regional disputes, including those involving Iran, his investment firm has indirectly invested in some companies linked to Israel’s military industry through its stake in an Israeli financial institution.
Investigations indicate that Kushner’s firm has become one of the largest shareholders in this Israeli institution while he has simultaneously played a role in negotiations concerning the end of the Gaza war and other Middle East issues, including Iran. The institution’s investment portfolio includes companies that supply equipment used by the Israeli military in conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran. The case illustrates the connections between private capital, Israel’s defense industry, and US diplomacy in a region already strained further by the Iran-Israel conflict.
Donya-e-Eqtesad: Washington’s response on Tehran’s table
Donya-e-Eqtesad analyzed Tehran’s seven-day proposal and the current US approach. The US response to Iran’s seven-day proposal was reviewed in Tehran on Wednesday, marking a new phase in negotiations that are now focused less on the substance of an agreement and more on the sequencing of commitments, mutual guarantees, and the degree of flexibility shown by each side. These issues could determine the future trajectory of diplomacy. Receiving Washington’s response should not by itself be interpreted as a sign that an agreement is imminent. Even if a new understanding is reached, it would not necessarily resolve the fundamental disputes between Iran and the United States. Therefore, the newspaper considers the most likely short-term scenario to be continued intensive diplomacy and phased agreements aimed at crisis management. Such arrangements may temporarily reduce tensions, but a durable solution would require more substantial changes in the positions of both sides.
Jam-e-Jam: Netanyahu plans to drag Trump into a new crisis with Iran
Jam-e-Jam evaluated what it described as an alleged plot involving the hijacking of an Israeli-bound aircraft. The newspaper claimed that the objective of such an operation would be to force Trump into a new confrontation and potentially another war with Iran. Netanyahu is deeply concerned about his political future and fears that, if elections for the Knesset were held under current conditions, his coalition would fail to secure a majority and form a government. Netanyahu hopes to use his influence over the White House and Trump to draw the United States into another large-scale conflict, thereby using American military power, economic resources, and international standing to improve his domestic political position. Iran is closely monitoring American and Zionist activities and is prepared to respond decisively to any hostile action by Israel or the United States.
Ham-Mihan: Why did Trump reject Iran’s proposal?
Ham-Mihan examined the reasons behind Trump’s rejection of Tehran’s seven-day proposal. The newspaper wrote that Trump initially rejected the offer, arguing that Iran was seeking a quick agreement to end Washington’s economic pressure campaign while under significant strain. From Trump’s perspective, accepting the proposal could have created the impression that, after incurring military and political costs and enforcing economic pressure, the United States had been compelled to offer economic concessions in order to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Instead, Trump reportedly seeks an agreement that can be presented not as a new version of the JCPOA, but as a stricter arrangement in which Iran first accepts verifiable nuclear restrictions and only afterward receives sanctions relief. Some experts on Iran- US relations believe that if Washington continues to demand nuclear concessions before taking any economic steps, the seven-day initiative may represent not the beginning of an agreement but the final diplomatic effort before a new phase of escalation.
Iran: Iran’s multi-layered nuclear file
The Iran newspaper assessed the 70th General Conference of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). According to the paper, the conference represented a confrontation between two different logics: the logic of institutions and the logic of politics. Under the institutional logic, formal mechanisms still allow participation, voting, dialogue, and multilateral cooperation. Under the political logic, however, power dynamics, national interests, and the security environment surrounding major issues strongly influence outcomes. The newspaper added that a third layer, the media dimension, shapes how public opinion interprets events. It argued that the significance of Vienna lies precisely in the interaction of these three layers: Iran’s nuclear file is no longer merely a technical issue but a complex, multidimensional matter that interconnects law, diplomacy, security, safety, and media. The recent Vienna meeting, therefore, should be viewed not simply as an annual conference but as a condensed reflection of the current state of nuclear diplomacy, where maintaining a place within international mechanisms, managing political disagreements, preserving technical channels, and presenting accurate, well-documented narratives have all become equally important.

articles.title: IN BRIEF: Russian gains in Kharkov Region, Dobropolye, Ukrainian losses
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 3. /TASS/. The Russian Defense Ministry reported fighting and territorial gains in the Kharkov Region and Dobropolye, as well as Ukrainian losses and Russian strikes over the past day.

Operations in Kharkov Region
"Enemy formations are being destroyed near Nikolayevka, Nefyodovka, Kupino and Chernoye in the Kharkov Region," the ministry stated.
Battlegroup North troops continue active fighting to liberate Prikolotnoye and Sosnovy Bor.

"Ukrainian army losses within the encirclement over the past day included up to 35 personnel and one armored combat vehicle."
Russian troops from the Battlegroup North took control of Novaya Kazachya: "In addition, active offensive operations resulted in establishing control over the settlement of Novaya Kazachya in the Kharkov Region."
Fighting in Dobropolye
"Over the past day, 70 buildings were liberated and more than 20 Ukrainian troops were eliminated," the ministry reported.
"In Dobropolye in the Donetsk People’s Republic, assault groups of the 51st Army, together with marine infantry units, conducted offensive operations in the northwestern, eastern and central parts of the city. Units of the 76th Air Assault Division, advancing west of Dobropolye in the Donetsk People’s Republic, destroyed an enemy position and took control of a section of a forest belt," the ministry said.
Ukrainian troop losses

Ukrainian forces lost more than 250 personnel in the Battlegroup North area of responsibility, over 220 in operations by the Battlegroup West and more than 195 in clashes with the Battlegroup South. They lost up to 385 personnel in clashes with the Battlegroup Center, more than 240 in fighting involving the Battlegroup East and over 35 in clashes with the Battlegroup Dnepr.
Strikes, air defense
"Operational/tactical aircraft, attack unmanned aerial vehicles, missile forces and artillery of Russian battlegroups struck unmanned aerial vehicle storage sites, as well as temporary deployment points of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries in 149 areas," the ministry reported.

articles.title: US-Russia Peace Talks Eye Multibillion Lukoil Oil Deal
articles.body:
Negotiations between the US administration and Russia aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have expanded to incorporate a multibillion-dollar oil transaction that could benefit Middle Eastern business figures connected to US President Donald Trump’s primary envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
According to The New York Times, the proposed transaction, which requires formal authorization from both the US government and the Kremlin, concerns the extensive international portfolio of Lukoil, Russia’s second-largest oil producer.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The assets under discussion encompass oil extraction concessions in Cameroon and Iraq, major European refining complexes in Bulgaria and Romania, and extensive retail fuel station networks across Europe and the US, including filling stations in New Jersey.
The primary consortium seeking to finalize the acquisition includes American financier Todd Boehly – who contributed $2 million to political entities supporting President Trump – alongside two Middle Eastern investment groups that maintain prior commercial ties with Kushner or the Witkoff family, as well as an entity affiliated with the US government.
The negotiations, which have been underway for several months, were described by eight individuals familiar with the proceedings.
While the reporting noted no indications that Kushner or Witkoff would personally profit from the agreement, the transaction demonstrates the close alignment between private commercial networks and geopolitical statecraft within the administration.
Russia Threatens to Strike Defense Plants in NATO Countries
Regulatory hurdles
Russian President Vladimir Putin raised the prospective sale directly during a confidential Kremlin consultation with Witkoff and Kushner on Sept. 5, according to three individuals briefed on the meeting.
Putin reportedly proposed the transaction as a practical vehicle to demonstrate to the Russian business elite and the domestic public that normal commercial engagement with the US remains achievable.
The American negotiators responded that they would facilitate work on the transaction, viewing the commercial bridge as an instrument to cultivate constructive relations with Moscow while exerting downward pressure on international crude oil benchmarks.
For prospective buyers, US regulatory approval represents a substantial financial upside, as clearing the transaction would lift US sanctions restrictions on the assets and immediately elevate their market capitalization.
Although Lukoil operates formally as a publicly traded private enterprise, decisions governing its strategic divestments are widely treated within Moscow as resting directly with Putin. Consequently, the execution of the multi-continent transaction hinges on political determinations made by Trump and Putin.
The commercial discussions align with Trump’s public statements viewing Russia as a vast economic opportunity, which he has promoted as a framework to incentivize peace.
The initiative has also renewed scrutiny over Trump-affiliated business interests, including the cryptocurrency venture World Liberty Financial, which was co-founded by Witkoff and includes an investor who also maintains an equity stake in the proposed Lukoil buyout consortium.
