articles.title: Pete Hegseth just took his personal crusade to a new level | Arwa Mahdawi
articles.body:
Apart from money and McDonald’s, there’s nothing Donald Trump seems to love more than a “big, beautiful” wall. The government is currently spending billions of taxpayer dollars to fulfill the president’s fantasy of lining the US-Mexico border with 30ft steel bollard walls and high-tech surveillance.
What the Trump administration is apparently not so keen on is the wall of separation between church and state. While the president may hawk bibles as a side hustle, he is not exactly devout; he serves only mammon. The top levels of his government, however, are stuffed full of religious fanatics who appear hellbent on remaking the country as a Christian theocracy.
Chief among these is the defense secretary and former Fox News personality Pete Hegseth. When he isn’t screeching about “beardos, weirdos, and wimps”, the man is cosplaying as a megachurch pastor. Hegseth, who has been married three times and paid $50,000 to a woman who accused him of rape in 2017 (he denies the accusation), found God relatively recently. He joined an evangelical church in 2018 and is now busy imposing his own brand of religion on the Pentagon, framing the war on Iran as a modern crusade and instituting monthly prayer services.
Sometimes he blends Pulp Fiction with the Bible at these services; other times he prays for “overwhelming violence of action against those who deserve no mercy”. The Jesus that told people to love their enemies, it seems, is far too woke (and bearded) for Hegseth.
This week, Hegseth took his personal crusade to a whole new level, announcing a new Pentagon Office of Religious Affairs, which reports directly to him. The military he said, was putting on “the full armor of God”. The Pentagon insists that it will not “compel religious participation”, but given Hegseth’s broader efforts to imbue Christianity into the armed forces, it’s hard not to be alarmed. Americans United for Separation of Church and State, which has sued the Pentagon over its worship services, is certainly worried. “All of [Hegseth’s] actions combined with this latest announcement make clear that Hegseth is advancing a Christian Nationalist agenda in the military,” the group said in a statement.
And that agenda seems to go well beyond the military. Hegseth has close ties to Doug Wilson, an extremist pastor and self-described Christian nationalist who thinks that women should not be allowed to vote. In an interview with NPR, Wilson said he doesn’t think his full vision for turning the US into a Christian theocracy will be realized for about 250 years, but he’s taking it step by step. His main focus now is banning abortion and same-sex marriage. While he’s still not a mainstream figure, the likes of Hegseth are pushing him out of the fringes fast. The defense secretary invited Wilson to lead a worship service at the Pentagon in February and has amplified a CNN video where the pastor said women should submit to their husbands.
It’s also not just Hegseth and his extremist pastor that we have to worry about. The Missouri senator Josh Hawley proudly said in a 2024 speech that he is “advocating Christian nationalism” and has been pushing to overturn access to abortion medication in the name of these beliefs. The House speaker Mike Johnson is connected to strongly Christian nationalist views. Meanwhile, JD Vance recently appeared on an evangelical podcast where he said is doing as much of “God’s work as possible” and is OK “if that leads to the end times”, which are apparently “coming”.
I’m an atheist, but the way things are going, the end times are beginning to sound appealing. Let’s just pray it starts with the end of this administration.
The underground world of US abortion pill mules
Nineteen states and Washington DC have codified shield laws that protect health providers who prescribe and mail the abortion medications mifepristone and misoprostol to people in states with abortion bans. But these protections are under attack: in the latest attempt to curtail access to the medication, three attorneys general in anti-abortion states (Louisiana, Alabama, Arkansas) filed a lawsuit with the US supreme court challenging these laws. It’s not surprising then that some activists are bypassing the legal and medical systems and taking matters into their own hands: using volunteers to obtain abortion pills abroad and then distribute them to community support networks across the US. “It really doesn’t matter what [state and federal authorities] do legally – we will continue,” one activist told Mother Jones. They added: “There may come a time where we are one of the only, if not the only, option for the nation.”
Margot Robbie is changing her legal name after a decade of marriage
“We don’t know why she has done this, but it has nonetheless caused a stir,” writes the always hilarious Rebecca Shaw in the Guardian about Margot Robbie becoming Margot Ackerley. “We got the usual discourse of blah blah tradition, blah blah patriarchy, blah blah women’s individual choice and so on.” Instead of engaging in this discourse, Shaw has a very practical solution for how married couples should choose a surname.
Laws on intoxication and consent scrutinized after Cornell rape allegations
New York is one of 19 states that has “voluntary intoxication” laws, which some people argue effectively serve as a legal loophole protecting sexual offenders. If you as a victim were voluntarily under the influence of drugs or alcohol, you cannot claim that you were mentally incapacitated during an assault unless you can show that you were unconscious or otherwise physically helpless. After the Cornell gang-rape allegations became national news, this law is now facing increasing scrutiny. The prosecutor Matthew Van Houten has said that that the fact the Jane Doe in the case voluntarily took drugs is partly why criminal charges were never brought. Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, has criticized this aspect of the law and appointed the state attorney general Letitia James to oversee the case after she “lost faith” in Van Houten.
The horror of the Cornell rape case is how ordinary it is
“Sexual assault … reveals that law is applied selectively, according to the needs of power,” writes Moria Donegan. “Every court and every university, and every institution will say: ‘We take sexual violence extremely seriously.’ And every one will find, with uncanny consistency, reasons not to take it very seriously at all.”
Take a look at the latest Google Maps satellite images of Gaza
… and then tell me this isn’t a genocide. While it isn’t a mainstay of the news, South Lebanon is also systematically being wiped off the map by Israel.
Influencer Alix Earle says she’s never read a book
“Like, maybe Dr Seuss,” she added in a chat with Interview Mag. I had never actually heard of Earle before seeing this headline, but I have certainly heard about the US literacy crisis. No doubt Earle is exaggerating for attention, but this sort of proud anti-intellectualism is so depressing. No wonder Trump is the president.
The US is spelled wrong in a White House accord on ‘super intelligence’
The president and some top tech titans signed a voluntary accord on “super intelligence” this week to allay fears about AI. Alas, they managed to misspell the United States as “Unites States”. Is the “super intelligence” in the room with us now? Forget AI, it’s Trump’s intelligence I’m worried about.
- Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

articles.title: DPRK conducts exercise involving launch of intermediate-range strategic missiles — KCNA
articles.body:
PYONGYANG, October 3. /TASS/. The DPRK has conducted an exercise involving the launch of intermediate-range strategic missiles, Kim Yo Jong, a department director of the Central Committee of the Workers' Party of Korea, said, according to the KCNA news agency.
"At dawn today, an exercise involving the launch of intermediate-range strategic missiles toward the east coast of our country was carried out," the statement said.
According to Kim Yo Jong, officials from the General Missile Bureau reported to the head of state, who personally observed the exercise, that new technologies enable the missiles to follow at least four different flight trajectories depending on the target and mission. She also reiterated Pyongyang’s previously stated claims about the missiles’ ability to alter their trajectories at low altitudes and their use of artificial intelligence technologies.
"In other words, this effectively means that it is impossible to evade such a strike," Kim Yo Jong said. She added that when a wave-like trajectory was employed, enemy detection systems lost track of the target after the initial ascent phase.
The DPRK official also addressed assessments of the missiles’ flight range. She noted that South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff reported a range of more than 700 kilometers, while Japan’s Ministry of Defense estimated it at approximately 680 kilometers. Pyongyang views the discrepancy as evidence of the missiles’ distinctive flight characteristics and the limitations of existing surveillance systems.
Kim Yo Jong said the DPRK had observed a similar scenario four times, adding that this, in Pyongyang’s view, confirms the effectiveness of the special flight mode employed by the missiles.

articles.title: Commander of Unmanned Systems Forces Madiar: Army has hardened, time for the rear to grow up too
articles.body:
Commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Robert (Madiar) Brovdi has urged Ukrainians not to fall for illusions regarding a swift ceasefire and a long-awaited peace, emphasizing that Russia is continuing to escalate the war.
"Pull yourselves together, dear Ukrainians, it's time to turn your brains on," Brovdi wrote on Facebook on Saturday.
According to him, a "weary and frightened people" are currently being targeted with an "illusion about a quick ceasefire and dreamed-of peace" precisely at a time when Russia is raising the level of escalation and threatening other countries.
"Opinions are being shaped virtually in unison with the Valdai chatter," he stated.
Brovdi emphasized that the Russian leadership does not seek peace, but is currently exploiting opportunities to strike Ukraine's rear. "Putin is definitely not about peace. He wants blood, up to completely destroying us. And today he is using the 'jet-shahed' window of opportunity, dismantling the rear specifically, because on the front, to put it mildly, he has had few successes throughout all of 2026," the USF commander wrote.
He stressed that Ukraine must assess the situation rationally rather than relying on expectations of a quick end to the war.
At the same time, he stated that the Defense Forces are working to close the current "window of opportunity" for Russian troops.
"The enemy's current window of opportunity will be closed by the Defense Forces through countermeasures, including re-armament, which takes time. How much? Depends on a number of factors—I won't say more for now," he wrote.
According to Brovdi, the situation at the front remains difficult, but Russian troops are suffering losses. "The front is hard, the worm is pushing and will keep pushing, but it is being destroyed on an escalating scale," the commander stated.
He also urged Ukrainians in the rear to be prepared for a long war and to rely on their own strength.
"The army has hardened, so it's time for the rear to grow up too. Do not believe in illusions and miracles—let's rely on our own strength and on each other; that is the only way we will preserve our statehood and our Motherland. And the shed under a white flag offered by jackals will be burned down on the very first dark night. Adults will understand me," Brovdi emphasized.
Ahead of this, several Ukrainian politicians publicly called for ways to end the war, intensify negotiations with Russia, and find possible compromises.
In particular, MP Oleksiy Honcharenko stated that Ukraine should begin negotiating with Russia step-by-step, addressing individual issues. Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov stated that Ukraine must simultaneously strengthen its defense capabilities and seek a path to peace that will protect the country from a new attack. Head of the Parliamentary Committee on Finance, Tax, and Customs Policy Danylo Hetmantsev stated that the terms of peace should be determined by the results of combat operations and negotiations, and the final decision on them, in his view, should be made by the people in a referendum.

Russian Strike Hits Major Pharmaceutical Distributor's Warehouse Near Kyiv, Fifth Such Attack in a Month
A warehouse belonging to Venta, one of Ukraine’s largest pharmaceutical distributors, caught fire near Kyiv following a Russian strike, UNIAN reported on October 2.
The facility stored medicines from international and domestic manufacturers, including Bayer, Sanofi, Pfizer, Teva, Darnytsia, and Farmak.

The full extent of the damage and its potential impact on the national drug supply remain unknown. In September, reports surfaced regarding reduced stocks of certain medications amidst ongoing Russian attacks.

Distributors have restructured logistics, and government regulations now allow medical supplies to be dispersed across multiple storage sites rather than concentrated in single locations.
Prior to this incident, a Russian attack on September 3 damaged the Biokon logistics complex in the Boryspil district of the Kyiv region, which is considered the largest specialized pharmaceutical warehouse in the country, according to Ekonomichna Pravda.
On the night of September 8, Russian forces used two ballistic missiles to hit a Kyiv warehouse belonging to Optima-Pharm, another major distributor, which they had already destroyed in 2025.
On September 13, Russian forces struck Universal Logistic, the second-largest medicine depot in Ukraine.
The following day, September 14, an attack hit a warehouse owned by BaDM, another top pharmaceutical distributor. The strike marked the fourth attack on Ukrainian pharmaceutical storage infrastructure since the beginning of September.
Russia’s primary military target remains Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. However, since October 2025, Russian missiles and drones have been increasingly targeting Ukraine’s pharmaceutical supply chain—with warehouses coming under systematic attack.

articles.title: Iran has ‘legitimate right’ to civilian nuclear program – China
articles.body:
Iran has ‘legitimate right’ to civilian nuclear program – China
Iran has the right to pursue a peaceful nuclear program as a party to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), Beijing has said.
China’s deputy permanent representative to the UN, Sun Lei, made the statement to the General Assembly on Thursday.
“As a non-nuclear-weapon State party to the Treaty on the NPT, Iran should honor its commitment not to develop nuclear weapons, and its legitimate right to the peaceful use of nuclear energy should be respected,” Sun said in a plenary meeting on the use of the veto.
The debate followed a vote in September in which China and Russia blocked a resolution submitted by the US to extend the mandate of a UN sanctions watchdog panel on Iran sanctions.
The monitoring body was reinstated as part of the ‘snapback’ mechanism invoked in August by the UK, France, and Germany (the E3), aimed at reimposing sanctions. China and Russia consider the snapback legally invalid and maintain that the sanctions were not restored.
According to Sun, China used its veto to “uphold a correct understanding of right and wrong,” support a political settlement of the Iranian nuclear issue, address non-proliferation concerns, and promote long-term peace and stability in the Middle East.
The stalemate over Iran’s nuclear program stems from Washington’s unilateral withdrawal from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), and subsequent failures by the E3 to exhaust diplomatic options under the plan before invoking the snapback, the diplomat said.
Under the 2015 agreement, Iran agreed to curtail its enrichment activities in exchange for sanctions relief. President Donald Trump pulled the US out of the agreement in 2018 during his first term and reimposed sanctions on Iran.
In February, the US and Israel attacked Iran in what Trump described as an effort to prevent the country from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
Russia condemned the attack and maintains that Iran’s nuclear program is peaceful.
President Vladimir Putin, speaking at the annual Valdai forum on Thursday, said a Russian proposal to transfer Iran’s enriched uranium to Russia remains on the table. The US initially agreed to this but later toughened its position and refused, he said.
“If all the participants in this process ultimately conclude that this would help defuse tensions in any way, we are ready to engage in that work,” Putin stated.

articles.title: Russia strikes key Kiev bridge (VIDEOS)
articles.body:
Russia strikes key Kiev bridge (VIDEOS)
The Russian military has struck Kiev’s Northern Bridge over the Dnieper River to undermine Ukraine’s military logistics, the Defense Ministry said.
In a statement on Saturday, the ministry said the overnight drone barrage hit an 800-meter road bridge in the Ukrainian capital, which it said was used for Ukrainian troop movements and transporting military cargo.
Officials also said drones struck the Gostomel logistics center in Kiev Region where military supplies are stored. Another attack hit a dry-cargo vessel carrying dual-use equipment as it sailed through the northwestern Black Sea toward Odessa, the statement added.
Kiev Mayor Vitaly Klitschko confirmed that the Northern Bridge was hit, adding that the road surface and trolleybus contact network were damaged and that traffic was suspended. Videos shared by Ukrainian media show major traffic jams in one of the capital’s districts.
There are eight major road and rail bridges connecting the eastern and western parts of Kiev. Earlier this week, Russia targeted the Pivdennyi (southern) Bridge, saying it was “facilitating troop movements and the logistical delivery of military cargo for the Ukrainian military units in Donbass.”
A local official told Strana.ua that the bridge carries up to 90% of transit road traffic between Ukraine’s left- and right-bank regions and also handles a significant share of military shipments.
Following the strikes, Ukrainian MP Vladimir Kreidenko said lawmakers are considering ferries and temporary pontoon crossings if serious damage to the bridges leads to prolonged traffic disruptions.
Russia has intensified strikes on military-related logistics and defense industrial base in recent weeks in response to Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s 40-day PR ‘pressure campaign’, which included long-range strikes targeting oil refineries and civilian infrastructure deep inside Russia.

articles.title: Ukraine to step up strikes on Russian oil refineries in response to Putin's 'new doctrine' – Zelensky
articles.body:
Ukraine to step up strikes on Russian oil refineries in response to Putin's 'new doctrine' – Zelensky
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said this in an interview with Reuters, Ukrinform reports.
According to Zelensky, Ukrainian intelligence has obtained documents showing that Russian leader Vladimir Putin had issued a "new doctrine" of military attacks on a much broader range of civilian targets ahead of this winter.
"We saw documents and we know that they allow them attack infrastructure ... logistics ... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities. This is the goal of the operation," he said.
Driving the shift in policy, Zelensky said, was Putin's desire to appear strong at a time when his military was losing ground in a key frontline region and sustaining higher levels of casualties.
Over the past week, the Ukrainian capital has come under persistent attack by Russian drones and missiles targeting energy and telecoms assets, road and rail infrastructure. For the first time, Russia has targeted the bridges across the Dnipro river connecting east and west Kyiv.
The president stressed that Ukraine would respond to the change in tactics by Moscow, but would not respond in kind by targeting civilian infrastructure indiscriminately.
"We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners: what gives money to them for this war. But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects," Zelensky said.
Reuters reported that the Kremlin was not available to comment on Saturday. But in a statement urging foreign nationals to leave Kyiv, the Russian Foreign Ministry said Moscow would continue to systematically hit targets in what it said were retaliatory strikes for Ukrainian attacks on Russia in recent months.
After the Trump administration invited Putin to attend a G20 summit in Miami in December and discussed business deals with Russian envoys, Zelensky urged Washington not to normalize relations with Russia before ensuring a return to peace.
He said he would be happy to meet Putin for peace talks at the G20, but he warned the U.S. not to believe in "illusions" that Russia would end hostilities if it gained control of Donbas.

Kyiv • UNN

Agents of the "ATESH" partisan movement conducted reconnaissance of the Russian Armed Forces Air Defense Military Academy in Smolensk, where specialists for Russian air defense systems are trained. articles.title: A Nobel laureate’s deal: free Russia’s prisoners, fund the missiles hitting Ukraine
articles.body:
Dmitry Muratov, the Nobel Peace Prize laureate and co-founder of Russia's shuttered Novaya Gazeta, has lent his name to an idea that sounds like pure humanitarianism. Russia frees some of the people it jails for opposing the war; in return, the United States eases its sanctions on the Russian economy.
The scheme did not even start in an American office. According to The Atlantic, which reported the plan on 29 September, it was Muratov himself who urged Donald Trump's envoy, John Coale, to try it. Coale had used the same model on Belarus, where some 500 prisoners were released, sanctions softened, and trade talks reopened.
Now, with Trump's approval, he wants to run it on the Kremlin.
“A direct investment in ammunition flying across the border”: Belarusian defectors warn US sanctions relief is funding Russia’s war
The prisoners should go free. There is nothing to argue about there. No one jailed for anti-war words, for journalism, or for political dissent belongs in a cell. But here is the small detail: the price for their freedom is easing the pressure on a state that is waging war, not on the United States, which is being asked to ease the sanctions, but on Ukraine.
And here is where the real humanitarian arithmetic begins. We do not yet know which sanctions would be lifted. Whichever they are, the logic is the same: Moscow lets some of its political prisoners go, and Washington gives the Russian economy some breathing room in return. People walk out of Russian prisons, and the Kremlin gets more oxygen.
More money for the Russian state in wartime is not merely a figure in a bank report. It is more resources for the army, for missiles, for drones, for the war's continuation. And Ukrainians are the ones who feel it.
I can picture the Kremlin ghoul rubbing his hands at an idea like this. Now he can be not just president, but the director of a prisoner market: release a hundred today, jail three hundred tomorrow, so there is something to trade next time. New dissidents, journalists, activists, and merely inconvenient citizens he can pack away far faster than the West can lift a sanction.
A tidy little business model: Russia produces the prisoners, the West buys them back with its policy, and Ukraine settles the account.
Because if easing sanctions widens Russia's room to finance the war, then Ukrainians effectively get a very strange bill for someone else's humanism: a Russian political prisoner walks out of prison, and a Ukrainian gets a fresh portion of missiles and drones on their head.
By the way, about those Ukrainian civilians. By the estimates of international and Ukrainian rights groups, Russia is holding, or has held, some 16,000 of them illegally. The real figure may be higher, since not every case can be documented.
This is exactly where Muratov, as a Nobel peace laureate, might find his powers of persuasion useful. Why not put in a word for the Ukrainians in Russian prisons? The same people seized in occupied territory during "filtration," taken from their homes, buried under fabricated cases, held for years without a proper trial.
And among them are children.
And here onto the stage steps Russia's Baba Yaga of "child protection": Maria Lvova-Belova, the so-called presidential commissioner for children's rights. She herself told Putin, in public, about a boy from Mariupol she had taken into her care after he was removed from the occupied city. Ukraine and international organizations view such cases as part of a wider system of unlawful transfers of Ukrainian children to Russia. The International Criminal Court has issued a warrant for her arrest on exactly those charges: the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children.
That is what Russian care for children looks like: take a Ukrainian child from Mariupol, carry him off to Russia, and set about turning him into a Russian. If this is how Russia's children's commissioner works in public, it is frightening to imagine what happens where there are no cameras and no international warrants.
Nobody is offering to lift a single sanction for them.
And Muratov's pacifist initiatives are not new, either. After the full-scale invasion, he was among the authors and promoters of the ceasefire appeals. One public statement, signed by 51 Nobel laureates, called for an end to the fighting, which Muratov later described as a plea for a "genuine ceasefire" before talks.
On paper it all looks wonderful: stop shooting, stop killing one another, make peace. But there is one small problem. Russia did not wander into this war alongside Ukraine. Russia launched the full-scale invasion itself.
And in these appeals, Muratov did not demand that the Kremlin withdraw its troops from Ukraine. He did not demand the de-occupation of Ukrainian territory. He did not put the question of responsibility for the aggression and the war crimes to Russia. The formula was far more convenient: just stop shooting.
But "stop killing each other" is a beautiful phrase for people who would rather not notice who attacked whom.
It turns aggressor and victim into two symmetrical sides, as though Ukraine and Russia had simply quarreled and now both must show wisdom and stop firing. There is just one nuance: if, after such a "peace," the Russian army remains on occupied Ukrainian territory, that is not an end to the aggression. It is a pause with a Russian flag on Ukrainian soil.
Now add the prisoner proposal on top. Russia does not withdraw its troops. Ukraine does not get its occupied territory back. The Kremlin answers for nothing. But a few Russian political prisoners are released, and for that, Russia's sanctions are eased too. And Ukraine, meanwhile, is simply supposed to stand to one side and rejoice that humanism has triumphed.
Except there is a difference of principle. A Russian political prisoner can walk out of a Russian prison. A Ukrainian civilian can stay in one. And a Ukrainian soldier can be killed by a weapon Russia bought thanks to that same sanctions relief.
And then a very simple question arises for the great humanist and Nobel laureate: why should the freedom of Russia's political prisoners be bought at the expense of the freedom, the safety, and the lives of Ukrainians?

articles.title: Tory conference 2026: What POLITICO reporters are watching for
articles.body:
BIRMINGHAM, England — Britain’s largest opposition party wants to show it’s still on the electoral pitch during an annual gathering that kicks off Sunday.
Despite Conservative Leader Kemi Badenoch consolidating her position and seeing improved personal ratings, the party is still far from its government heyday, and faces an ongoing challenge on the right from Nigel Farage’s populist Reform UK.
Here’s what POLITICO’s team of reporters will be watching for as the Conservatives gather in Birmingham.
Advertisement
U.K. Political Editor Dan Bloom
My biggest question for Badenoch’s speech at 11 a.m. Wednesday will be: can she end Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s honeymoon?
Since July, Labour has jumped to 26% in the polls while the Tories lag behind Reform on 19%. There will simply be fewer lobbyists and hangers-on than at Labour’s jamboree.
Badenoch will spend this week arguing that Burnham, with his crusade against “40 years of neoliberalism,” has ushered in the kind of classic left-right ideological fight that she relishes. Expect her to bang on about cutting welfare to fund defense — two weak points for Labour. And the self-described “badass Kemi” plans to be more abrasive than Burnham, who went out of his way not to attack anyone in his speech.
I reckon two things will decide if she can cut through: her personal brand, and how far she can differentiate the Tories from Labour and Reform (plus, well, her own party from 2024). She will try to paint the Tories as the party of fiscal responsibility but that’s a crowded marketplace. It’s worked for the Conservatives in the past but we aren’t in two-party politics anymore — though admittedly, the five-party split has become less dramatic since the summer.
There will be economic policy announcements but perhaps not on the scale of last year’s pledge to scrap stamp duty. Badenoch has talked about getting rid of inheritance tax but aides appear to be suggesting an announcement isn’t ready.
I can’t wait to see the peacocking by would-be candidates for a general election. Tory aides are shouting from the hills that they are on a “war footing” and candidate selection is ramping up. Some of the high-profile Tories who were rejected for being too centrist are swerving this year’s conference, but former West Midlands Mayor Andy Street will be prominent on the fringe. Critics complain that Badenoch has bulldozed the transepts off her party’s ideological church.
Advertisement
And, of course, I’d ask questions about a coalition. There is no love lost between the Tories and Reform but all recent polls suggest they would have to team up to have any chance of running a government. Will she pull any punches against Farage … or Restore Britain chief Rupert Lowe, whose vote-splitting might help her in the end?
Senior Foreign and Defense Correspondent Esther Webber
I’ll be really interested to see how the party is positioning itself against what we know so far about Ed Miliband’s agenda as foreign secretary — so whether there’s any dissent over new sanctions introduced by Labour on Israeli E1 settlements.
Miliband has just begun to signal a potentially more conciliatory approach to China as an alternative locus of power and investment versus the U.S., so I’ll be looking at whether the Conservatives think this is a weak point where they can redouble attacks on Labour.
There’s also the question of artificial intelligence regulation and which camp the Tories are situating themselves in. Will they agree with the government on the need for a globally coordinated effort, or back U.S. President Donald Trump’s zero-regulation stance?
Finally, here’s a side plot: Are there any signs that former Home Secretary Priti Patel, traditionally a conference fan favorite, is actually doing anything in her new role in coordinating cooperation between the Tories and other parties internationally?
London Influence Reporter John Johnston
With little detail so far about Burnham’s plans for business, and many corporate execs pondering if Farage’s Reform has hit its peak, this Tory conference will be a vital opportunity for the party to try and show it is building back towards being a credible alternative.
Advertisement
Since the 2024 general election, many businesses and lobbying firms have sent only a skeleton staff to Tory conference. But I’ve heard that extra corporate passes and tickets to the standalone Business Day have been snapped up in the last few months. So, attendance may be healthier — even if most still won’t be splashing out on panel events or exhibition stands.
Business leaders remain skeptical about the prospect of an early general election. But as the official opposition, the Conservatives have the potential to help industry shine a spotlight on concerns and push issues up the political agenda if one comes. At last year’s conference, many public affairs pros felt the Tories lacked the ideas, unity and leadership to do that. My focus this year will be figuring out if that assessment has shifted.
Energy Reporter Abby Wallace
The Conservatives have come a long way from the party that, in government, enshrined net-zero targets in law. Badenoch has been clear about the direction she wants to take the party in: ditching legally-binding climate targets and drilling for more oil and gas in the North Sea.
The party’s leader has even suggested that former colleagues who still support the target will not be welcome back on the Tory benches. I’ll be looking out for whether that U-turn at the top has fully filtered through the party.
While energy bills have surged on the back of war in Iran, the party has been pressing Labour ministers to prioritize cutting costs in the system. For the Conservatives, that means ditching some support for renewables and a bigger role for gas and nuclear in the future. I’ll be keeping an ear on whether there is any pressure from the opposition for ministers to intervene ahead of what will be a difficult winter of price rises too.
The future of the North Sea, including looming decisions on Rosebank and Jackdaw, will no doubt spring up on the fringes — especially after the Conservatives clinched the Aberdeen South by-election following a campaign focused on oil and gas drilling.
Advertisement
Financial Services Reporter Eleanor Myers
Andrew Griffith will be stepping up this party conference, having been promoted to shadow chancellor earlier this year to replace his more mild-mannered colleague Mel Stride.
Griffith was a bigwig in business before he entered parliament, and as a former City minister, I’ll be watching whether he focuses his ire on the prospect of Labour raising bank taxes in the budget, which is now less than a month away.
Griffith will make his big speech on how to get Britain growing again at 2 p.m. Monday. Growth was the favored buzzword of former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, and has been heartily adopted by her successor John Healey, although how to achieve it remains a challenge amid soaring debt and rising interest rates. I’m interested to see whether the Conservatives propose a solution.
Senior Technology Reporter Frank Hersey
This conference is a chance for Badenoch’s team to establish any sort of differentiation between Tory tech policy and that of the other parties. This has been getting harder as parties’ approaches have coalesced. Labour committed to a pro-growth agenda for AI under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer with planned regulatory reforms to match. Tory plans for a social media ban for under-16s were eventually (and reluctantly) grasped by Labour. The Tories were further hemmed in by Reform banking the low-tax, low-regulation space.
I’ll be looking to see if the party can get ahead in any policy areas or if it has to pick new ones to do so. Among all the parties, there’s perhaps most interest in what the Conservatives say on tech — as their policy ideas in this space are feeling overdue.
Senior Trade Reporter Sophie Inge
The fightback against Burnham’s pledge to explore closer ties with the EU is expected to continue in Birmingham, after Badenoch warned that Britain shouldn’t be “having arguments which started 10 years ago.”
Deputy Leader Alex Burghart has already pledged to “reverse” the Brexit reset, warning that plans for an agrifood deal with the bloc risk undermining the U.K.’s trading relationship with the U.S., among other countries.

articles.title: Poroshenko calls on EU to speed up conversion of defense funding into military contracts
articles.body:
Ukrainian MP and leader of the European Solidarity party Petro Poroshenko, during a meeting in Brussels with EU Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubilius, discussed deepening defense cooperation between Ukraine and the European Union and called for faster financing and implementation of joint defense projects.
"Russia's tactic of massive use of jet-powered drones requires a rapid search for effective and cost-efficient means of interception and countermeasures, including modern detection systems, electronic warfare capabilities and counter-drone solutions. Particular attention was paid to new technologies, joint Ukrainian-European developments and their rapid scaling, including through the full use of the potential of the Ukraine-EU Drone Alliance," Poroshenko wrote on Facebook following the meeting.
According to him, the parties also discussed EU financing for Ukraine's defense sector and the timely coverage of expenditures on the procurement of drones, missiles, ammunition and air defense systems.
"My main message to our partners is that European funding must be converted into military contracts as quickly as possible, contracts into production - preferably joint production - and production into real capabilities on the battlefield," Poroshenko emphasized.
Separately, he called for the swift integration of Ukraine's defense-industrial complex into the European defense architecture, noting that this is in the interests of both Ukraine and the security of the European continent.

articles.title: Russians launch massive Shahed, Iskander strike on Mykolaiv, injuring 3, 2 in critical condition – official
articles.body:
Russian occupation forces carried out a massive attack on Mykolaiv over the past day using an Iskander-M ballistic missile and Shahed-type strike drones, injuring three civilians and damaging port and civil infrastructure, Mykolaiv Regional Military Administration Head Heorhii Reshetilov reported on his Telegram channel.
"As a result, three men aged 21, 47, and 62 were injured. As of this morning, two of the victims are in the hospital in critical condition, while another is continuing treatment outpatiently," the Regional Military Administration head reported regarding the situation as of 07:00.
According to the administration, the strikes caused destruction to port and municipal infrastructure facilities: an administrative building, production and warehouse premises, a hotel and restaurant complex, an office building, a car service station (service center), a private house, cars, and windows were blown out in apartments of an apartment building.

articles.title: Russia attacked Ukraine with 157 drones - how many destroyed and what is known about the strikes

Russia attacked Ukraine with 157 drones - how many destroyed and what is known about the strikes
Kyiv • UNN
Overnight, Russia launched 157 drones at Ukraine; air defense forces destroyed or suppressed 131 of them. Strikes were recorded at 12 locations.
Russia struck Ukraine with 157 drones during the night of October 3. Of these, 131 were shot down or suppressed. UNN reports this, citing data from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
What Russia used to strike and where the attack came from
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of October 3 (from 18:00 on October 2), the enemy attacked with 157 Shahed-type attack UAVs (45 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parodiya-type decoy drones from the following directions: Bryansk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk — Russia, the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk, and the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea — Hvardiiske.
How the air defense forces responded
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 09:00, air defense forces had shot down/suppressed 131 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, and drones of other types
What is known about the strikes
Hits by the enemy’s air attack assets were recorded at 12 locations, while downed targets (debris) fell at 5 locations.
"In addition, in the morning, the enemy attacked the Odesa region with loitering munitions of the Bandероль type. The consequences of the attack are being clarified," the statement said.
The attack is ongoing; several enemy UAVs are in the airspace.

"Russia's war is dangerously reaching Moldova"
I condemn Russia's attack on Ukraine this morning. Its war is dangerously reaching Moldova

articles.title: Italy’s Ustica enigma: Can French files solve mystery crash blamed on stray missile?
articles.body:
Italy’s Ustica enigma: Can French files solve mystery crash blamed on stray missile?
France’s decision to share defence documents with the Italian judiciary has raised hopes of a breakthrough in investigations into the 1980 crash of a passenger jet near the island of Ustica, which a former Italian president claimed was mistakenly shot down by a French fighter jet. Sceptics caution that the files are unlikely to shed light on one of Italy’s most enduring mysteries, let alone reveal a culprit.
A rocky outpost of Italy in the Tyrrhenian Sea, the island of Ustica owes its name to the smouldering volcanic lava that gave its striking rock formations their dark hue.
For many Italians, however, the picturesque island is synonymous with a notorious plane crash that claimed 81 lives, and the intricate cover-up that buried its causes in a thick fog of lies, decoys and mysterious deaths.
The fate of Itavia Flight 870, which plunged into waters off Ustica on June 27, 1980, remains a subject of fierce debate after countless expert reports and judicial enquiries spanning several decades. The most widely accepted theory suggests the plane was caught up in an aerial dogfight and mistakenly shot down by a fighter jet, which a former Italian president has claimed was French.
News this week that French authorities would hand over defence documents to Italian investigators has been greeted as a potential gamechanger in Italy, where prosecutors and plaintiffs have long accused France and other Western allies of withholding evidence.
The 11th-hour twist led prosecutors on Wednesday to abort plans to shelve the latest investigation into the crash, throwing a lifeline to families of the victims who have relentlessly lobbied Italian governments and the judiciary to pursue the case.
Cover-up
The DC-9 plane operated by the now-defunct Itavia carrier was in the final stretch of its journey from Bologna to Palermo on a clear summer evening when it suddenly broke up and crashed into the sea, killing all 77 passengers and 4 crew members, all of them Italian.
The incident is known in Italy as the strage di Ustica, a term commonly used to refer to the deadly terrorist attacks that rattled the country in those years, many of which also remain shrouded in mystery.
Watch moreVictims of Italy’s deadly ‘Years of Lead’ demand justice
“At first, it was labelled an ‘accident’ or a ‘tragedy’. But as efforts to cover up the incident became apparent over time, people started calling it a ‘strage’ (massacre),” said historian Cora Ranci, who has written a book about the Ustica affair and the many smokescreens she says have hampered investigations.
Like other unsolved civilian massacres, she added, the Ustica affair “has contributed to the erosion of trust between citizens and institutions in Italy, fuelling the sense that those in power are bound by a code of silence and that their actions are shrouded in secrecy”.
Following the crash, officials hastily concluded that it had been caused by mechanical failure, precipitating the demise of the already struggling carrier Itavia. Judicial inquiries resumed only years later under pressure from victims’ families, spurred by an investigative journalist convinced that the plane had been shot down.
Progress was slow, hampered by the fact that tracking data and radar scans had been wiped clean at all but one of the various Italian bases within range of the incident, leaving investigators with little hard evidence to work on. Four air force generals were eventually tried on charges of treason and withholding evidence, though none were convicted.
The untimely deaths of at least 15 military personnel and others connected to the case – through transport accidents, shootings, stabbings and suicides by hanging – furthered muddied the waters, compounding the sense of a conspiracy to hide the truth.
In 2013, Italy’s highest court ruled that the plane had been brought down in an aerial battle, either by a missile or through a near-collision, without identifying a culprit. It ordered the state to compensate families of the victims, adding that cover-ups in the investigations were considered “definitively ascertained”. The ruling was in line with the conclusions of an earlier, decade-long inquiry, which determined that the intended target of the operation was a smaller aircraft travelling in the DC-9’s slipstream to evade radar detection.
“We’ve known for years that the passenger plane was downed in a combat operation,” said former senator Daria Bonfietti, the head of the association of families of the victims that lobbied the authorities to recover the wreckage and reopen investigations decades ago. But, she added, “we still don’t know who did it.”
The Libya link
Despite the court rulings, some remain deeply sceptical of the missile scenario, leaning instead towards the theory of a bomb exploding on board the plane. They point to the numerous terrorist attacks that shook the country in those years, including the strage di Bologna, a train station bombing that killed 85 people and injured score more just weeks after the Ustica crash.
Potential culprits cited by proponents of the bomb theory – which has never been upheld in court – include far-right activists, Palestinian militant groups and Muammar Gaddafi’s Libya.
The late Libyan strongman is also at the heart of the missile hypothesis, which gained further traction in 2007 when former Italian president Francesco Cossiga claimed that the passenger jet had been shot down by French military planes who were after Gaddafi.
Cossiga, who was prime minister in June 1980, cited Italian intelligence but offered no evidence to back up the allegation. He claimed Italian sources had tipped off Gaddafi, ensuring that he was not on board the smaller plane allegedly tailing the Itavia flight.
Proponents of the Libyan link say it is substantiated by the recovery, three weeks after the Ustica disaster, of the wreckage of a Libyan MiG fighter on a mountain in Calabria, which may have been chased and downed on the same night as the DC-9.
“We know from declassified documents that Italy at the time was covertly allowing Libyan aircraft to fly though its airspace to Yugoslavia for purposes of training and maintenance,” said Ranci, adding that it was common practice for those jets to evade detection by tailing commercial flights. On top of creating dangers for civilian planes, this tacit agreement infuriated the Americans and even more so the French, who were fighting a proxy war with Gaddafi’s Libya in Chad.
The Ustica crash came months after France’s embassy in Tripoli was ransacked and after a botched Libyan attempt to shoot down a French surveillance aircraft over the Mediterranean, which sent tensions spiralling.
Bonfietti, whose elder brother was on board the Itavia flight, said successive judicial inquiries had established that multiple military aircraft were operating over the Tyrrhenian on the day of the crash, including US, French and other NATO aircraft. “Now we need those countries to tell us what they were up to and why they kept quiet about it,” she said.
Watch moreGladio: NATO’s secret cold war operation in Italy
“If Gaddafi was indeed their target, it’s obvious that whoever carried out the operation could not openly claim it – not in a Cold War context,” Bonfietti added. “Instead, they decided to cover up what happened and pretend the plane experienced a mechanical failure.”
Locating the Foch
Allegations of French involvement resurfaced in 2023 when former Italian prime minister Giuliano Amato urged France to come clean on the mysterious plane crash, asking President Emmanuel Macron to look into the matter.
“If he shows that the allegation is unfounded, so much the better. If it is true, he should apologise,” Amato, who served as deputy PM at the time of the incident, told a news conference, suggesting it would be easier for someone Macron’s age to overcome old taboos.
Bonfietti said she had personally asked Italy’s current Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni to raise the issue with Macron when they met for a summit in June. According to Italian media reports, it was those talks that helped pave the way for the release of French documents.
The former senator said she hoped the new files would help expose what she described as France’s “past lies”, including about the whereabouts of a French aircraft carrier that Cossiga claimed was involved in the Ustica incident. Italian prosecutors say testimony from witnesses contradicts French claims that the Foch carrier was docked at Navy headquarters in Toulon on June 27 and that the Solenzara base in Corsica had closed and ceased all radar recordings hours before the Ustica crash.
“If the Foch was instead in the Tyrrhenian, as witness accounts suggest, it would have been in a position to detect and record what happened,” said Ranci, adding that the same applied to a US Navy carrier stationed in the Tyrrhenian – which US officials claimed had switched its radar off that night – and an AWACS mobile radar station believed to have been flying overhead.
Contacted by FRANCE 24, France’s defence ministry said it had “always responded to requests from the Italian judicial authorities” in connection with the case. It said it “recently confirmed (to Italian authorities) that a batch of documents could be used in legal proceedings”, adding that these documents “had been brought to the attention of the Italian authorities several years ago”.
The ministry did not say whether classified documents previously withheld would this time be handed over.
Analysts have voiced scepticism that the French documents would lead to any breakthrough, stressing that the decision to make them available to Italian prosecutors in no way constitutes an admission of guilt. According to Professor Gregory Alegi, a professor at LUISS University in Rome and a prominent critic of the missile hypothesis, France’s willingness to share more information “suggests they know they have nothing to fear”.
Some families of victims have expressed hopes that French cooperation might open new lines of investigation, urging prosecutors to also pursue the terrorism lead. All agree the French move will at least ensure the inquiry is not shelved.
“It’s quite possible the French sent us nothing new – their shopping list or something – but the important thing is they sent us documents and so investigations go on,” said Bonfietti. “We owe it to our loved ones to keep fighting for the truth.”

articles.title: Russia turns helicopter missile into truck-mounted weapon
articles.body:
- Russia fired its new truck-mounted Izdeliye 347 launcher with a modified LMUR missile at mock artillery positions during the Tsentr-2026 exercise.
- The Defense Ministry says the system can hit stationary and moving targets up to 20 km away, with operator guidance in the final phase.
Russia has fired a guided missile from its attack helicopters off a truck, using a new ground launcher called Izdeliye 347, or “Product 347,” against mock artillery positions during its Tsentr-2026 exercise.
The Russian Defense Ministry said on Oct. 2 that the system carries a modified version of the LMUR light multipurpose guided missile and can hit stationary and moving targets up to 20 km (12 miles) away. During the main stage of the drills at the Chebarkul training range in the Chelyabinsk region, crews used it to strike artillery positions that had been found by aerial reconnaissance.
The ministry said the launcher is mounted on a truck and that an operator can steer the missile onto the target in the final part of its flight. It did not say how many missiles each launcher carries, what chassis it uses, who builds it, or when it could enter service.
The LMUR, also known as Izdeliye 305 and the Kh-39, is built by the KBM design bureau in Kolomna, part of Rostec’s High Precision Systems holding. It weighs about 105 kg (231 pounds) and carries a 25 kg (55-pound) high-explosive fragmentation warhead. The basic version has a stated range of 14.5 km, and a longer-range variant reportedly reaches beyond 25 km.
Russia fields the missile on its Mi-28NM and Ka-52M attack helicopters and has used it widely against Ukrainian forces. Its main advantage is that it does not need to see the target at launch. The missile flies toward given coordinates using satellite navigation, then sends video from its thermal seeker back to the operator, who picks out the target and guides it in. That lets helicopter crews fire from well behind the front, out of range of most Ukrainian short-range air defenses.
A ground version would give Russian units the same kind of long-range, man-in-the-loop strike capability without risking a helicopter. The concept is similar to Israel’s Spike NLOS, which is fired from helicopters, vehicles and ships.
Russia has tried this before. Several years ago, the Defense Ministry worked on a project codenamed Baikal to adapt the LMUR for ground launch. That design used an armored tracked vehicle, similar in concept to the Khrizantema-S anti-tank system, and was also meant to engage slow, low-flying aerial targets. Its fate was never made public.
Izdeliye 347 takes a different approach, putting the missile on an unarmored truck instead of a tracked combat vehicle.
The launcher was one of several new or rarely seen systems Russia showed at Tsentr-2026, which ran from Sept. 28 to Oct. 3 and involved more than 47,000 troops, according to the Defense Ministry.

articles.title: North Korea launches ballistic missile after Seoul demands apology over wounded soldiers
articles.body:
North Korea fired a ballistic missile towards the sea on Saturday, South Korea and Japan said, a day after it rejected Seoul’s accusation of its mines wounding soldiers.
The missile was launched from the Wonsan area at about 6.30am towards the East Sea – also known as the Sea of Japan – and flew more than 700km (434 miles), the South Korean military said. Seoul and Washington were analysing the test for details, it added.
Japan’s coast guard, citing the defence ministry, said the object may have been a ballistic missile and appeared to have come down, warning ships to take precautions.
South Korea’s military said it heightened its monitoring of any further missile tests and would share intelligence with the US and Japan. The South Korean presidential office’s national security council convened an emergency meeting on Saturday to assess the situation.
Pyongyang’s Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of ruler Kim Jong-un, issued a statement on Friday that dismissed Seoul’s demand for an apology for what it said were North Korean mines that seriously wounded South Korean soldiers in the demilitarised zone – the heavily guarded buffer between the two Koreas.
South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, had urged Pyongyang on Thursday to return to dialogue, despite his military demanding an apology a day earlier. Kim Yo-jong responded by calling Seoul “really despicable” and ridiculing Lee’s latest overture, calling it “the climax of the farce that everyone should watch”.
Kim also warned that Pyongyang was “ready for anything” Seoul might do over the mine blast – remarks followed the next morning by North Korea’s ballistic missile launch.
South Korea said this week that North Korean mines caused the blast that injured three South Korean soldiers on a reconnaissance mission inside the 4km-wide buffer zone that stretches across the Korean peninsula.
The missile test might be an attempt by Pyongyang to draw a response from South Korea to the sister’s statement, said Cheong Seong-chang, vice-president at the Sejong Institute in Seoul, a research centre on North Korean affairs. North Korea might also have tested a new type of missile, he added.
North Korea has launched missile tests on more than 10 occasions so far this year. Some came after North Korea protested against joint military drills between Seoul and Washington.
North Korea has ramped up hostility against the South in recent years, disavowing unification as a national goal and calling South Korea its “primary foe”.
With Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Russia Orders Surge in European Hybrid Attacks
articles.body:
Russia has ordered its intelligence services to “step up” hybrid operations across EU and NATO countries, including possible sabotage targeting military facilities, critical infrastructure and communications systems, Ukraine’s military intelligence agency has warned.
The Military Intelligence of Ukraine (HUR) said Moscow planned to use agents recruited across Europe by Russia’s GRU military intelligence service and FSB security service to carry out the operations.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The intelligence services of aggressor state Russia have been instructed to step up their activities in EU and NATO countries,” HUR said in a statement on Friday.
It said the operations were aimed at undermining support for Ukraine and weakening NATO’s capabilities.
“Military facilities, critical infrastructure and communications systems are among the targets being monitored by Russian intelligence services,” the agency said.
“Potential targets include Starlink satellite internet receiving stations located in European countries,” it added.
HUR said it had warned Ukraine’s international partners about Russia’s plans.
Starlink facility targeted in Poland
The warning comes just over a week after a fire at a Starlink satellite communications ground station in Wola Krobowska, a village in central Poland, which Polish authorities are investigating as suspected Russian-linked sabotage.
No EU Membership for Ukraine on Jan. 1, 2027, Brussels Admits
Prosecutors say the fire was deliberately set, allegedly to disrupt Starlink internet traffic and communications in Poland and other countries in Central and Eastern Europe. No one has yet been charged in the investigation.
Starlink, a satellite internet system operated by billionaire Elon Musk’s US aerospace company SpaceX, has become a key part of Ukraine’s war effort, providing internet connectivity for frontline communications, drone operations and battlefield command.
Sabotage fears grow
The EU, the majority of whose member states also belong to the Western military alliance NATO, has been on heightened alert for acts of sabotage and other hybrid attacks since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of neighboring Ukraine in 2022.
Concerns have grown amid a recent uptick in such incidents. Last month, Berlin said Russia was behind a foiled drone attack targeting Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany, a key logistics hub for NATO and Kyiv.
Moscow has repeatedly denied involvement in hybrid operations against European countries.
