articles.title: Russia shows Shturm robotic tank system in big exercise
articles.body:
- Russia used uncrewed T-72B3M-based tanks from its Shturm robotic assault system to support assault troops during the Tsentr-2026 exercise.
- The tanks are remotely controlled from a separate crewed vehicle on a tank chassis, with a reported control range of about 3 km.
Russia has used uncrewed tanks from its Shturm heavy robotic assault system in combat drills for the first time, sending remotely controlled T-72-based vehicles to support assault troops during its Tsentr-2026 strategic exercise.
Russian President Vladimir Putin was shown the vehicles at the Chebarkul training range in the Chelyabinsk region, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Oct. 2. The ministry said the machines are built on the T-72B3M tank chassis and have uncrewed fighting compartments, in two versions: one with a tank-type turret and one armed like a BMPT tank support vehicle. During the main stage of the drills, they provided fire support to assault units.
The Shturm system pairs remotely controlled combat vehicles with a crewed control vehicle, all built on T-72 or T-90 tank chassis. The combat vehicles can still be driven by a crew on board if needed. The most visible feature of the main version is a shortened 125 mm gun, designed so the turret can swing freely between buildings in urban fighting. It also carries a bulldozer blade, all-around armor against shoulder-fired anti-tank weapons, and launchers for rocket flamethrowers or other weapons on the turret. A version with a 152 mm gun is reported to be in development.
During the drills, operators controlled the armored group from a safe distance using joysticks, FPV headsets and tablets over a multichannel, jam-resistant link, the Rostec weapons project “Russian Weapons” told Rossiyskaya Gazeta. Russian outlet ANNA News reported that each vehicle was driven by three operators working as commander, gunner and driver, seated in the separate control vehicle.
That control setup is one of the system’s main limitations. The robotic tanks cannot operate on their own. They depend on a dedicated crewed control vehicle, essentially a second tank chassis without a turret, which has to stay close enough to keep the radio link. Earlier Russian reports put the control radius at about 3 km (1.9 miles), meaning the crew still has to work near the fight in an armored vehicle of its own.
The Defense Ministry has not published any data on how the link performs under heavy electronic warfare, the main threat to remote-controlled systems on the battlefield in Ukraine, where both sides jam drones and ground robots daily.
Uralvagonzavod began work on Shturm under a Russian Defense Ministry order around 2018. The first images of a test vehicle appeared in July 2025 at the company’s plant in Nizhny Tagil, with a crew on board. At the time, The National Interest questioned whether the remote control and autonomy features were ready.
The Tsentr-2026 exercise, which ran from Sept. 28 to Oct. 3 and involved more than 47,000 troops, also featured T-14 Armata tanks, the Zarya laser air defense system and other robotic vehicles, according to the Defense Ministry.

articles.title: Iran army says prepared to face any scenario
articles.body:
Iran army says prepared to face any scenario
TEHRAN– Iran’s Armed Forces are closely monitoring developments and remain fully prepared to respond to any scenario, the spokesperson for the Islamic Republic of Iran Army said on Saturday, as he referred to repeated threats by the country’s adversaries.
Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia made the remarks during a visit to the Army’s 65th Airborne Special Forces Brigade, a unit widely recognized for its specialized capabilities and role in missions requiring a high degree of operational readiness.
Highlighting the brigade’s position within Iran’s defense structure, Akraminia said its personnel, combining commitment, specialized training and operational capabilities, have turned the unit into an important asset for both the Army and the country.
He stressed that the missions assigned to the 65th Brigade extend beyond conventional tactical operations, arguing that the unit’s activities can produce consequences at the strategic level and affect Iran’s national security interests as well as the wider regional and international environment.
Against the backdrop of continued tensions and threats, the Army spokesperson said Iran’s military capabilities have been undergoing continuous development and that the Armed Forces are prepared to confront whatever circumstances may arise.
Akrami-Nia also addressed the calculations of the United States and Israel in the conflict with Iran, saying the resilience of the Iranian Armed Forces, coupled with the steadfastness of the Iranian people, had disrupted the adversaries’ calculations.
According to the Army spokesperson, the United States and Israel had initially anticipated that Iran’s defensive capabilities could be dismantled and their objectives achieved within a matter of days. He said those calculations did not materialize.
Akraminia further argued that the objectives pursued by Iran’s adversaries went beyond the country’s nuclear and missile programs or their confrontation with the Resistance Front. He said the broader objective was to undermine the Islamic Republic and fragment Iran as a country, but that none of those objectives had been achieved.
The remarks come as Iranian military officials have repeatedly emphasized the importance of maintaining a high level of readiness amid continuing regional tensions and threats of renewed confrontation. Iranian authorities have also stressed that the country’s defense posture is based on deterrence and the ability to respond to threats against its territorial integrity and national security.
The Army spokesperson attributed the Armed Forces’ ability to withstand the pressure to their faith, motivation and spirit of resistance. He also pointed to the role of public solidarity in sustaining the morale of military personnel.
Akraminia said the nightly presence of people in public squares during the conflict was not merely a manifestation of national unity and cohesion, but also had a direct psychological effect on servicemen stationed on the frontlines, strengthening their morale and determination.
His comments underscored the Iranian military’s continued emphasis on preparedness, national cohesion and the integration of specialized military capabilities into the country’s broader defense posture.

articles.title: Russian tank shoots down attacking drones in war games
articles.body:
- A Russian T-90M used its Arena-M active protection system to shoot down FPV and fixed-wing drones in a staged column attack at Tsentr-2026.
- Ukrainian troops have reported Arena-M intercepting drones in combat, but its known configuration carries only 12 interceptor munitions.
A Russian T-90M tank used its Arena-M active protection system to shoot down attacking drones during the Tsentr-2026 strategic exercise, in a staged attack on a tank column at the Chebarkul training range in Russia’s Chelyabinsk region.
In the demonstration, several types of drones, including fixed-wing models and standard first-person-view (FPV) quadcopter drones, simulated a strike on a column of tanks. The T-90M’s onboard system detected and destroyed the incoming drones. The test took place under controlled exercise conditions, and Russia did not say how many drones were launched, how many were intercepted, or whether any got through.
Arena-M is a hard-kill system, meaning it physically destroys threats instead of jamming them. A radar on the tank watches for incoming projectiles, calculates their path and fires a small defensive munition that breaks up the threat with a spray of fragments before it hits the armor. The system was built by the KBM design bureau in Kolomna to stop anti-tank rockets and guided missiles, which fly much faster than drones. The baseline version can intercept projectiles traveling up to 1,000 meters per second.
Small drones are harder for that kind of radar to track. They move slowly, reflect little radar energy and often dive onto the tank from above, where older systems did not look. KBM has worked to close that gap. In 2025, Russia said Arena-M received a software update with a dedicated mode for intercepting drones, and in early 2026 a new variant designed to counter one-way attack drones and loitering munitions completed development.
The system has already been used in combat in Ukraine, where T-72B3A and T-90M tanks fitted with Arena-M have been seen on the front line, Meta-Defense reported. Ukrainian troops have acknowledged that it works. One Ukrainian unit reported that Arena-M on a single Russian T-72B3A tank destroyed seven FPV drones, and that it took 15 to 20 drones to knock out a tank fitted with the system along with cage armor.
That points to the system’s main weakness. Arena-M’s known configuration carries 12 interceptor munitions. Once they are used up, the tank has to rely on its armor, anti-drone cages and electronic warfare, and FPV drones are cheap enough for Ukrainian units to launch in large numbers against a single target.
Arena-M has been fitted to some T-90M, T-72B3 and T-80BVM tanks. Uralvagonzavod first showed a T-90M with the system in February 2025, and photos of production T-90Ms with Arena-M being transported on public roads appeared in July 2026. But a batch of new T-90M and T-72B3M tanks shown leaving the factory in September did not carry the system, suggesting it is not yet standard on every new tank.
Tsentr-2026 ran from Sept. 28 to Oct. 3 and involved more than 47,000 troops, according to the Russian Defense Ministry. President Vladimir Putin visited the Chebarkul range on Oct. 1.

articles.title: US claims it ‘kicked out’ Iranian diplomats
articles.body:
US claims it ‘kicked out’ Iranian diplomats
The US has expelled two more members of the Iranian delegation that attended the UN General Assembly in New York after they allegedly ignored an order to leave the country, AFP and Axios reported on Saturday, citing a State Department official.
US and Iranian negotiators separately met with mediators last month without reaching a breakthrough, leaving the Middle East bracing for a potential resumption of hostilities. American media reported that after the sides failed to reach an agreement on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio ordered Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and other diplomats to leave the country earlier than planned.
“Two more members of the Iranian delegation were found still in [New York] long after the United Nations General Assembly had passed. They have now been kicked out of the US,” a US official told AFP, adding that Rubio “means business.”
According to Axios, one diplomat left on Friday night and the other on Saturday morning.
The Iranian mission to the UN had previously disputed Washington’s account of the delegation’s departure, saying its members had left in accordance with a schedule communicated to the US before the General Assembly session.
“Having achieved nothing, the State Department has resorted to propagating baseless and worthless news,” the mission wrote on X on Thursday.
US President Donald Trump has resumed threats to “annihilate” Iran’s leadership in recent weeks, hinting that he could order new strikes unless Tehran accepts his peace terms.
Iranian officials and the military have said they are prepared for further escalation.
“After one failure after another, the worst president in American history just keeps talking – and talking – and now his words have even outrun his own fantasies. You can win every day in your own imagination. But reality is shaped by Iran – by its people, its soldiers, and its missiles,” Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, wrote on X on Friday.
The standoff comes as Washington reinforces its military presence in the Middle East. The USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and USS Makin Island amphibious ready group are heading to the region, adding roughly 9,000 to 10,000 sailors and Marines.
The USS George Washington and USS George H.W. Bush are already operating there. If both remain when the Theodore Roosevelt arrives, the US could have three aircraft carriers in the Middle East by late October.
Some US officials reportedly believe Trump could resume major combat operations after the midterm elections in early November. The war remains unpopular among Americans, with 71% of registered voters saying the Trump administration lacks a clear strategy for ending the conflict, according to a recent Fox News poll.

articles.title: The G7 Is Releasing Emergency Fuel Reserves. How Much Will It Help Americans?
articles.body:
The Group of Seven (G7) countries said Friday that the nations would release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products in the coming months, starting with “substantial” amounts of diesel. The move comes amid a global shortage largely attributed to slowdowns of the passage of oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
A joint statement from the G7 nations—Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the U.S.—confirmed that the International Energy Agency (IEA) will coordinate the release over the next four months.
It calls the move a part of “decisive, coordinated measures to stabilize immediate energy supplies” amid record-high fuel prices driven by the war in Iran and the recent escalation of fighting between Russia and Ukraine.
Read More: Once Again, Energy Is Power
“Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil,” President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social on Friday. “The process will begin immediately.”
In talks leading up to the announcement on Friday, Trump had been pushing European partners for the release, citing high fuel prices for Americans. Last month, the Trump Administration threatened to temporarily suspend its exports of diesel—earning immediate backlash from countries that rely on it, including Canada, Mexico, and much of Europe.
European leaders and oil executives at the time said that such a ban would be disastrous for long-term oil flow. For that reason, experts believe the threat helped pressure those nations to release their fuel reserves.
The agreement could offer some relief for Americans even if the released diesel stays in Europe, because Europe buys some of its diesel from the U.S. Releasing European reserves could ease competition for U.S. diesel and potentially reduce prices for American buyers.
This is especially critical as the cost of Brent crude oil sits at $102 per barrel as of Oct. 3 and on-highway diesel hit a high of $6.529 per gallon as of last month, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
But how much relief consumers will actually see—and how quickly—will depend on what type of fuel is released, how much reaches the market and when, and whether supply disruptions persist.
What is actually being added to the market?
Although the G7 shared how much fuel it would release, it did not specify the full breakdown of the release by fuel type. Its statement did say, however, that there will be a “frontloaded” and substantial release of diesel fuel within the first 20 days.
While crude oil must be refined into products like gasoline before consumers can use it, diesel is already a finished fuel. That means a diesel release could address the immediate shortage more directly.
The planned release could help ease shortages of both crude oil and refined fuels, with supplies disrupted by the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
The supply of crude oil has been heavily disrupted this year after the U.S. and Israel launched joint strikes that ignited a war with Iran in February. In response, Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in March. More recent negotiations to end the war have largely failed to address differing opinions on ownership and control over the Strait. This has critically restricted the passage of oil-carrying vessels through the waterway, with daily shipping traffic in the single digits last month, down from pre-war averages of roughly 138 to 140 daily transits.
Diesel, meanwhile, is essential to U.S. transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing: Most goods, food, and manufacturing supplies across the country are transported by heavy-duty trucks and trains running on diesel engines. The war in Iran has driven diesel prices up and lowered supply, but Russia and Ukraine’s targeting of one another’s energy infrastructure has further exacerbated the issue.
While the U.S. in particular does not heavily rely on Russian diesel, America is vulnerable to the volatility caused by Russia removing it from the global market. Trump has claimed outright that Ukraine’s targeting of Russian oil infrastructure is to blame for diesel shortages.
What could Americans feel, and when?
Jason Bordoff, founding director of the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University, says it’s difficult to predict the consumer impact given the scarce details shared so far.
“It makes a big difference if the release is in the next two weeks or if it's four months from now,” Bordoff says.
“I think if we saw some announcement tomorrow from Germany or France that gave concrete, specific numbers for a substantial amount—50 million barrels or so—of diesel, then it could have a real impact if this release actually happens in a timely fashion,” Bordoff says.
At the same time, Jeff Colgan, a professor of political science at Brown University, cautions that American consumers may see limited benefits.
“Releasing diesel could make a difference on price, especially in tight markets in Europe,” Colgan says. “But American consumers are unlikely to see much of a price drop from this policy move unless the diesel share of that 100 million barrels is very large.”
With a timely release of diesel, Bordoff predicts that Americans could see a drop by as much as 25 cents per gallon after a few weeks—but, he adds, the markets seem pretty unsure that that will actually happen.
And market perception is central to whether or not prices drop in the short term.
“I think they’re saying: Show me the barrels, so I have confidence this is real, and it's going to happen quickly,” he says.
David Bieri, an economist and associate professor of urban affairs and planning at Virginia Tech, tells TIME that international interventions like this help “signal” to markets that governments are a credible safety net in prolonged periods of uncertainty.
“That's the main mechanism, because they want to influence market sentiment,” Bieri says. “Then, futures markets begin to price more optimistically, and then eventually the hope is that prices will come down.”
The effect Bieri is describing has already begun: The price of diesel futures in the United States fell 8% on Friday morning, a sign of more optimism in the market.
Bordoff adds that they are also, in part, a response to Trump dropping his threat of a diesel export ban—a threat that was lifted as a condition of the G7 agreement.
The release itself may not impact the markets “an awful lot,” Bieri says, given the broader context of the war with Iran.
“In fact, consumers might not necessarily notice it, ever. That's how insignificant the quantity itself is,” he says of the 100 million barrels. “But it's the importance of the cooperative signal that hopefully will make things better this fall.”
Bieri also cautions that any savings could take time to reach consumers, as carriers and other distributors may use lower fuel costs to rebuild their margins.
“[They] have been bleeding on increased fuel costs,” he says. “This is going to be, if anything, a welcome reprieve for their profit margins, and they're not going to pass that on immediately to consumers.”
What happens if the supply gap is still there when releases taper off?
This October announcement is not the first of its kind: Following the initial market shock of the war in Iran, IEA member countries announced a 400-million-barrel release in March—80% of which has already been released. Notably, the latest announcement did not clearly establish how much of the forthcoming release would be additional to earlier commitments.
In March, the IEA said that the majority of the barrel release would be crude oil; however, reports show that Europe has primarily contributed refined oil, like diesel—which could suggest more of the same in this latest round.
In either event, such fuel releases are just a matter of sticking a bandage over the larger issue of two unresolved wars and continued global energy disruption, says Bordoff.
“We're going to continue to have oil, gasoline, and diesel price shocks until that conflict comes to some sort of resolution, and energy flows can get going again,” he says. “Inventories, and stocks and other schemes like waiving state fuel taxes or something can help on the margin for temporary disruptions, but at some point this isn't temporary anymore.”
Michael Noel, economist at Texas Tech University, agrees with Bordoff, telling TIME that “unless something dramatic happens to end the Ukraine and Iran conflicts, the supply shortage will persist.”
Negotiations between Iranian leadership and the Trump Administration have stalled multiple times in the last six months. Trump said on Sept. 9 that he expected a resolution to come after the midterm elections, which take place in the U.S. on Nov. 3.
“I think the war's going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer,” he said last month. “Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward.”
Axios reported, however, that senior Trump Administration officials met at Camp David to discuss the war on Friday. The talks come as the U.S. last week added economic pressure in the region with a series of sanctions aiming to curtail funding streams and stymy industrial lifelines for Iran.
Experts argue that the fuel crisis and volatility exposes the need for the U.S. to adapt to a changing energy ecosystem. Notably, Colgan says that would include “the national security advantages of clean technologies like EVs, batteries, and renewable energy.”

articles.title: Israeli forces attempt to assassinate Hamas' 'new Gaza leader'
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israeli forces attempt assassination of senior Hamas leader in Gaza
Israeli forces have attempted to assassinate a senior Hamas leader Ali al-Amoudi in Gaza, Israeli media reported on Saturday.
The attacks took place on Friday evening, when Israeli airstrikes killed five Palestinians, including four women and a child, though al-Amoudi's fate remains unclear.
Hamas has not issued a statement acknowledging an attempted assassination.
After Hamas' Gaza leader Khalil al-Hayya was elected to succeed slain leader Yahya Sinwar in August 2026, al-Amoudi was considered the most likely candidate to take over as the group's chief in Gaza, a source close to Hamas told The New Arab in August.
The source noted that al-Hayya remains the official head of Hamas in Gaza, while al-Amoudi serves as his deputy. Israeli media reports on Friday alleged that al-Amoudi is in charge of the the group in Gaza.
Al-Amoudi has remained relatively out of the spotlight for years, though is considered to have been close to slain Hamas leader Sinwar. He was released from Israeli detention as part of the 2011 prisoner swap involving captured Israeli soldier Gilad Shalit, and later progressed to higher positions within the movement.
He was also among the key figures within Hamas who pushed within the group for acceptance of UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process Nikolay Mladenov's roadmap for Gaza in late July.
The assassination attempt comes as Israel continues its attacks on Gaza, despite a ceasefire agreement that came into force last October. Israeli forces have killed more than 1,400 Palestinians in Gaza since the truce deal, and has increased its area of military control in the enclave.

articles.title: North Korea launches ballistic missile over 700 kilometers as hostilities heat up
articles.body:
North Korea fired a ballistic missile toward the sea off its east coast on Saturday, South Korea and Japan said, its latest missile launch this year, which came a day after it rejected Seoul's accusation that its mines wounded soldiers.
The missile was launched from the Wonsan area at around 6:30 a.m. on Saturday and flew more than 700 kilometers (434 miles), the South Korean military said in a statement. Seoul and Washington were analyzing the test for details, it added.
Japan's coast guard, in an emailed statement citing the Japanese defense ministry, said the object may have been a ballistic missile and appeared to have come down, warning ships to take precautions.
South Korea's military said it has raised its monitoring of any further missile tests and will share intelligence with the US and Japan.
The South Korean presidential office's national security council convened an emergency meeting on Saturday to assess the situation after the missile launch, the office said in a statement.
North Korea tested missiles at least 10 times this year, ramps up hostility
North Korea has launched missile tests on more than 10 occasions so far this year. Pyongyang has sometimes said it was testing new types of weapons systems. Some of the tests have come after North Korea protested joint military drills between Seoul and Washington.
The launch came after Pyongyang's Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of leader Kim Jong Un, issued a statement on Friday that dismissed Seoul's demand for an apology for what it said were North Korean mines that seriously wounded South Korean soldiers in the Demilitarised Zone, a heavily fortified area between the two Koreas.
South Korea said this week that North Korean mines caused the blast that seriously injured two South Korean soldiers on a reconnaissance mission inside the 4-km-wide (2.5-mile) border that stretches across the Korean Peninsula.
The missile test may be an attempt by Pyongyang to draw a response from South Korea to the sister's statement, said Cheong Seong-chang, vice president at the Sejong Institute in Seoul, a research center on North Korean affairs. North Korea may also have tested a new type of missile, he added.
North Korea has sharply ramped up hostility against the South in recent years, disavowing unification as a national goal and calling South Korea its "primary foe."

articles.title: Trump says Iran has 'virtually given up' any plans for nuclear weapons
articles.body:
Ahmet Salih Alacaci
04 October 2026•Update: 04 October 2026
US President Donald Trump suggested on Saturday that Iran has “virtually given up” any plans to develop nuclear weapons, one of his administration’s most frequently stated objectives in the war with Tehran, now in its eighth month.
Trump also claimed oil prices were currently decreasing, long elevated after Israel and the US launched strikes against Iran on Feb. 28.
“Oil is coming down. Oil is right now lower, and it's been lower than it was under the Biden administration, and they did nothing about the fact that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon,” Trump told reporters as he departed the White House to attend a rally in the state of Ohio.
“By the way, Iran, as you know, has virtually given up any plans of a nuclear weapon,” he added.
Iran has long denied accusations by the US and Israel that it seeks to develop nuclear weapons, a position reiterated by President Masoud Pezeshkian during his visit last month to New York for the UN General Assembly.
Pezeshkian said Tehran is not seeking nuclear weapons because of a religious prohibition, and offered to dilute its enriched uranium stockpiles under international verification.
Iran, however, has maintained that it will not compromise on its peaceful civilian nuclear program or make structural concessions unless the US lifts economic sanctions.

articles.title: Russia rebukes US, defends Iran’s ‘inalienable’ nuclear rights
articles.body:
Russia rebukes US, defends Iran’s ‘inalienable’ nuclear rights
TEHRAN – Russia has strongly rebuked the United States over its calls for Tehran to abandon its peaceful nuclear program, reaffirming that the Islamic Republic possesses an inalienable right to pursue peaceful nuclear energy under international law.
In a post on X on Friday, Mikhail Ulyanov, Russia’s permanent representative to Vienna-based international organizations, slammed Washington for relying on “wrong assumptions” regarding non-proliferation norms and the mandate of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).
“Iran is not obliged to abandon its nuclear program. It is Iran’s inalienable right,” Ulyanov emphasized. “Unfortunately, the position of the Republican administration is based on wrong assumptions of non-proliferation norms and the IAEA activities.”
The Russian diplomat made the remarks in response to US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz, who claimed Tehran had “broken the rules” by enriching uranium to 60 percent.
Iran has maintained a firm, principled stance regarding its peaceful atomic activities, particularly in the aftermath of the unprovoked US-Israeli military aggressions in June 2025 and February 2026. In both instances, the aggressors struck civilian and nuclear infrastructure in flagrant violation of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) and the UN Charter.
Following the initial aggression, which occurred amid indirect diplomatic engagements, the Iranian Parliament unanimously passed legislation in June 2025 suspending all cooperation with the IAEA. The decisive move came after the agency adopted a politically motivated resolution that set the stage for foreign strikes, followed by the UN nuclear watchdog’s refusal to condemn the illegal attacks on Iranian facilities.
Under the law, IAEA inspectors will not be permitted to resume monitoring unless verifiable security guarantees are established, subject to the approval of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC). Senior Iranian officials, including Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, have repeatedly stressed that neither Tehran’s legitimate nuclear rights nor its conventional deterrent capabilities are up for negotiation.
China also rallied behind Tehran. Addressing a recent UN General Assembly session, China’s deputy permanent representative to the UN, Sun Lei, reiterated that “Iran’s legitimate right to the peaceful use of nuclear energy should be respected.”
Sun held Washington responsible for the current crisis, pointing to its unilateral withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear deal (JCPOA), brutal “maximum pressure” campaigns, and military escalations during ongoing diplomacy.

articles.title: Pontoon crossings coming to Kyiv following Russian strikes on key bridges, media reports
articles.body:
Pontoon crossings coming to Kyiv following Russian strikes on key bridges, media reports
Following Russian attacks on vital bridges in central Kyiv, the capital plans to construct pontoon crossings across the Dnipro River, Ukrainian media reported on Oct. 3.
"Urgent solutions are a dam and a pontoon crossing, which are being built quickly," Ukraine's Reconstruction, Infrastructure, and Transport Minister, Mykola Kalashnyk, told Suspilny news about responding to the bridge attacks. "This work has already begun. A corresponding coordination meeting was held with the president."
From Oct. 1 to Oct. 3, Kyiv's Southern and Northern bridges over the Dnipro River were targeted in multiple Russian drone strikes amid Moscow's unrelenting attacks on the civilian infrastructure across Ukraine. This week alone, the capital had 56 air raid sirens, lasting over 87 hours in total, emergency services said on Oct. 2.
Kalashnyk said that the construction of pontoon crossings could take up to three months and would help traffic move through the capital, which remains heavily restricted after the bridge attacks.
The Kyiv City Military Administration (KMDA) announced new restrictions on movements over Kyiv's bridges during air raid alerts on Oct. 3.
"On average, about 600,000 cars cross the left and right banks [of the Dnipro] during the day and the task is to maintain this throughput," Kalashnyk said. "Therefore, the locations where construction will begin have been determined accordingly."
Kalashnyk also revealed that plans for constructing underground tunnels beneath the Dnipro were being considered, though construction could "cost tens of billions of hryvnias."
Before constructing alternative crossings, Kalashnyk said that protecting the capital's existing bridges should remain the priority.
"Our first task is to provide protection from the sky, which we are doing in coordination with the military," Kalashnyk said. "The first step is to prevent strikes. The second part is to provide protection. The third is rapid recovery. And the fourth is to make decisions regarding alternative reserve crossings, i.e., the construction of new alternative bridge infrastructure facilities."
To counter Russia's growing use of jet-powered attack drones, Ukraine will be able to produce up to 400 interceptor drones by the end of October, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with the Financial Times published on Oct. 2.

articles.title: U.S.-Russia talks on Ukraine have expanded to a multibillion-dollar oil deal — media
articles.body:
U.S.-Russia talks on Ukraine have expanded to a multibillion-dollar oil deal — media
Kyiv • UNN
The United States and Russia are discussing the possible sale of Lukoil’s international assets worth billions of dollars as part of negotiations to end the war. No final decision has been made, and the transfer of the assets would require OFAC approval.
Talks between the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump and Russia on ending the war against Ukraine have expanded and now include a possible multibillion-dollar deal to sell the international assets of Russia’s "Lukoil." UNN reports this, citing The New York Times and Reuters.
According to reports, the issue of the deal was raised personally by Kremlin head Vladimir Putin during a meeting at the Kremlin with U.S. presidential envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Details
According to the NYT, the matter concerns Lukoil’s large portfolio of assets outside Russia, including oil fields, refineries, and networks of gas stations in various countries. The deal would require approval from both the U.S. government and the Russian side. Those reportedly interested in the assets include a group led by American billionaire and investor Todd Boehly. It also includes two Middle Eastern business groups that previously had business ties with Kushner or the Witkoff family, as well as a U.S. government entity.
According to the publication, Putin discussed the possible deal on September 5 during a meeting with Witkoff and Kushner at the Kremlin. One of the NYT’s sources said that the Kremlin chief proposed completing the sale of the assets as a demonstration that Russians could once again conduct major business with the United States.
Reuters, for its part, notes that at the time of publication, the White House, the U.S. Treasury Department, and Lukoil had not responded to requests for comment. There is also currently no final decision on the sale of the assets.
Context
Lukoil was placed under U.S. sanctions in October 2025. At the time, the U.S. Treasury Department said the restrictions were intended to increase pressure on Russia’s energy sector and reduce the revenues Moscow could use to finance the war against Ukraine.
At present, the U.S. Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control allows negotiations on the sale of Lukoil International GmbH to be conducted and conditional agreements to be concluded until October 22, 2026. At the same time, this license does not allow the assets to be actually transferred to the buyer: a separate OFAC authorization is required to complete the deal. The U.S. side’s conditions also include a complete severing of the acquired assets’ ties with Lukoil and the blocking of funds that are to be paid to the Russian company until the possible lifting of the sanctions.
It should also be noted that in late September, Russian special envoy Kirill Dmitriev also held talks in Washington with U.S. officials regarding the war against Ukraine and possible energy projects between the United States and Russia after the end of hostilities.
Recall
In late September, Kirill Dmitriev, a representative of Russian dictator Vladimir Putin, held talks with U.S. officials on ending the war in Ukraine, including possible joint energy initiatives between the United States and Russia in the postwar period.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine has refuted reports alleging that Western nations are preparing contingency plans to evacuate or relocate foreign embassies from Kyiv to western Ukraine or Poland, MFA spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi confirmed.
Responding to media inquiries, Tykhyi stated that foreign diplomatic missions have not communicated any intentions to transfer operations away from the capital, reiterating that established international protocols govern any prospective relocation of diplomatic staff.

“If any diplomatic missions intend to move, they inform us in advance as prescribed by standard procedures,” Tykhyi said, as reported by the Center for Countering Disinformation. “As of Friday evening, no such appeals or notices have been received from the foreign diplomatic corps.”
The ministry’s clarification followed a report published by The Guardian citing anonymous senior Western diplomats who indicated that contingency blueprints were being drafted to relocate embassy staff to the western city of Lviv or eastern Poland if Russia begins deliberately targeting foreign diplomatic facilities in the capital.

However, one senior Western diplomat cautioned that “the situation is obviously deteriorating fast,” alleging that Moscow seeks “to freeze Kyiv out, to throw it back into the stone age” through concentrated bombardments ahead of winter.

The diplomatic discussions surface amid an escalating Russian aerial campaign targeting transit bottlenecks, energy networks, and municipal utilities across the Ukrainian capital.
On Friday, Oct. 2, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko warned that maintaining municipal functions under Russian missile and drone attacks has become an urgent matter of “safety and survival,” speaking after a convened session of Kyiv’s Defense Council.
“The capital is in a very dramatic situation. We can no longer pretend that we can live as we would in peacetime,” Klitschko stated, emphasizing that municipal authorities and emergency responders are coordinating measures to preserve life-support systems under continuous strikes.
Travel advisories
Despite elevated operational strains and repeated air raid alerts across the capital, Western governments have maintained regular diplomatic operations in Kyiv.
In an updated travel advisory issued on Aug. 28, the US Department of State maintained its Level 4: “Do Not Travel” advisory for Ukraine due to active hostilities and recurring Russian missile and drone bombardments across non-frontline regions.
However, the State Department explicitly confirmed that the US Embassy in Kyiv remains open, staffed, and fully operational.

EU Pours €130 Million Into Border Surveillance Drones
The European Commission is adding €130 million ($146 million) to an EU scheme that helps member states buy drones and counter-drone systems, as part of a broader push to strengthen border oversight.
The announcement brings total European Union investments in border surveillance tech past €500 million ($563 million), as reported by Euronews.

The funding allocation was introduced during a meeting of justice and home affairs ministers in Luxembourg, marking their first face-to-face talks on border management and migration since the crisis in Ceuta earlier this summer.
EU Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration Magnus Brunner emphasized that deploying emerging technologies like drones is vital for both securing external boundaries and safeguarding critical infrastructure.
Back in February, the Commission rolled out an action plan addressing drone-related security and counter-drone mechanisms, offering national governments €250 million ($281 million) in funding for monitoring land and sea borders, according to Euronews.
That initiative covers up to 90% of costs for projects including drone purchases, anti-drone installations, system integration into national networks, and tools designed to mitigate hybrid threats.
Brussels separately directed €170 million ($191 million) to the EU border agency Frontex and national agencies through the Border Management and Visa Instrument to buy unmanned monitoring gear.
At the same time, Greece suggested temporary suspensions on the right to apply for asylum during emergencies caused by mass irregular migrant arrivals. The proposal holds backing from member states including Poland, Germany, Austria, and Denmark.
Brussels is also expected to widen the scope of Frontex, particularly in handling crisis responses and monitoring digital hybrid threats, with a mandate review planned for later this year. European leaders will further address migration policy and border governance during the European Council summit set for October 15–16, Euronews reported.
Germany had recently partnered with Kyiv to tap into Ukrainian expertise on Russian hybrid warfare.
Under a new security agreement, Ukrainian specialists will share operational experience in counter-drone defense, counterespionage, and cybercrime, with German police set to train at specialized counter-drone facilities inside Ukraine.

articles.title: Russian Armed Forces use laser systems to counter Ukrainian jet-powered UAVs — expert
articles.body:
LUGANSK, October 3. /TASS/. The Russian Armed Forces have begun deploying laser systems to counter Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), while interceptor drones and electronic warfare systems are also being used against them, military expert Andrey Marochko said during a live broadcast on his VKontakte social media page.
"In addition to mobile fire groups, advanced electronic warfare systems are being deployed, along with laser systems - albeit in limited numbers - designed specifically to target jet-powered drones. We also have interceptor drones capable of bringing down Ukrainian UAVs. There are drones that hunt other UAVs of the same class, including fixed-wing drones designed to intercept Ukrainian drones," the expert said.
Marochko also claimed that the Russian Armed Forces have surpassed the Ukrainian military in both the number of long-range UAVs launched and the effectiveness of their strikes.
